56_marg11: The beginning of the gospel, etc. Jerome. A gospel is a good announcement, which properly pertains to the kingdom of God and to the forgiveness of sins; whence: “Do penance, and believe the gospel, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
56_marg12: The four gospels are one, and one is four. So the book of Mark too is called a gospel, and likewise those of the others, because all are one and one is all.
56_marg13: Jerome. Jesus: in Hebrew, soter; in Greek, saviour; in Latin, salvator.
56_marg14: Christ: in Greek; Messias: in Hebrew; anointed: in Latin; that is, he is called king and priest, of the stock of King David and of the Levitical line.
56_marg15: Of the Son of God, etc. Bede. Matthew says, “Son of David, son of Abraham,” Mark says, “Son of God,” so that we may rise gradually from lesser things to greater. And Matthew, who writes the human generation, fittingly called him Son of man. But Mark, who begins his book from the start of evangelical preaching, fittingly calls him “Son of God.” For the gospel belongs to God alone. Here it is to be noted that the evangelists wrote with one Spirit, but each set for himself a different beginning and end of writing. Matthew begins at the nativity and ends at the resurrection. Mark reaches from the beginning of Christ’s preaching to the ascension and the preaching of the disciples. Luke from the birth of John to the ascension of the Lord, when the disciples in Jerusalem await the coming of the Holy Ghost. John begins from the eternity of the Word of God and completes at the resurrection of the Lord.
56_marg16: As it is written, etc. Mark sets before his account the testimonies of the prophets, by which he asserts that these things are old and not new, but foreknown and foretold by the prophets. In this he invites the Jews, who had received the law and the prophets, to the gospel, and calls the Gentiles, who held the gospel, to reverence for the law and the prophets; so that no one, like the heretics, should receive one without the other.
56_interl39: The Spirit to the Father about the Son, through Malachias; or the voice of the Father to the Son about John.
56_marg17: John is called ‘angel’ not by community of nature, as Origen falsely claims, but by dignity of office; just as priests too, of whom it is said: “For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”
56_marg18: Note that this testimony, “Behold I send my angel,” etc., belongs to Malachias in both respects; yet he says it is Isaias’, because, though the words are not the same, the sense is found in Isaias, and more plainly in this verse: “A voice of one crying in the desert.” For the angel who is sent before the face of the Lord is “a voice of one crying in the desert.” He prepares the way, saying: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord,” etc. Yet the name of Isaias could have come to mind divinely in place of Malachias’, and Mark did not wish to correct it, because all the prophets spoke with one Spirit, as with one mouth.
56_interl41: angel: a messenger who announces about Christ: “He that shall come after me is preferred before me, because he was before me.”
56_interl42: before the Son, or before his presence or incarnation
56_interl43: John, of whom the Lord says to the Jews: “There hath not risen among them that are born of women a greater than John,” etc.
56_interl45: to the deaf who stop their ears to the voice
56_marg19: Isidore. To the Jews, who are deaf and placed far away on account of their sins, worthy of the outcry of indignation.
56_marg20: Isidore. In the desert the voice and cry is made, because the house of Judea is a desert, deserted, empty, swept, without the Spirit of God, without prophet, king, or priest. Whence Jesus and John seek what was lost in the desert. Where the devil conquered, there he is conquered; where man fell, there he rises again.
56_marg21: Isidore. Do penance and preach. Whence he speaks of the Parasceve before the sabbath, that is, penance before rest. Hence also the beginning of the preaching of John and of Christ: “Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand,” because on the seventh day God rested from all his works. For it is necessary for us to blot out the seven vices, as the seven nations, through penance, so that we may possess in rest the desirable land.
56_marg22: Jerome. The way of the Lord by which he enters among men is penance, through which God comes down to us and we go up to him. Whence: “Angels ascending and descending are mentioned upon the Son of man.”
56_marg23: Isidore. He commands that, walking the royal way, we love our neighbours as ourselves, and ourselves as our neighbours. He who loves himself and not his neighbour declines to the right; he who loves his neighbour and not himself, to the left. Many do good and do not correct, like Eli. Others correct but do not do good, like the scribes and Pharisees who sat on the chair of Moses. Hence the mouth of the turtledove is commanded in the law to be turned back to the armpits, so that the mouth is not separated from the work, nor the work from the mouth.
56_interl47: which you have bent crooked by turning aside to the right or to the left
56_marg24: The paths after the way: because the moral commandments are explained after penance, according to Mark or Matthew; the way is prepared by faith, baptism and penance. The paths are rightly marked by the austere signs of clothing, belt, food, drink and the most humble voice. Whence: John was, etc.
56_marg25: Isidore. ‘The grace of God.’ He begins from the grace of God. Whence there follows: baptizing: sins are forgiven through baptism; whence: “Freely you have received, freely give”; and the Apostle: “By grace you are saved.”
56_marg26: So that by his own baptism, by which sins could not be loosed, he would go before the baptism of penance, by which sins are loosed.
56_marg27: Baptizing, etc. The baptism of penance. He gave baptism unto remission of sins. Yet he preached it, but did not give it. As by his preaching he went before the preaching of Christ, so by the baptism of penance he went before the baptism of remission.
56_marg28: What is completed by the bridegroom is begun by the groomsman. Whence catechumens, that is, the instructed, begin through the priest, and are anointed with chrism through the bishop. Now the bride is brought in by the friend of the bridegroom, as Rebecca was brought to Isaac by a servant, veiled in a white mantle.
56_marg29: Jerome. Jordan: a foreign descent, where sins are absolved. For the ark passed through it into a foreign land, and with the middle part in the flowing sea, the other part is raised up in the form of a mountain. So we, once estranged from God, are humbled by baptism and raised up to heights. Because ‘he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.’ The part that flows into the sea is made bitter, because the ark of God, that is, the body of Christ, does not profit those not cleansed, but changes them for the worse.
56_marg30: Jerome. “Praise and beauty are before him,” that is, of the bridegroom. Whence the bride dismounts from the camel, when the Church humbles herself to Christ, who was prefigured by Isaac, at whose birth God made Sara laugh. As it is said to Mary, who is first with God: “Blessed art thou among women.”
56_marg31: Those who confess their sins are baptized. For those who desire to receive baptism ought to promise the newness of a better life. Whence, when Paul preached, it is said: “And many of them that believed came confessing and declaring their deeds.” And to Peter it is said: “Kill and eat”; as if to say: kill the evils that were in them, and so, cleansed and promising the Christian religion, change them into members of the Church.
56_interl50: deservedly they went out and were baptized by John, because John was clothed, etc.
56_interl51: a garment fitting for a preacher
56_marg32: Jerome. The prophet’s clothing, food and drink signify the whole austere life of preachers, and that the Gentiles are to be joined, within and without, to the grace of God, which is John. Camel’s hair: the rich of the Gentiles. Leather belt: the poor, dead to the world. Locusts: the wise of this world, who, leaving the dry stubble to the Jews, draw up mystical grain, and in the heat of faith dwell in the woods. The faithful, prepared out of the uncultivated forest, are compared to wild honey, because all things come from the grace of the gospel of God, in which there is no distinction of the Jew and the Greek.
56_marg33: Morally. Clothed in camel’s hair, etc., because he did not cherish sins, but sharply rebuked them, saying: “O generation of vipers,” etc. A leather belt about his loins, because “they that are Christ’s have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences,” etc. He ate locusts and wild honey, because his preaching was so sweet that he was even thought to be Christ. But this opinion soon fell away, because it became known that he was not Christ but Christ’s forerunner. For in honey there is sweetness; in the locust, a lively flight, but soon falling away.
56_interl55: It does not befit dwellers in the wilderness to seek delicacies of food, but only to supply necessity.
56_marg34: Jerome. What is stronger than the grace by which sins are washed away? That grace, which forgives sins seven times and up to seventy times seven, is indeed the first; but it forgives sins once through baptism. Mercy, however, reaches the wretched from Adam to Christ through seventy-seven generations, and up to one hundred and forty-four thousand.
56_interl61: which he made for himself out of our mortality
56_marg35: Bede. It was the custom among the ancients that if someone refused to take her who was suited to him as wife, the other, who came to her as bridegroom by right of kinship, would unloose the shoes of the one who refused. But Christ is the bridegroom of the Church, of whom the same John says: “He that hath the bride, is the bridegroom.” Since, therefore, men thought John was Christ, he rightly says he is not worthy to unloose the thong, as if to say: I am not able to unshoe the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not claim for myself the name of bridegroom.
56_marg36: The thong of his sandals: namely, the mystery of the incarnation, by which “the Word was made flesh”; whence the flesh of Christ, whence the soul, whence the spirit takes its beginning, so that he becomes a true man “in all things without sin”; that he is a true God in the true God, without beginning; that is, the Son of man who is in heaven. And how he comes forth “as a bridegroom coming out of his bride chamber,” that is, leaving the virginal womb closed behind him. Whence, when the true bridegroom came, John’s house is called ‘the house of the unshod.’ Whence: “In the form of a dove the Holy Ghost descended.” Of the bride it is said: “My bride”; “my friend, my neighbour”; “my beloved”; “my dove.” The bride in the patriarchs, the friend in the prophets, the neighbour in Mary and Joseph, the beloved in John the Baptist, the dove in Christ and the apostles, to whom it is said: “Be ye therefore wise as serpents,” etc.
56_marg37: The heel: the last part of the body. For at the end, for righteousness, the Saviour was made incarnate. Whence: ‘Into Idumea will I stretch out my shoe,’ because unless the knowledge of the Spirit is joined to it, no one through the grace of forgiveness investigates the mystery of the incarnation.
56_interl62: that is, the mystery of God’s incarnation
56_interl63: because I am a mere man
56_marg38: Bede. John does not yet openly say that God, or the Son of God, is, because his hearers were unlearned; but little by little, through the glorified humanity, he leads them to faith in the divinity, saying: “But he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost.” But afterwards, when he saw they were now more capable, he openly preaches the Son of God, saying: “I gave testimony,” because this is the Son of God.
56_interl66: Bede. Not only on the day of baptism, but daily, as we advance through the grace of the Spirit.
56_marg39: I baptize you with water; he with the Spirit of God, a river always full, always level, of which: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful.” The Spirit who is borne over the waters, not under them, differs greatly from the water, as much as the soul that rules differs from the body that is ruled. But “he remained upon him,” the Spirit, this is the anointing of Christ according to the flesh, of which: “Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” Oil cannot be under water, nor the Creator under the creature. Oil rises from the bitterness of the root into food for light, a remedy for a wound, a refreshment for the hungry. Whence it comes about that the anointing of Christ, from the bitterness of passion, came to the glory of resurrection. Whence the Apostle: “For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus,” etc., as far as: “For which cause God also hath exalted him.”
56_marg40: For three reasons: that he might fulfil justice and humility; that he might approve John’s baptism; and that, sanctifying the waters of the Jordan by the descent of the dove, he might show the Holy Ghost to be present in baptism.
56_interl72: which are opened to the baptized, and were closed to Adam by the interposed cherubim and the flaming sword, which is quenched in the water of baptism.
56_marg41: Mark, “as the hart panteth after the fountains of water,” leaps, gathers the tops of the meadows, carries palms on his head, and like the honey-making bee briefly tastes the flowers of the field (to which the odour of the true Isaac is likened). Whence he relates that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, was received for baptism by John in the Jordan, and at once, coming up from the water, saw the heavens opened, the Spirit descend like a dove and remain in him; that by a voice from heaven the Father was pleased with the beloved Son; and that the Spirit drove him into the desert, where he was tempted by Satan forty days and forty nights, and dwelt with the beasts, the angels ministering. Christ showed this order by deed before voice, which we must follow as we hasten toward angelic fellowship. For we ought, drawn from the fickleness of the swinging world by the odour of pleasure and the cleanness of the flower, to run with the young maidens after the bridegroom; and so through the sacraments of baptism we are absolved by the grace of forgiveness from the two fountains of love of God and of neighbour, and, ascending in hope, we gaze with the clean eyes of the heart upon heavenly secrets. Then, with “a contrite and humbled spirit,” we receive the Holy Ghost, descending with a simple heart to the meek, and remaining with a love that never falls; and the voice of God is addressed to us, his beloved: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.” Then the Father is pleased in us, with the Son and the Holy Ghost, when we become one spirit with God, whence: “That they may be one, as we also are one.” Then the Spirit drives us into the desert, to be tempted by Satan for forty days, so that patience may produce trial, trial hope, and hope love; since, as it is said, “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood; but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness.” Then the beasts will be at peace with us, when in the ark of our soul we tame the clean with the unclean, and lie down with lions like Daniel, since the spirit is not against the flesh, nor the flesh against the spirit. After these things the ministering angels, who “always see the face of my Father who is in heaven,” are sent for consolation, saying: “Thy prayer is heard”; and: “Be not affrighted; you seek Jesus of Nazareth”; and: “Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise,” etc.; and: “To him that overcometh I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.”
56_marg42: Bede. The mystery of the Trinity is shown in the baptism: the Son is baptized, the Spirit is in the dove, the Father sounds in the voice. The heavens are opened not by an unlocking of the elements, but to spiritual eyes. The dove sat upon Jesus, lest it be thought the voice was made to John and not to him. He beautifully added: “and remaining on him”; for this is proper to Christ, that, having once filled him, the Spirit always remains in him. But to the faithful it is sometimes given to work miracles, and sometimes taken away; yet for them, for the work of justice and for keeping the love of God and neighbour, he is never absent. Whence the Spirit will remain with us and be in us according to the measure of faith. Of Christ, however, it is said: “Full of grace and truth.”
56_marg43: And remaining on him, etc. The Spirit remains in him not from the time he was baptized but from the time he was conceived. But that he descended at baptism signifies to us that spiritual grace is given in baptism; to those who are reborn for the forgiveness of sins “of water and the Spirit,” a fuller grace of the Spirit is usually given from heaven through the laying on of the bishop’s hand.
56_marg44: Bede. It is not taught that he did not know, but it is shown to us that we ought to believe that he himself, namely the one who came as a man with the others to be baptized, is the true Son of God; and therefore we too can be baptized in the Spirit, through the water of absolution and the Spirit of sanctification, and be made sons of God: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.” It is fitting that the Spirit descended in the form of a dove, a simple animal and without gall, because it seeks the simple and does not dwell in impure minds.
56_marg45: Bede. Lest there be doubt which spirit, Luke deliberately puts it first: “And Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost, returned from the Jordan.” Then he adds: “and was led by the Spirit into the desert,” lest it be thought that an unclean spirit could have done anything against him.
56_interl76: that we too may flee the allurements of the world.
56_marg46: Bede. It signifies the whole time during which the devil tempts his members. For the world, divided into four parts, serves the Lord by keeping the ten commandments and fighting against the devil. Four times ten makes forty. The adversary is everywhere and always present, and never ceases to hinder our way.
56_interl79: so that we, after baptism, may gird ourselves not only for good deeds to be done but also for evils to be endured.
56_marg47: And he was with beasts, etc. We too, if in the desert of holy living we bear with men’s beastly ways with an undefiled mind, merit the mystery of the angels, by whom, released from the body, we may be carried up to heaven.
56_marg48: Isidore. “We have received grace for grace”; the carnal things are beheaded, the spiritual things are made alive. When the shadow ceases, the truth is present. John in prison, the law in Judea; Jesus in Galilee, salvation among the Gentiles.
56_marg49: Let no one think that John was handed over immediately after the forty days’ temptation and the Lord’s fast. For in John’s gospel it is found that the Lord taught and worked many miracles before: “This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee.” And again: “For John was not yet cast into prison.” It is said that John, having read the other evangelists and found that they had truly written history, but of one year only, the year in which he also suffered after John’s imprisonment, passing over the year whose deeds the three had set out, narrated the deeds of the earlier time, before John was handed over.
56_interl85: which leads to the kingdom of God.
56_marg50: Jerome. “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Poverty follows an earthly kingdom; for the poverty of Christians there is an everlasting kingdom; whence: “My kingdom is not of this world.” For all earthly honour is foam, smoke, sleep.
56_marg51: Concerning this: “But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son,” etc.
56_marg53: Repent. Jerome. The sweetness of the fruit makes up for the bitterness of the root; the hope of harbour delights amid the perils of the sea; the hope of health eases the pain of medicine. Whoever desires the kernel must break the nut. Let him do penance who wishes to cling to the eternal good. Those who have merited to reach the palm of indulgence can proclaim the praises of Christ. Whence preachers are chosen after penance.
56_interl89: Works are not done so that there may be faith, but faith so that works may follow.
56_interl91: Fishermen are sent first to preach, so that the faith of believers may be held to be in the power of God, not in the eloquence or learning of men.
56_marg54: Jerome. Simon ‘obedient,’ Andrew ‘manly,’ James ‘supplanter,’ John ‘grace.’ By these names we are turned into the image of God: obedience, that we may obey; manliness, that we may fight; supplanting, that we may persevere; grace, that we may keep it: “Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.” These are called the four cardinal virtues: through prudence we obey, through justice we act manfully, through temperance we tread down serpents, through fortitude we merit the grace of God.
56_marg55: Whom does worldly eloquence not intoxicate? It is hard for powerful, noble and rich men, and far harder for the eloquent, to believe God. Their minds are blinded by riches and wealth and luxury, and, surrounded by vices, they cannot see the virtues and the simplicity of holy Scripture; they judge it not by the majesty of its meanings but by the lowliness of its words.
56_marg56: Four fishermen are called: Simon, Andrew, James and John: “Leaving all things, they followed him.” By this four-horse chariot we are carried to heaven, as Elias was; by these four corners the first Church is built; by these four Hebrew letters the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, is known to us. By these likewise it is commanded that we hear the Lord calling and forget the people of vices, and the house of our paternal tradition, which is foolishness with God, and the spiders’ web, in which the empty air held us, almost fallen, like gnats. Let us flee the ship of our former way of life. For Adam our father according to the flesh is covered with dead skins; when that is laid aside with its deeds, and we follow the new, we are covered with the skins of Solomon, in which the bride glories that she is beautiful.
56_marg57: It is asked how he called first Peter and Andrew, and after a little, James and John, as Matthew and Mark relate, since Luke says that James and John were partners of Peter in the great catch of fish, and that Jesus said to Peter, “From henceforth thou shalt catch men,” and that they followed him at once, “having brought their ships to land.” But what Luke says happened first, and what was foretold to Peter, that he would catch men, not that from then on he would not fish. For they returned to the catching of fish, and afterwards, as Matthew and Mark relate, they were called two by two: first Peter and Andrew, then the others. For then they followed him not as men anxious to return to ships drawn up on the land, but as men called and commanded.
56_interl95: with the nets of the gospel.
56_interl102: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house.”
56_marg58: “And they entered into Capharnaum,” etc. Jerome. Mark, arranging the sayings of the gospel within himself, did not follow the order of history but kept the order of the mysteries. Whence on the sabbaths he tells of the first mighty work, saying: “And they entered into Capharnaum,” etc.
56_marg59: Jerome. Capharnaum ‘village of consolation,’ the sabbath ‘rest.’ The man in the unclean spirit is ‘the human race,’ in whom uncleanness reigned from Adam to Moses. For: “Whosoever have sinned without the law, shall perish without the law.” He who knows the Holy One of God is ordered to be silent. While indeed knowing God: “they have not glorified him as God, or given thanks; but became vain in their thoughts.” The spirit, tearing the man, went out from him, because as salvation draws near, temptation draws near. Pharaoh, let go by Israel, pursues him; the devil, despised, rises up into scandals.
56_marg60: In that he takes most care and teaches on the sabbath, he shows that he is not under the law but above it, and teaches us the true sabbath: that is, studying the salvation of souls, we abstain from every servile work, that is, from everything unlawful.
56_marg61: Bede. The scribes said what was written in Moses and the prophets. Jesus, as God and Lord of Moses himself, freely added to what was lacking in the law, or changed it. Whence in Matthew: “You have heard that it was said to them of old,” etc., “But I say to you.”
56_marg62: “What have we to do with thee,” etc. Bede. This is not a confession of the will but a wrung-out admission of necessity, as a runaway slave fears the sight of his master and begs off from blows. For the demons, seeing the Lord on earth, believed they were at once to be judged.
56_interl109: the presence of Jesus is torment to demons.
56_marg63: Bede. In a fitting order: the serpent’s tongue, which first spread poison, is shut first, lest it spread it any further; then the woman, who was first seduced, is healed of the fever of carnal desire. Third, the man who obeyed his wife to his harm is cleansed of the leprosy of error, so that the order of restoration in the Lord is the same as the order of ruin in the first man.
56_marg64: Bede. Or ‘shaking violently,’ as some copies have. Luke, however, says that it hurt him not at all. But what Mark says, ‘tearing,’ is the same as Luke: “When the devil had thrown him in the midst.” What he adds, “and hurt him not at all,” is to be understood as meaning that the shaking did not weaken him, as demons go out when some members are cut off or torn away.
56_interl112: that, going out, he had not hurt him any more.
56_marg65: Morally. We understand the man freed from the demon as the soul cleansed from unclean thought, and the woman, healed afterward of the fever, as the flesh restrained from the heat of desire by the precepts of continence.
56_marg66: “What thing is this? what is this new doctrine?” etc. They are stirred by what they see to inquire into what they had heard. For to this end the Lord himself does signs, and gave his disciples the power to do them, so that through this the gospel may be believed more surely, while those who promise heavenly things to earthly men do divine works on earth.
56_interl116: because he did such great things.
56_interl119: Allegorically. The synagogue, in a sense, committed to Peter as to the mother Church.
56_interl120: suffering from the heat of envy and persecuting the Church.
56_marg67: And at once they tell him of her, etc. Bede. Luke says: “And they besought him for her.” For the Saviour sometimes heals when asked, and sometimes of his own accord, so as to show that he is at hand against the passions of vices too, and always present to the prayers of the faithful; and that to devout petitioners he either grants the understanding of what is not understood, or forgives what is not understood. Whence: “Who can understand sins? from my secret ones cleanse me, O Lord.”
56_interl121: raised her carnal works to spiritual use.
56_marg68: The troubles of the sickness do not linger, as they usually do; the health given by the Lord’s command returns all at once.
56_marg69: And taking her by the hand. Peter’s mother-in-law, feverish, is raised up, taken by the hand. Fever is intemperance; from it we sons of the Synagogue are healed by the hand of discipline and the raising of desire; and we serve the will of him who heals us, who is inclining toward evening away from us.
56_marg70: Bede. Morally, that is, the members that had served uncleanness should serve righteousness.
56_marg71: Bede. The setting of the sun is the death of Christ. They brought to him all who were ill: for after his death he healed more through the apostles than while living in the flesh he preached to the Jews.
56_marg72: Christ, who says: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
56_marg73: At the door, etc. Jerome. Morally, the door of the kingdom is penance with faith, which works salvation for various diseases. For various are the vices by which the city of the world languishes.
56_interl125: Bede. To the sinner he said: “Why dost thou declare my justices,” etc.
56_interl126: lest anyone hearing the preacher should follow one who errs and mixes falsehoods into what he turns.
56_marg74: Bede. Luke says more plainly: “Devils went out from many, crying out and saying: Thou art the Son of God. And rebuking them he suffered them not to speak, for they knew that he was Christ.” So the demons know that he is Christ and confess him to be the Son of God. For the devil thought the man worn out by fasting, and by tempting could not test whether he was the Son of God. But afterwards, by the power of the signs, or rather, he suspected or understood. So he did not persuade them to crucify him because he was ignorant, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by his death. Whence Paul: “Which none of the princes of this world knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”
56_marg75: And rising very early, etc. Bede. As through the setting of the sun comes death, so through the dawn comes the resurrection of Christ; in whose clear light he went out into the desert of the Gentiles and prayed for unbelievers, because he was stirring their hearts to prayer.
56_interl131: it is not fitting for a preacher to be idle.
56_marg77: Bede. In this preaching is also understood that sermon given on the mountain which Matthew reports. For Mark adds: “And there came a leper to him,” about whom he says such things. By these it is understood that he is the one whom Matthew says was healed after the Lord came down from the mountain. For Matthew says: “And when he was come down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him: and behold a leper came and adored him, saying: Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.”
56_marg78: Bede. Humble, bashful. For each one ought to blush at the stains of his life, but let not shame restrain the confession; let him show the wound and ask for the remedy.
56_marg79: The leper, kneeling and begging the Lord’s will, is cleansed by him who “does not want the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.” Our leprosy is the sin of the first parent, which began at the head, when he desired the kingdoms of the world: “covetousness is the root of all evils.” Whence Giezi, following avarice, is spread over with leprosy. But this leprosy, shown to the priest “according to the order of Melchisedech,” is cleansed by an offering, when he says: “Give alms; and behold, all things are clean unto you.”
56_marg80: The leper signifies the human race which, according to Luke, is said to have been full of leprosy: “For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God”; that is, that the hand of the Saviour being stretched out, that is, the Word made flesh touching human nature, they may be cleansed from the variety of the ancient error. And those who for long were set apart from the people of God may be restored to the temple of God, and may be able to offer to the true priest, who is “a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech,” “their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God.”
56_marg81: Bede. In the will he grants power; he does not doubt, as an unbeliever might, about the Lord’s will, but, conscious of his own filth, he does not presume.
56_marg82: He who, shut out from the Lord’s law, asks to be healed by power, judges grace to be above the law. For as in the Lord there is the authority of power, so in him there is the constancy of faith.
56_interl132: shows the wound; asks for the remedy.
56_marg83: Bede. The law forbids touching a leper; but because the Lord is lord of the law, he does not obey the law but makes the law. He does not touch because he could not heal without touch, but so he proves that he was not subject to the law.
56_interl135: grace surpasses the law; he who frees others does not fear being defiled.
56_interl136: let us despise no one, even if we see stains.
56_marg84: “I will. Be thou made clean,” etc. Bede. He heals in that wonderful way in which he is asked.
56_marg85: Nothing in between the command and the deed.
56_marg86: “And when he had spoken, immediately the leprosy departed from him.” Nothing in between the deed and the command: “He spoke, and they were made.” You see that will is power. Therefore, as one having the power to heal and the authority to command, he does not shrink from proving it by working. For he says “I will” against Photinus; he commands against Arius; he touches against Manichaeus.
56_marg87: “See thou tell no one,” etc. Bede. Not because he wanted what he could not do, since “Whatsoever the Lord pleased, he hath done”; but he teaches that our benefits are to be restrained not only from the reward of money but also from favour.
56_marg88: Bede. That he may understand that he was healed not by the order of the law but by the grace which is above the law. He bids him offer, to show that he does not dissolve the law but fulfils it, since while walking according to the law he heals, above the law, those whom the remedies of the law did not heal. Nor ought the sacrifice, which signifies, to have ceased before, since what was signified had not yet been confirmed by the constitution of the apostles and the faith of believers.
56_interl140: to be offered according to the law
56_interl142: if he believe God, if the leprosy of impiety depart
56_interl143: he was forbidden to speak, but he, going out,
56_marg89: But he being gone out, etc. Bede. The salvation of one compels many to the Lord. A benefit cannot be kept silent, even when ordered to by him who gave it. The Lord commanded him to hide it. For he wills that we wish to lie hidden in the good things we do, which belongs to humility; and that we be made known against our will, so as to profit others, which belongs to great exaltation; since even if we ourselves wish it, works cannot be kept silent.
56_marg90: So that he could not openly go into the city, etc. Jerome. Jesus is not made known to those who serve with broad, shady praises and their own pleasures, but to those who go out with Peter and are in the deserts, which the Lord chose for prayer and for refreshing the people, who forsake the delights of the world and all that they possess, so that they may say: “The Lord is my portion.” But the glory of the Lord is made manifest to those who come together from everywhere, that is, through plains and heights, whom nothing can separate from the love of God.
56_interl144: he flees the tumultuous minds of the carnal
56_interl145: he visits those set apart from worldly cares
56_interl146: Allegorically. These are those whom nothing can separate from the love of Christ.
56_interl148: but, because he does not abandon even the carnal, he entered into Capharnaum
56_interl153: So that there was no room, etc. Bede. While the Lord was preaching in the house, they are not contained, nor at the door, because while Christ was preaching in Judea the Gentiles did not yet wish to enter to hear; yet to them, though placed outside, he directed the words of his teaching through his preachers.
56_interl159: Bede. Allegorically. The soul numbed by the softness of the flesh.
56_marg91: Jerome. Paralysis is a type of torpor, by which the sluggard lies in the softness of the flesh, having a desire for salvation, but is hindered by lazy and double thoughts, as if his limbs were enfeebled. The four virtues, which we have mentioned above, carry him to the roofs of divinity and wisdom, opened in the house of Christ’s flesh. In return for the service it is said that he carries the flesh which was carrying him, so that by another way he may return the more readily to his own country.
56_interl160: because all teaching is confirmed by the four books of the Gospel
56_marg92: Carried by four, etc. Bede. Because by four virtues the confidence of the mind is raised up to the Lord. Of these it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “He teaches sobriety and wisdom and knowledge”; and the virtues which others call prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice.
56_marg93: They uncovered, etc. The roof of the house in which Christ teaches is the loftiness of Scripture: “By what doth a young man correct his way? by observing thy words.”
56_marg94: The house of Jesus, according to another evangelist, is said to be roofed with tiles, because the spiritual sense is covered by the lowliness of the letter. It is let down with the bed before Jesus, because he who is still set in this flesh ought to know Jesus even so.
56_marg95: When Jesus had seen their faith, etc. Bede. One’s own faith avails much with God, where the faith of others has so much power that the man, healed inwardly and outwardly, rose up at once. And by the merits of others his own errors were forgiven him.
56_marg96: Wonderful humility: despised by all, dissolved in every joint, he calls him son. Or surely for this reason: because his sins are forgiven him.
56_marg97: He shows that he was struck by the disease because of sins, and therefore could not be healed unless these were first forgiven. As with the paralytic at the pool: “Behold thou art made whole: sin no more, lest some worse thing happen to thee.”
56_marg98: Men are afflicted with troubles of the flesh for five causes. Either to increase merits, as Job and the martyrs; or to keep humility, as Paul was by the angel of Satan; or for sins to be recognized and corrected, as Mary the sister of Moses. And this paralytic, who could not be healed unless his sins were first forgiven; or for the glory of God, like the blind man of whom: “Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents,” etc. And Lazarus, whose sickness was “not unto death, but for the glory of God”; or for the beginning of eternal damnation, as in Herod.
56_interl167: therefore they are envious, because he said: Thy sins are forgiven thee
56_interl168: sitting in unbelief, not rising to faith
56_marg99: Bede. They speak truly: God alone can do this, and God alone forgives sins also through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving sins; therefore he is truly God. They bear true witness, but they are deceived by denying the person of Christ. They err, therefore, because while they believe that he is God and forgives sins, they do not believe that he is Christ. But the Arians are more senseless, who do not dare to deny that he is Christ and that he forgives sins, yet do not fear to deny that he is God.
56_interl173: because he desires to save the unbelievers, he shows himself to be God by knowledge of hidden things and power of works
56_marg100: As if it belonged to the same power to heal the soul and the body.
56_marg101: Bede. As if to say: by the power by which I see the hidden things of the heart, I forgive those same sins. As though you should understand from yourselves what follows for the paralytic.
56_interl177: the spiritual thing, which God alone knows, who makes it
56_interl178: what can be seen with bodily eyes
56_interl179: so that the visible miracle may prove the invisible
56_marg102: Bede. God alone forgives sins, and the Son of man has power to forgive sins. Therefore the Son of man is the same God. Thus Christ, as man, forgives sins by his divinity, and by his humanity can die for sinners.
56_interl181: Bede. Separate the flesh from earthly things by continence, with hope of heavenly things.
56_interl182: paradise, which was man’s first house
56_marg103: Bede. He who had lain sick carries his bed home. With his soul healed by the forgiveness of sins, he returns with his body to the lasting keeping of himself, so that he may not again admit anything by which he might be struck.
56_interl183: The wonderful power of the Lord: salvation is in the command, without delay.
56_interl184: the condemned blasphemy is turned into praise
56_marg104: Bede. After the healing of the paralytic he goes out to the sea at Capharnaum, because he instructs not only the citizens but also the dwellers by the sea, and teaches that the wandering movements of the world are to be despised with the firmness of faith. There he taught a great crowd; there he made a publican an apostle; there he made sinners, corrected by penance, worthy of his feast, and by hearing his mysteries drew those separated from the waves of desires to the solitude of a quiet way of life, which is in hope of heavenly things. For what follows is: “And when he was passing by, he saw Levi,” etc.
56_interl187: that he may gather the seafarers
56_marg105: Jerome. Levi was added, because from the tax-booth of worldly business he follows only the word which says: “Every one of you that doth not renounce all that he possesseth, cannot be my disciple.”
56_marg106: Mark and Luke, out of modesty and for the honour of the evangelist, do not give the common name. He himself, according to what is written, “The just man is the first accuser of himself,” names himself Matthew and the publican, to show that no converted man ought to despair of salvation, since an apostle and evangelist was suddenly made out of a publican.
56_marg107: Levi the son of Alpheus is himself Matthew, from the tribe whence he sprang, called Levi.
56_interl190: to the care of the tax-booth
56_interl191: For telos is Greek; in Latin, tax
56_marg108: To the tax-booth, that is, to the care and management of the taxes. For telos is called in Greek; in Latin, tax.
56_interl193: a poor man follows the poor one
56_marg109: And leaving all things, he followed him, etc. Bede. Luke says more fully: “And leaving all things, he followed him.” He who would follow the poor Christ, not so much with a step of the body as with an affection of the mind, leaves all things; as Matthew did, who, eager to follow, despised not only the gains of the tax-booth but also the danger which could arise from the rulers of the world on account of unsettled accounts. For he who called him outwardly also kindled him inwardly, so that he might follow at once, and taught him the manner. Rightly, therefore, he who by obeying despised human business became a steward of divine talents.
56_interl194: Bede. And he made him a feast, which Luke tells of.
56_marg110: Bede. Luke: “And Levi made him a great feast in his own house.” For he who receives Christ within rejoices in the abundance of delights, and the Lord gladly enters and reclines in his affection. This is the spiritual feast of the good poor, in which the rich man goes hungry and the poor man feasts.
56_marg111: Those who collect public taxes, or who pursue the gains of the world, who, converted by the example of the publican, now presume of salvation, and who do not, like the Pharisees, abide in their vices and find fault, but do penance. Whence: For, etc.
56_marg112: Publicans are those who collect public taxes, or who farm the revenues of the treasury, or of the public purse and of the world, and also those who pursue profit through trade.
56_marg113: Morally. He goes to the feast of sinners, that he may have an occasion of teaching and may impart spiritual food. By going to sinners the humility of the Lord is shown; in the conversion of penitents the power of his teaching is made plain.
56_marg114: Through the calling of Matthew is signified the faith of the Gentiles, who, leaving the gains of the world, feast with the Lord at the banquets of charity and good works. Through the haughtiness of the Pharisees is signified the envy of the Jews at the salvation of the Gentiles, to whom it is said: “The publicans and the harlots shall go into the kingdom of God before you.”
56_interl197: the master answered for his disciples
56_marg115: They that are well have no need, etc. Bede. He calls himself the physician who was wounded by a wonderful kind of healing: “He was wounded for our iniquities ... and by his bruises we are healed.”
56_interl200: therefore I turn away from you
56_interl201: you who, as if you were just, shun sinners, and who, setting up your own justice, are not subject to the justice of God
56_interl202: those who acknowledge themselves sinners, seeing that they are not justified by the law, bow their necks to the grace of Christ. Therefore I turn to sinners
56_marg116: And the disciples, etc. Bede. The other evangelists say that the Pharisees and the disciples of John asked this. Here it seems to say that others asked, whom concern for the same matter had moved. Whence it is gathered that this was objected by many: by the Pharisees, by the disciples of John, by the guests, or by whoever else.
56_marg117: Mystically. The disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, because those who glory in the works of the law, or, what is worse, follow the traditions of men, or perceive the preaching of Christ only with the ear and not with love of the heart, grow faint in heart, fasting from spiritual goods. The disciples of Christ do not fast, because whoever is faithfully a member of Christ feeds on his body and is nourished by his blood. The Lord eats and drinks with sinners, but this is because abstinence increases the merit of one in whom there is no power of nature. But the Lord, who can by nature blot out sins, can make the eaters purer than the fasters. Yet Christ fasted that you might fast, and ate with sinners that, seeing his grace, you might recognize his power.
56_interl203: he premises the cause of the following question
56_marg118: Can the children of the bridegroom mourn, etc. Matthew says: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?” etc. The bridegroom is Christ, the bride is the Church, from which spiritual marriage the apostles were born, who cannot mourn or fast as long as they see the bridegroom with the bride. When the marriage has passed, and the time of the passion and resurrection has come, then they will fast.
56_marg119: Morally. As long as the bridegroom is with us, we are in joy, and we can neither fast nor mourn. But when, on account of sin, he withdraws and flies away, then a fast is to be proclaimed, then mourning is to be increased.
56_interl212: his presence profits more than bodily abstinence
56_interl216: Bede. Both from food and from love of the world.
56_interl217: therefore they do not fast, because
56_interl218: the stricter precepts of the new life
56_marg122: No man seweth a piece of raw cloth, etc. Bede. He calls the disciples old garments, that is, still carnal and not yet renewed by the firmness of faith. If a new patch, that is, a part of the teaching which pertains to the new life, is sewn on to them, it too is in some way torn, since a part of it is handed on out of season, namely that which concerns the fast from foods, whereas that teaches the general thing: not only abstinence from food but from every pleasure of the flesh.
56_marg123: The teacher must take care not to entrust the secrets of new mysteries to a soul not yet renewed but still enduring in the old age of malice.
56_interl219: to the apostles, given to the old custom
56_interl221: the new life conflicts with the old
56_interl222: because if anything good was in it, it perishes, pressed down as if by excessive weight
56_marg125: Allegorically. We are clothed outwardly with the garment, and refreshed inwardly with the wine. The garment is good works, by which we shine outwardly before men. The wine is the fervour of faith, hope and charity, by which, in the sight of God, the senses are renewed inwardly by newness.
56_interl225: they cannot bear it, because they are still carnal
56_interl226: spiritual teaching is not committed to the memory
56_interl227: and those who have them lose them
56_marg126: They were indeed new wineskins: after the ascension, by hoping and praying in longing for his consolation, they were renewed. Then they received the Holy Ghost, by whom, as with new must, the new bottles were filled.
56_marg127: Bede. Note first that the apostles break the letter of the sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, while they receive other disciples, reject Paul as if he were a transgressor of the law.
56_marg128: They are hungry, as men who, because of the crowd, have no time to eat. But they give an example of a more austere life: they seek not prepared feasts but plain food.
56_marg129: Mystically. The disciples pass through the cornfields, as prelates with holy care look around at their subjects, and carefully weigh how each may be drawn to faith, and whose salvation they hunger for. Whence, when Peter was hungry amid prayers, there was set before him the food he hungered for, and it was said: “Arise, Peter; kill and eat.” And there is a wonderful harmony of the sacrament: there, animals are commanded to be slain and eaten; here the disciples pluck the ears and, according to the other evangelists, rub them in their hands and eat. Whence: ‘Mortify your members, and put off the old man.’ For otherwise they do not pass into the body of Christ, and otherwise they do not feed the teacher with the fruit of their progress. To pluck the ears, therefore, is to root out the root of the mind from all earthly intention. To rub with the hands, by the examples of virtues, is to strip the mind of the desire of the flesh, as of the husks of ears. To eat the grains is to incorporate each one, cleansed, into the Church by the mouths of preachers. The disciples do this before the Lord, because the teaching of the doctor goes before and the grace of heavenly visitation follows. And rightly on the sabbaths, because preachers labour for the hope of rest, and admonish hearers to rest from worldly cares and labour for eternal rest.
56_marg130: Morally. They walk through the fields with the Lord, those who meditate on the sacred words, obeying the Lord. They hunger in the fields when they desire to find in them what, kindled the more by the love of God, they may be fed on as with bread, and this on the sabbaths. Whence: “Be still and see that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man that hopeth in him.” They pluck the ears and rub them, because they take up the testimonies of the Scriptures and search them, until they draw out the marrow of love, which is veiled under the lowliness of the letter as under the bristles of the ears. The Lord proves this of the sabbath; the foolish defenders of the sabbath condemn it, who love only the surface of the letter, know not the refreshment of the mind, and do not know the rest of souls. Whence he also says to them: “Have you never read, etc.”
56_interl230: he brings up the old history
56_interl233: Under Abiathar the high priest. Do not let it trouble you that others say Abimelech. For both were then present there: Abimelech the father and Abiathar the son, who, after his father had been slain by Saul, became the companion of David’s exile, and, while David reigned, was high priest, of greater name than his father; and so he was worthy that the Lord should mention him as high priest even while his father was living.
56_marg131: Bede. As if David and Abimelech were not blamed by us but excused for hunger, why do you condemn in these the cause that you approve in the others? Although there is a great distance between them: these rub ears, those eat the levitical loaves; and the day of the new moons was approaching the sabbath, when he, being sought at the banquet, fled from the king’s hall.
56_marg132: Figuratively. That David and his young men eat the hallowed loaves signifies that priestly food is to pass into the use of the peoples, because we ought to imitate the life of priests, and all the sons of the Church are priests, anointed to a holy priesthood, offering themselves as spiritual sacrifices to God.
56_marg133: And he gave them, etc. Following this, he judged it better to free men from the peril of hunger than to offer sacrifice: “I will have mercy and not sacrifice.” The salvation of men is a sacrifice pleasing to God.
56_interl237: Bede. Therefore the salvation of man is the first observance of the sabbath, as the usefulness of man requires.
56_marg134: Bede. The sabbath is so commanded to be kept that, if there is necessity, he who breaks it is not guilty. It is not forbidden to circumcise on the sabbath, because Josue was obliged to go round the walls of Jericho for seven days. The Maccabees fought on the sabbath: what is not lawful in the law, necessity makes lawful. So also today in fasts, if someone who is sick breaks a fast, he is not held guilty.
56_marg135: Therefore the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath also, etc. As if: if David the king and the priests, according to another evangelist, violating the sabbath for the service of the temple, are free from the charge of crime, how much more the Son of man, the true king and priest. And so, is the Lord of the sabbath not held guilty of the crime of plucking ears on the sabbath?
56_interl238: where there is the greater gift of knowledge, there is the greater danger of fault
56_marg136: Bede. The hand that was stretched out to the forbidden fruit dried up from good work; by the hands of Christ stretched out on the cross it has been restored to the sap of good works.
56_marg137: This man signifies the covetous, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive; who plunder and do not bestow; to whom it is said that they should stretch out their hands, that is: “He that stole, let him now steal no more; but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have something to give to him that suffereth need.”
56_marg138: Bede. Because he had reasonably excused his disciples, they watch him, so that if he heals on the sabbath they may accuse him of transgression, and if he does not, of cruelty or weakness.
56_interl241: so that he may be seen by all
56_interl242: whether to heal the man or not
56_marg139: Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? etc. Bede. He reproves those who violate the precepts of the law by a perverse interpretation, thinking that on the sabbath one must abstain from good, when the law says: “You shall do no servile work therein,” that is, sin. This precept is prefigured, because those who have done good through the six ages of the world will rest in the seventh only from evils. For the fruit of good work will not be idle: to rest in the praise of God.
56_marg140: Matthew says that they asked him; Mark and Luke say that he was asked. But they asked first, and Jesus, knowing their wickedness, set the man to be healed in the midst of them and asked, as Mark and Luke say. And then, while they were silent, he set forth the parable of the sheep and concluded that it is lawful to do good on the sabbath. And so: “looking round about on them with anger,” etc.
56_marg141: Bede. He signifies the whole man by a part, or because he did this for the soul, or because this healing of the hand signifies the salvation of the soul.
56_marg142: Bede. Not that the supremely merciful can destroy anyone, but not to save is to destroy. Just as it is said that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart, not that he hardened it, but that he did not soften him when he was hardened.
56_interl244: as if angry at their unbelief
56_marg143: Bede. Morally. The fruitless weakness of the soul is cured no better than by the giving of alms. Whence: “He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner.” And in Ecclesiasticus: “Let not thy hand be stretched out to receive, and shut when thou shouldst give.” For in vain does a man stretch out his hands in prayer to the Lord, who does not stretch them out to the widow who asks.
56_marg144: They reckon it a crime, out of great zeal for wickedness, that the hand was healed at his word. Nor can he be convicted of working on the sabbath who “spoke, and they were made,” since they themselves carry food on the sabbaths, hand over cups, and do the other things necessary for living.
56_marg145: And the Pharisees going out. Those who cannot do so by themselves seek companions in wickedness.
56_marg147: With the Herodians, etc. The servants of Herod, on account of the enmity which he himself practised against John, persecuted with plots and hatred Jesus, whom John preached.
56_marg148: Great vanities: he who lacks salvation takes counsel about the death of the Saviour.
56_interl248: because they are overcome by reason, they plot death
56_interl250: the physician yields to the mad people
56_interl251: he yields to those who hate, he draws near to those who love
56_marg149: He flees as a man, because his hour had not yet come, and the place for his passion was not outside Jerusalem.
56_marg150: Bede. The teachers of the people and the servants of the king pursue him with hatred; the untaught crowd follows him with love, and very many deserve to be healed.
56_interl260: Bede. The fame of his virtues
56_marg151: Allegorically. From the synagogue he withdraws to the sea, etc. He leaves Judea and comes to the Gentiles with his disciples, that is, with the apostles preaching; he approached the hearts of the Gentiles, and so he received the many who came to him and gave the salvation they desired. Whence it is aptly added: “And he spoke to his disciples.”
56_interl262: the Church gathered from the Gentiles
56_interl263: Ship. The Church gathered from the Gentiles, having passed over the waves of the world in mind; which, the more it widens the bosom of the heart to receive grace, the more securely it tramples the waves of the world.
56_marg152: They who disturb the peace of the Church press him. They who receive the faith with a true heart and love touch him. Those who touched him are said to have been healed; fleeing those who pressed, he went up into the ship.
56_marg153: Bede. Both those who have wounds and those with unclean spirits. But the sick, with a pious intention of salvation, the demoniacs, or rather the demons within them, were not only compelled by fear to fall down but also to confess his majesty. For, terrified by his presence, they could not conceal that they already knew him to be the Son of God. Saner than the Arians, who even today deny that the Son of God is.
56_interl268: “But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices, etc.?”
56_interl269: to the demons and to the healed
56_marg154: Bede. Not only the demons, who confess unwillingly, or those healed by him who confess willingly, but also the apostles, who were to preach through the whole world after the passion, are bidden to be silent before the passion, lest the divine majesty being preached, the passion be deferred, and so the salvation of the world.
56_interl270: that he is God, lest the passion be deferred
56_marg155: Bede. After he forbade the unclean spirits to preach him, he chose the saints who should preach him and cast out the wicked spirits.
56_marg156: This mountain signifies the height of justice, by which, through the place, he admonishes those who are to be instructed and those who are to preach to be raised to heavenly things; so also he gave the law on a mountain.
56_marg157: It is the custom of divine Scripture to speak allegorically, but let us so apply lofty things to our senses that we may discern the truth of history. For Christ alone is spiritually a mountain, abundant in the quality of heavenly things, from whom living waters flow, and whatever is believed to be the supreme good is founded in him, who is the mountain of all mountains and the holy of holies, whom he daily invites to himself. Those are called up to the mountain who are lofty both in merit and in word, so that the place agrees with their lofty merits.
56_interl272: it is not by merits but of divine grace
56_interl273: “You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you;”
56_marg158: that three sets of four should preach faith and charity through the four parts of the world. Whence: “On the east, three gates: and on the north, three gates: and on the south, three gates: and on the west, three gates.”
56_marg159: God loved the beauty of Jacob; when the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel, that there should be twelve on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, to whom was given the power which the Son received from the Father according to the flesh, so that they should do the works that he himself did, and greater works than these.
56_marg160: He also gave power to raise the dead, as Matthew says, so that the power being shown might give faith to the word, and that those who preached new things might do new things. But now that the number of the faithful has grown, many hold to the life of virtues and do not have the signs of virtues, because a miracle shown outwardly is in vain if there is no one who works within; for: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers, but to unbelievers.”
56_marg161: Bede. Not now for the first time, but when he was brought by Andrew, he said: “Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter.” But this evangelist makes you attentive, saying that the Lord so surnamed him; for otherwise you would think he was so called by chance, not by the providence of God. God willed that he be called first by another name, so that the vitality of the sacrament might be noted from the change of name; that is, in Greek or Latin ‘Petrus’, which in Syriac is Cephas, and in both languages named from ‘petra’ (rock), of which: “And the rock was Christ.” For as the apostles are called the light of the world from Christ the Light, so Peter is from the rock. Simon, putting away the sorrow of his denial, namely when he saw the Lord after the resurrection. Or, hearing of the sadness of death, namely when it is said to him: “Another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldst not.”
56_marg162: And he imposed on Simon the name Peter. From obedience he rose to knowledge: “For he that hath, to him shall be given, and he shall abound.” And James, who has supplanted the desires of the flesh. And John, who received by grace what others by labour. And he imposed on them the name Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder, whose exalted merit deserves on the mountain to hear the thunder of the Father thundering through the cloud concerning the Son: “This is my beloved Son”; so that through the cloud of the flesh they too might scatter the fire and lightning of Christ on the earth as rain, since the Lord made the lightning into rain, so that mercy may quench what judgment burns. Whence: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord.”
56_interl277: James. Who, when the Lord called him, supplanted the care of the flesh, and despised the flesh itself when Herod slaughtered it.
56_marg163: Bede. In whom is grace, or the grace of the Lord, who, on account of the special grace of love which he earned by virginal glory, reclined on the breast of his Redeemer at supper.
56_marg164: Bede. One of them, thundering, uttered a theological voice, which no one had known how to utter before: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. He left it so heavy with such weight that, had he wished to thunder somewhat more, the world itself could not have contained it.
56_interl279: Bede. Manly, from the Greek aner, which is man, because he manfully clung to the Lord.
56_marg165: Jerome. He who manfully does violence to his own ruin, so that he always has the answer of death in himself and always has his soul in his hands.
56_interl280: the mouth of a lamp, or of lamps
56_marg166: Jerome. He who is the mouth of a lamp is one who gives light by the mouth with what he has received, to whom is given the work of an enlightened mouth. Scripture often records this kind of expression when names are given on account of mysteries, which the evangelist now inserts, speaking vehemently in the person of God.
56_interl282: son of him who suspends the waters; preachers of heavenly things, whence they may more richly intoxicate the hearts of earthly men
56_marg167: Jerome. He is the son of him who suspends the waters, that is, of him who said: “I will command my clouds that they rain not.” But the name of son of God is acquired through peace and love: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called children of God”; and: “Love your enemies, that you may be the children of God.”
56_marg168: Given. To him is granted not only remission of sins but also to be in the number of the apostles, as: “The lion and the ox shall eat together, and the wolf with the lamb.”
56_marg169: Note that the other evangelists put Matthew first, and do not call him a publican. He himself places himself after Thomas and calls himself a publican.
56_interl284: abyss, or twin; in Greek, Didymus

56_marg171: Thomas: an abyss, because he penetrated the depth of power in the resurrection. Or ‘twin’ in Greek, which is called ‘Didymus’, that is, doubtful, on account of his doubting heart, because he scarcely believed the resurrection.

56_marg172: That is, of the learned or thousandth one, of whom: “A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand.”
56_marg173: James of Alphaeus, that is, James the lesser, son of Alphaeus, brother of the Lord.

56_marg175: James of Alphaeus, who is also called the brother of the Lord, because Mary of Alphaeus was the sister of the mother of the Lord, whom John calls Mary of Cleophas, perhaps because Alphaeus and Cleophas are the same. 56_interl286: a little heart, that is, guardian of the heart
56_marg176: Guardian of the heart. Luke names this one in the gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles Jude of James, because he is the brother of James, the brother of the Lord. Whence it is said: “the son of Mary, mother of James, and of Joseph, and of Jude, and of Simon.”
56_marg177: And Thaddeus, who is corculus, that is, a cultivator of the heart who keeps his heart with all watchfulness. For God is seen through the purity of the heart, as through clean glass.
56_interl287: to distinguish him from Simon Peter
56_marg178: Bede. Simon the Cananean, from Cana, a village of Galilee, who is also Simon the Zealot, that is, emulator. Cana: zeal; Cananean: Zealot.
56_marg179: And Simon the Cananean, who is also Simon the Zealot, bearing or having sorrow: “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.” He fulfils a threefold mourning who seeks the consolation to come. He weeps for his own sins with David and Mary; with Paul he weeps “with them that weep.” And he weeps much with John, who said: ‘And I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open the book and to loose the seals thereof.’ But he is called Zealot whom the zeal of the house of God consumed, as Phinees, and the scourge ceased.
56_interl288: the fall of this one confirms others in humility
56_interl290: And Judas Iscariot who. He who does not blot out his sin by penance, nor is it blotted out by memory. Whence: “And let not the sin of his mother be blotted out; let it be before the Lord always.”
56_marg180: Judas: ‘confessing’ or ‘glorious’. Scariot: memory of death. There are many proud and glorious confessors in the Church, the first of whom is Simon Magus, and other heretics whose mortal memory is celebrated in the Church, that it may be blotted out.
56_marg181: Judas Iscariot: from the village in which he was born, or from the tribe of Issachar. Issachar: ‘hire, price’, namely of perdition. Scariot: memory of death, because he betrayed God not suddenly but premeditated. He is chosen among the apostles providentially, because great is the power of truth, which not even an adversary minister weakens. The Lord willed to be betrayed by a disciple, so that you, betrayed by a companion, might bear it with moderation: that your judgment went astray, that your kindness was lost.
56_marg182: For these apostles keep watch in threes on each of the four sides around the tabernacle of the Lord, and carry the holy words of the Lord on the shoulders of their works, so that they may carry one tabernacle with many dwelling-places to the land of promise. The example of one of them humbles them to fear, as the fall of Lucifer humbles the angels, as in: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom,” but: “He that glorieth, may glory in the Lord.”
56_marg183: And they come to a house, etc. Bede. Those who have taken up the care of others ought to guard carefully the house of conscience, so that from it they may first rule themselves, and then others.
56_marg184: The house in which they gather is the primitive Church. The crowds who hinder them from eating bread are sins and vices, because: “He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.” Whence the Lord is turned to fury when he says: “Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life.”
56_interl291: the happy occupation of the Saviour, the happy zeal of the crowd flocking together
56_marg185: The crowd besieges him; his own people despise him as mad.
56_marg186: In this the salvation of the Gentiles is noted and the envy of the Jews is condemned, of whom: “He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
56_interl295: which others make great, his own despise, because: “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country.”
56_interl297: because they could not grasp the height of his wisdom, they thought he spoke with an alien sense
56_interl298: and in this the disciples were mistaken
56_marg187: Bede. If some through slowness of mind do not understand the word of God, still hope of salvation remains, if perhaps they understand. But those who are unwilling to understand, and pervert what they understand, have no hope. Whence: Scribes, that is, the wise, etc.
56_marg188: This signifies that he is to be persecuted by his fellow citizens even unto death. We read above that a crowd followed him from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan and about Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles. And the scribes from Jerusalem blasphemed, because the crowd of the Jewish people had led him through with palms and praises, while the Gentiles desired him. The scribes and elders of the people were plotting his death.
56_marg189: He himself suffers what he taught us to suffer, saying: “Blessed shall you be when men shall curse you.”
56_marg190: “Man of flies,” or “having flies”: by which name they surnamed the prince of demons, on account of the filth of sacrificial blood.
56_interl302: so that he proves by reason that he is neither out of his mind nor casts out demons by Beelzebub
56_interl303: so that they may not understand until they are seized
56_marg191: Bede. Let them choose what they will. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them withdraw from his kingdom, which cannot stand divided.
56_interl307: that the demons fight against one another
56_interl308: things fall apart chiefly through discord
56_interl315: You say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub, but: “No man can enter into the house of a strong man, etc.”
56_marg192: The world placed in the wicked one, in which it rested without contradiction up to the coming of the Saviour, as in a peaceful empire.
56_interl320: those snatched from the devil he gathered into the Church and set in order through distinct ranks of dignity. Then: “And then he shall plunder his house,” etc.
56_marg193: He plundered the house, because he distributed all parts of the world possessed by the devil to the apostles and their successors, as if they were divided provinces, that they might convert peoples to the faith.
56_interl321: you say that I have an unclean spirit, but
56_interl322: this is against Novatian, who denies pardon to the lapsed in martyrdom
56_interl326: that is, one who, understanding God’s works and unable to deny them, contradicts out of envy and says that the works of the Holy Ghost are Beelzebub
56_marg194: Because he does not deserve to do penance so as to be received, who, knowing Christ, said that he was the prince of demons, because he is never released from prison who has not paid the last farthing of the word before the end of life. For the penny of eternal life is founded on four parts: that what you believe in the heart you confess with the mouth, and what you confess you complete in deed, and what you have completed you do not cease to teach: “For he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”
56_marg195: Matthew says: “Whoever shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost, or speak a word against the Holy Ghost, shall not have forgiveness, neither in this world nor in the world to come.” Where he shows that some things are relaxed in the future. This is to be understood of lesser sins, such as idle talk and excessive laughter, for which even this life has merited pardon.
56_marg196: Bede. Not because it is not a spirit, or because it is a spirit but not God, or God but less than the Father and the Son. For this comes not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance. But: “Because they said: He hath an unclean spirit,” etc.
56_marg197: This is against Origen, who promises pardon to all sinners after judgment, when countless ages have passed.
56_marg198: Isaias: “They shall be sent into the pit, they shall be sent into prison, and in the last they shall be visited.” From this authority, misunderstood, Origen, bursting into presumption, was condemned, because in a certain way he judged the goodness of the Holy Ghost to be foolish, in that he would not judge the wicked, namely by equating them with the good, as not to be punished beyond judgment.
56_interl328: because like the devil he attacks the majesty of God against his conscience
56_interl329: because he sins eternally who never repents
56_interl334: Bede. He was at rest in spiritual understanding.
56_marg199: Not sons of Mary, ever virgin, as Helvidius lies, nor of Joseph by another wife, as others prattle, but kinsmen.
56_marg200: Mystically. The mother and brethren, the people of the Jews, from whom Christ came according to the flesh, stand outside in the literal sense. The crowd in the house, the Gentiles, in the spiritual mystery. The Jews wish to see Christ outside, because, not seeking spiritual understanding, they compel him, or seek him, to go out to teach carnal things.
56_interl336: we too, if we stand outside, shall not be known
56_marg201: Who is my mother and my brethren? Bede. He does not refuse obedience to his mother, who says: “Honour thy father and thy mother.” But he shows that he owes more to the paternal mysteries than to maternal affections; he showed by example what he said in words: “He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me.” Nor does he unjustly despise his brethren, but he set spiritual work before kinship, teaching that the bond of hearts is better than that of bodies.
56_interl337: that he may make them attentive
56_marg202: Jerome. So that we may know that we are his brethren and his mother too, if we do the will of his Father, that we may be co-heirs; for he distinguishes not by sexes but by deeds. Sister and brother by believing, mother by preaching; while through preaching the love of Christ, as it were Christ himself, is begotten in the heart of the hearer.
56_interl338: for both sexes of the faithful
56_marg203: Whence Matthew, after the preceding sermon, immediately added: “The same day, Jesus going out of the house, sat by the sea side,” etc.
56_marg204: Bede. Going out of the house where he is said to have a demon, he teaches by the sea, to show that he would leave the Jewish people for their guilt of unbelief and pass over to the Gentiles. Whence it is aptly placed before: because while he was preaching in the house, his mother and brethren stood outside.
56_marg205: He began to teach by the sea, so that the place might indicate listeners who are bitter and unstable. And therefore he speaks in parables, so that those who did not understand might, by asking the apostles whom they despised, learn the mystery of the kingdom they lacked. The sea is the world, which, tasted, is bitter, and restless with the waves of vices. But the predestined are snatched away by the Lord himself, who sweetens bitter things, turns sad things into joy, and sickness into health.
56_interl340: Bede. The crowding of peoples flocking to the faith.
56_marg206: Bede. The Church, which is in the sea among unbelievers, which God illumines by the grace of his visitation and consecrates as a dwelling dear to himself.
56_marg208: Jerome. These are they who lately came to hear the word, and thence, from devotion of soul, have followed away from the bitterness of the reprobate as from the sea; but they are not yet with the Lord in the ship, because they are not yet imbued with the heavenly mysteries or sacraments which they desire.
56_marg209: [1.1] A parable is a comparison, made under some likeness, of things differing in nature from one another. He speaks in his usual wisdom, so that those who could not grasp heavenly things might be able to perceive them through an earthly likeness heard. [1.2] In Greek it is called ‘similitudo’ when we indicate by some comparisons what we wish to be understood, as when we compare a hard man to iron, a swift man to the winds and to birds. [2] The same happens with the thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold fruit, that is, the law, the prophets and the gospel, in which the mystery of the kingdom shown on the mountain stands on the mouth of three witnesses, that is, of Moses and Elias and Jesus.
56_interl341: from the bosom of the Father
56_marg210: Christ into the world. Or from Judea to the Gentiles. Whence Habacuc: “Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people,” etc.
56_interl343: the word, by himself or through his own
56_marg211: Some fell by the way side, etc. Luke: “And it was trodden down, and the fowls of the air devoured it.” The way is the mind, worn down by the fear of carnal thoughts. Whence the seed perishes and bears no fruit, and is snatched by birds, that is, by demons. They are called birds of the air either because of their celestial and spiritual nature, or because they dwell in the air.
56_interl345: the hardness of an impudent mind
56_interl346: the gentleness of an obedient spirit
56_interl347: because on hearing the word they delight for an hour
56_interl348: the uprightness of a spirit exercised in heavenly discipline and regularly trained to obey
56_interl350: of firm desire, because they take delight for only an hour in the word once heard
56_interl351: the hearts of the rich, anxious with care
56_interl353: nor can the word bear fruit
56_interl356: by the faith of the holy Trinity
56_interl357: in married people, which the index finger and thumb signify, to signify thirty, joined as in a gentle kiss
56_interl360: signifies that he has spoken of high things
56_interl365: those who are with me, not those who are outside
56_interl368: who are unwilling to come near
56_interl369: not in the ship with me
56_interl370: not only words but also deeds, because they could not grasp the spiritual things that were hidden in them
56_interl377: as if: therefore they are not converted, nor are their sins forgiven them
56_interl379: And these are they, etc. He sets out the differences among those who hear the word. There are some, such as the Gentiles, who do not hear at all.
56_interl381: because they receive it with no faith and no understanding, or only as an occasion for testing some advantage
