56_marg212: These test the advantage and taste the desire, but adversities hinder what they dread.
56_interl387: by riches, which sting with various cares, because those who possess much need much
56_interl391: And the lusts after other things, etc. Because it is commanded; for it is enjoined: “Thou shalt desire wisdom; keep the commandments,” etc. And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord: he shall delight exceedingly in his commandments.” These are good desires; he who desires the rest goes astray.
56_interl392: that is, they choke the throat of the mind, and do not allow a good desire to pass into the heart
56_interl394: Bede. These receive, keep and bear fruit.
56_interl395: faith in the Trinity in the hearts of the elect
56_interl396: the perfection of good work, because the adornment of the world was completed in six days
56_interl397: Bede. Eternal blessedness, because the hundred is carried from the left to the right by digital reckoning.
56_interl398: as if: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God”
56_marg213: Jerome. The lamp: the word of God. The measure or the bed: ‘the hearing of the disobedient.’ The lampstand: the apostles, whom the word of God enlightened. What is hidden and secret becomes open when it is handled by the Lord.
56_marg214: The measure: our life, measured by divine foreknowledge. The bed: the flesh, in which the soul rests. The lamp: the word, which enlightens. Whoever, out of love of present life and fleshly allurement, hides the word of God, covers the lamp as if under a measure or a bed, because he places fleshly desires before it.
56_marg215: So that the preaching of truth may rule, and bodily servitude be subject, through which nevertheless the teaching appears higher, as a lamp through a lampstand.
56_marg216: As if: do not be ashamed of the gospel, because nothing is hidden that will not be made open in judgment, when “God will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts”; where for you there is praise from God, but for them eternal punishment.
56_interl405: of understanding the word of God
56_interl406: let him commit it to memory
56_interl407: let him not withdraw himself, let him not turn what he has heard to fables
56_interl408: as if: do all that you can diligently, because: “In what measure you shall mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
56_marg217: Jerome. For according to the measure of faith the understanding of mysteries is divided to each one, and the gift of knowledge will be added to us, and virtues will also be added. “For he that hath, to him shall be given”: namely, he who has faith will have virtue, and he who has the work of the word will have understanding of the mystery. And on the contrary, he who does not have faith is lacking in virtue, and he who does not have the work of the word, his understanding is wanting; and he who does not understand has now lost what he heard, as if he had not heard.
56_interl409: in the present: the sense of understanding and the effect of working; and in the future: the gifts of eternal reward will be added
56_interl410: as if: give heed to the word you have heard: For he that hath, etc.
56_interl412: the understanding of what he loves
56_interl414: by natural talent or the practice of letters
56_interl415: Bede. That is, he will rejoice in no true sweetness of wisdom.
56_marg218: Jerome. Divine Scripture shows heavenly mysteries through earthly likenesses, as the whole body of the gospels stands. The kingdom of God is the Church, which is ruled by God, and itself rules men and tramples vices, as a centurion having soldiers under him. The man casting the seed is the Son of man; the seed is the word; the earth, human hearts; the sleep of the man is the death of the Saviour. The seed rises by night and by day, after Christ’s sleep: the number of believers, through prosperity and adversity, germinates more and more and grows in work, while he does not know. This is a figurative expression, and very frequent in divine things: “he does not know,” that is, makes us not know who will bring forth fruit at the end, while he says: “He that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved.” For the earth bears fruit of its own accord, while God waits for our will, saying: ‘If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments.’ First the blade, that is, fear: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”; then the ear, that is, tearful penance. Then the full grain, namely charity: “Love is the fulfilling of the law,” and: “When the fruit is brought forth, he putteth in the sickle.” The sickle is death or judgment, which cuts all things, since the harvest, that is, the consummation of the age, is at hand, in which the just, who sowed in tears, will rejoice.
56_interl425: because it lies in the choice of man
56_interl431: Bede. The preaching of the gospel, which leads to the kingdom of God, of which it is said: ‘The kingdom shall be taken away from you,’ etc.
56_marg219: Jerome. He compares this seed again to the grain of mustard, which is least in fear, great in charity, which is greater than all herbs, because “God is charity,” and “All flesh is grass,” and “He that is weak, let him eat herbs.” And it makes branches of mercy and compassion, under whose shade the animals of heaven delight to dwell.
56_interl432: Bede. In the heart of the believer or in the world.
56_marg220: When it is sown in the earth, etc. Sown by Christ, or by a man, in the earth or in the field, that is, in his heart. Here ‘man’ is our sense and mind, which, cherishing the grain of preaching with the moisture of faith, makes it sprout in the field of his breast.
56_interl434: Is less than all the seeds, etc. As if preaching contemptible things, and at first it is not believed, because he preaches God to be a dead man, crucified. Compared with the eloquence and wisdom of the philosophers, this is found to be less.
56_marg221: It surpasses the nature of herbs in height, breadth and age. It is high, because it lifts up to heavenly things. Broad, because it has occupied the whole world; aged, because it cannot be brought to an end.
56_marg222: Bede. Than all herbs. The philosophical disciplines, which the more openly they grow, become the more worthless, because “as the green herbs they shall quickly fall.”
56_interl438: preachers arising from the preaching itself
56_interl440: the protection of God, of which: “I sat down under his shadow, whom I desired,” etc.
56_interl442: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat.”
56_marg223: Not that he made no speech open to the crowds, but because no speech of his is found in which something of a parable is not found.
56_interl444: spiritual things to the spiritual, who are worthy to understand
56_marg224: Jerome. For they were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost sanctuary of wisdom, who, with the tumults of thoughts set aside, remained in careful attention to virtues. For wisdom is to be learned in a time of leisure.
56_interl446: as the setting of the true sun drew near
56_marg225: Bede. Allegorically. The sea: the surge of the world; the little ship: the cross, by which we rise above the waves of the world and reach the shore of the heavenly homeland. The other ships which are said to have been with the Lord, neither taken out to the deep nor to have endured the storm, signify those who are so steeped in the faith of the Lord’s cross that, as if unskilled and not yet struck by tribulation, they keep the mysteries of faith received in peace; or those who, after frequent storms of tribulations, use the calm of peace for a time. For perhaps those ships had been lately made and led only into harbour, or led back to harbour after the perils of the sea.
56_marg226: In the hinder part of the ship. Jerome. The stern, with dead hides, holds the living, keeps back the waves, and is made firm by wood; that is, the Church is saved by the cross and death of the Lord.
56_marg227: The stern is the beginning of the holy Church, in which the Lord sleeps in bodily death, though “he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.” He rebukes the wind and the sea, of whom it is said: “Thou rulest the power of the sea.” The wind and the sea are demons and persecutors, to whom he says: ‘Be still,’ when he restrains the edicts of wicked kings as he wills, because it is not in man to direct his own steps. The great calm is the peace of the Church after pressures, or contemplation after active life.
56_interl451: the body, on which divinity as its head lies inclined
56_marg228: Bede. While the disciples were sailing, Christ fell asleep, because while the faithful were meditating on the rest of the coming kingdom, and, with the second breath of the Holy Ghost or the oars of their own effort, were casting the waves of the world behind their backs, suddenly the passion of Christ came on. As he ascended the stern of the cross to take the sleep of death, the waves of the blasphemers rise up, roused by demonic storms; yet his patience is not disturbed by them, but the disciples are troubled, tremble and are in peril.
56_marg229: Morally. Steeped in the sign of the cross, we resolve to leave the world, we embark on the ship with Jesus, and we try to cross the sea. But he who “shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel” sleeps while we sail, because amid the efforts of the virtues, by the onslaught of demons or of wicked men or of our own thoughts, the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope wastes away, and the flame of love grows cold. But let us run back to the helmsman; let us diligently rouse him who does not serve but commands the winds, who will calm all things, who will grant the harbour of salvation.
56_interl453: Bede. Lest, the resurrection being delayed longer, they should utterly perish.
56_interl455: as if: is it no concern to you?
56_interl456: from death: ‘That, through death, he might destroy him who had the empire of death’
56_marg230: By the resurrection he restrained the rage of the Jews, who, shaking the head, cried out: ‘If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross.’
56_marg231: Peace, be still. Note that every creature feels the command of the Creator. Not that all things are animate, as heretics falsely claim, but by the majesty of the founder, what is insensible to us is sensible to him.
56_interl460: peace in the Church after pressures, or contemplation after active life
56_marg232: Bede. As if: why do you fear while I am present? Similar to this is that after the resurrection “he upbraided their incredulity and hardness of heart, because they did not believe them who had seen him risen again.” And again: “O foolish, and slow of heart to believe in all things which the prophets have spoken. Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory?”
56_interl461: therefore fearful, because: Have you not faith yet? etc.
56_marg233: Matthew: “But the men wondered, saying: What manner of man is this,” etc. Therefore it was not the disciples but others who were in the ship who wondered at him, doubting about him to whom the sea and wind obeyed. Or even the disciples themselves were rightly called men, because they did not yet know the power of the Saviour.
56_marg234: Bede. Gerasa, a famous city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, joined to Mount Galaad in the tribe of Manasses, not far from the lake of Tiberias, in which the swine were cast down. It signifies the nations whom the Lord, after his resurrection, deigned to visit by sending preachers. Whence Gerasa, or Gergesi, is rightly interpreted either as ‘driving out the tenant’ or as ‘a stranger drawing near’, because the people of the nations drove out the tenant, that is the devil, by whom they had long been inhabited, and he who was far off has been made near in the blood of Christ.
56_marg235: The Gentiles, who are deluded by demonic teachings, worship idols.
56_marg236: Isidore. This man is the most desperate of peoples, the people of the nations whom the Apostle enumerates: puffed up, proud, unclean, bloodthirsty, idolatrous, shameful, bound neither by the law of nature, nor of God, nor by human fear. His name is ‘Legion’, that is, ten thousand who fall at the right hand of the Father, which is Christ. To him the herd of swine is entrusted; these, without any regard for mercy, are together choked in hell by the command of untimely death. Many flee from these, who used to feed them. For when a fool is beaten, the wise man becomes wiser or more prudent.
56_interl463: because the nations delight in dead works, that is, in sins
56_interl464: Bede. The bodies of the faithless, whose souls are dead by sins, are sepulchres.
56_interl465: by divine laws, because he was not worthy
56_marg237: Bede. Chains and fetters signify the heavy and harsh laws of the nations, by which sins were restrained in their public affairs. When the chains were broken, as Luke writes, he was suddenly driven by the demon into the desert, because even with those laws transgressed, they were carried off by desire to those crimes which already exceeded common custom.
56_interl471: Bede. By the words of most hardened unbelief.
56_interl472: since, seizing rocks, the frenzied men were cutting themselves
56_marg238: Concidens, with the vowel lengthened: it is written with ci, from cedo, not from cado.
56_interl474: Bede. As if: nothing in common with us.
56_interl475: This against the Jews, who say: ‘By Beelzebub he casts out devils.’
56_interl476: This against Arius, who denies the Son of God.
56_interl477: they believe and tremble: the Son of God
56_marg239: Torment me not, etc. Bede. To cease from harming a man is a great torment to him; and he lets him go with a torment the more grievous, the longer he has possessed him.
56_marg240: What is thy name? Bede. He does not ask as one ignorant, but so that the power of the healer may appear more welcome once the public plague he had endured has been confessed. But also the priests of our own time, who cast out demons by exorcism, are accustomed to say that patients cannot be cured unless they openly confess, as far as they are able to recall, everything they have suffered from demons, whether by sight, hearing, or any sense of body or mind, whether awake or asleep.
56_marg241: Legion, etc. Bede. It signifies the Gentile people enslaved to countless cults of idolatry, to which is opposed: “And the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.” Whence rightly, at the building of Babylon the unity of tongues was split by the spirit of pride, and in Jerusalem by the grace of the Holy Ghost the variety of tongues was gathered into one; and the former is called confusion, and this the vision of peace, because one faith and piety, bringing peace throughout the whole world, confirms the elect among many tongues and nations, while more sects than tongues confound the reprobate by dividing them.
56_interl479: but that he would send them into the herd of swine; and this is: ‘For he was,’ etc.
56_marg242: Bede. Luke: ‘And they besought him that he would not command them to go into the abyss.’ They knew, therefore, that it would at some time come to pass that by his coming they would be sent into the abyss, not foretelling the future, but recalling the words of the prophets spoken about themselves; and so they feared that the glory of Christ, which they marvelled at, would tend to their own damnation.
56_marg243: Bede. Swine signify ‘unclean men’, who, lacking voice and reason, feed on the mountain of pride and delight in filthy acts, over whom demons can have dominion through the worship of idols. For unless someone lives like a swine, the devil does not receive power over him, unless perhaps for testing, not for destruction.
56_marg244: So that the destruction of the swine might be an occasion of salvation for men. For the shepherds, seeing it, at once announced it to the city.
56_interl480: Bede. Power having been received from God; for otherwise they would not harm even the cattle.
56_marg245: Bede. Because the Church is now glorified, and the people of the nations freed from the dominion of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ, sunk in blind and deep curiosity, carry on sacrilegious rites in hidden places.
56_marg246: Bede. Let the Manichean blush, if the souls of men and beasts are of the same substance and from the same author, since for the salvation of one man two thousand swine are suffocated.
56_marg247: Because certain leaders of the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim his power among the nations, astonished and marvelling.
56_marg248: Bede. Luke: ‘Sitting at his feet,’ which signifies those who have been corrected of their sins, with fixed attention of mind, to gaze upon the footsteps of the Saviour, that they may follow them.
56_marg249: Through zeal for virtues, which he had lost in his frenzied mind. Whence the prodigal son, returning to his father, is at once clothed with the first robe and a ring, because whoever has repented with a true heart can, by the gift of Christ’s grace, recover the former works of justice, from which he had fallen, together with the ring of inviolate faith.
56_marg250: For many, delighted by ancient sweetness, say that they honour the Christian law but are unwilling to suffer it, because they cannot fulfil it; yet they marvel that the faithful people has been healed from its former way of life.
56_marg251: Rabanus. As Peter: ‘Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,’ etc. Lest they touch the ark of God, as Oza.
56_interl481: conscious of their own frailty, still weak, they could not bear the weight of his wisdom
56_interl482: ‘To be dissolved and to be with Christ is by far the better.’
56_interl483: because to remain in the flesh is necessary for the sake of others
56_marg252: Bede. So let each person, after the resurrection from sins, return to a good conscience and serve the gospel for the salvation of others, that afterwards he may rest with Christ, lest, while he too hastily wishes to be with Christ now, he neglect the mystery of preaching, which is suited to the redemption of his brethren.
56_marg253: The healed man is sent to his house, that is, to the spiritual observance of the law, and preaches in the Decapolis, that is, keeps the decalogue, while the Jews are converted from the Roman kingdom, now, that is, they are of the Church, who also cling to the letter of the decalogue only, because the moral precepts are to be observed according to the letter.
56_marg254: Matthew says two; Mark and Luke say one, cured of a demon, because one of them was of more illustrious name and more famous, and therefore his cure is more famous. Allegorically: the two nations signify two of Noe’s sons. For when Noe begot three sons, one was taken into the possession of God, two were given to idols.
56_marg255: Jerome. After these things Jairus the ruler of the synagogue comes, because ‘when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel shall be saved.’ Jairus, ‘enlightening’ or ‘enlightened’, that is, the Jewish people, having put aside the shadow of the letter, illumined and enlightened by the Spirit, falls down at the feet, that is, humbling himself before the incarnation of Jesus, he prays for a daughter; he who lives for himself makes others live. Abraham and Moses and Samuel pray for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers.
56_marg256: Jairus: ‘enlightening’ or ‘enlightened’, because he enlightened the people with words of life, and in order to be able to do this he was enlightened by the Holy Ghost.
56_interl488: the head of Christ is God; the feet are the incarnation
56_marg257: Bede. Luke: ‘For he had an only daughter, almost twelve years old, and she was dying.’ The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the synagogue, formed by the legal institution alone, as if born the only daughter of Moses. She was dying in her twelfth year, that is, as the time of puberty drew near, because, nobly brought up by the prophets, when she came to the years of understanding and ought to have begotten a spiritual offspring for God, she was struck suddenly by the languor of errors and desperately abandoned the spiritual ways.
56_marg258: While he goes to heal the girl, he is pressed by the crowd, because, offering the Jews the admonitions of salvation by which he would raise up their sick conscience, he is burdened by the harmful custom of the carnal peoples.
56_interl495: the woman with an issue of blood
56_marg259: And a woman, etc. While the Lord goes to the ruler’s daughter, a woman diseased for twelve years snatches away health; afterwards the daughter is healed and raised, because the salvation of the human race was so dispensed that first some of Israel, then the fullness of the nations, ‘and so all Israel would be saved.’
56_interl496: Bede. It is to be noted that the girl of twelve years and the woman who bled for twelve years: when the former was born, the latter began to fall ill. For at nearly the same age of the world, the Synagogue began to be born among the patriarchs, and the nations began to be defiled by idolatry.
56_marg260: The bleeding woman, cured by the Lord, is the Church from among the nations, defiled by the great flow of carnal pleasures and already separated from the assembly of the faithful. While Christ was deciding to heal Judea, she anticipated with sure hope the salvation already prepared and promised to others.
56_marg261: Bede. False theologians, philosophers, and teachers of the secular laws, who promised to give precepts useful for living. The demons too, offering counsel as if to men, pressed themselves on them to be worshipped as God; the more they spent the strength of their natural industry in listening to these, the less they could be healed. But when they heard that the people of the Jews was sick and that the true physician had come from heaven, they began to hope for and seek a remedy for their sickness.
56_marg262: Bede. ‘If any man minister to me, let him follow me.’ And elsewhere: ‘You shall walk after the Lord your God.’ Or because she did not see God present in the flesh, but afterwards came to the grace of acknowledging the faith. And by touch, that is, by participation in his sacraments, she deserved to be healed of her sins. For the fountain of blood, the origin of sin, is the beginning of an unclean thought, from which all sin arises. But the Lord cleanses not only works but also evil words and the root of thoughts, with the evangelical sacraments, as with his own garments, the fountains of obscene blood.
56_marg263: Bede. Only the faithful woman touches the Lord, whom the crowd, following him everywhere, presses. Because he who is burdened by the disorderly crowding of various heresies, or by perverse morals, is touched only by the faithful heart of the Church. Whence: ‘Do not touch me, for I am not yet ascended to my Father.’ For to touch him truly is to believe him equal to the Father.
56_interl499: the root of an unclean thought
56_marg264: He asks so that the salvation he had given the woman, the power of faith being declared and acknowledged, may profit many.
56_marg265: By the seventh power the dead is raised, but on the way the bleeding woman touches the hem; she had lost her substance, along with her health, on physicians who did nothing to help. God rested on the seventh day from all work. When the dead is raised within, and half-alive outside, the flow of blood makes sterility along with the crowds. Whence to the Church of the nations: ‘Rejoice, thou barren, that bearest not.’ She comes up behind, that is, after the resurrection, and touches the hem, as the bells and the pomegranates that hang at the extreme edges of the high priest’s tunic. The bell signifies ‘confession’, the pomegranate ‘the will to martyrdom’ and ‘the whiteness of virtues’.
56_marg266: ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the just: and his ears unto their prayers.’ ‘This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.’
56_marg267: Bede. Behold to what the question was tending: namely, that the woman should confess the truth of her long-lasting infirmity, and of her sudden belief and healing, and so she herself might be confirmed in faith and give an example to others.
56_interl503: Bede. He does not say ‘will make’; for in believing she has already been made whole.
56_interl504: Bede. By persevering in the same faith: ‘For he who has persevered,’ etc.
56_marg268: Bede. When the woman was healed, the girl is at once announced dead, because, the Church of the nations having been cured of the stain of vices and named a daughter for the merit of faith, the Synagogue was at once dissolved by the death of unbelief, because it did not believe in Christ, and by the death of envy, because it grieved that the Church believed.
56_marg269: Bede. For many today, seeing the state of the Synagogue, do not believe it can be restored, and do not think prayer should be made for its restoration. But what is impossible for men is possible for God. Whence it follows: ‘But Jesus, etc.’
56_marg270: The ruler of the synagogue is the company of the teachers of the law, of whom: ‘The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses.’ If they are unwilling to believe, even the synagogue subject to them will be saved.
56_marg271: Bede. The mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers and mockers, but to the faithful who honour them. Whence elsewhere: ‘And wisdom is justified by all her children.’
56_marg272: Bede. ‘But let all them be glad that hope in the Lord: they shall rejoice for ever, and thou shalt dwell in them.’ The Synagogue has lost this joy through its merited unbelief, and therefore lies dead among the weeping and wailing. But Jesus does not allow her to perish utterly. Whence it follows: ‘And going in, etc.’
56_marg273: To me, in whose ordering the soul, once received, lives, and the flesh that is to be raised rests. Hence it is the custom among Christians that the dead, who are not doubted to be going to rise, are called sleeping. Whence: ‘We would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who are asleep.’
56_marg274: Although the soul that sins dies, yet that one whom the Lord foresees for eternal life may not unfittingly be said to have been dead to us but to have fallen asleep to him.
56_marg275: Bede. Morally. The crowd is cast out so that the girl may be raised, because unless the multitude of worldly cares is cast out of the heart, the soul lying dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself through all its thoughts, it does not in any way gather itself to consider itself.
56_interl507: Bede. He first cleanses the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood; otherwise the girl would not rise.
56_marg276: Talitha cumi: it is Syriac, that is, ‘damsel, arise.’
56_marg277: In the Syriac language which the evangelist gives, it is no more than ‘damsel, arise.’ But perhaps, to express the force of the Lord’s command, he added: ‘I say to thee, arise’, and cared more to convey the sense of the speaker than the words. So often the apostles and evangelists, when they take up some testimony, set down the sense rather than the words.
56_marg278: It is said to the girl: ‘Talitha cumi,’ that is, ‘damsel, arise.’ It is said to the ruler of the synagogue: ‘Thy daughter is dead.’ Jesus: ‘The damsel is not dead, but sleepeth.’ Both things are true: she is dead to you, but she sleeps to me. The girl was twelve years old, and the woman had suffered for twelve years; the sins of unbelievers appear at the beginning of the faith of believers. Whence it is said: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice.’
56_marg279: Morally. That Christ raised three dead signifies three kinds of souls. He raises the girl still shut up in the house, that is, the soul that has given only consent, not yet an act, to evil delight. He raises the young man already carried out beyond the gate, that is, the sinner who has already carried consent through to act. He raises Lazarus already stinking, and the soul that by long habit of sinning smells foul and corrupts others by its reputation. He speaks to the girl with few words, because he easily raises her whom he declares not dead, and shows that a soul like hers is quickly raised. He strengthens the young man with more words when he says: “Young man, I say to thee, arise,” because such souls sometimes revive with more difficulty. At the tomb of Lazarus he groans, is troubled, and weeps: “He cried with a loud voice: Lazarus, come forth.” In the same way, one pressed down by long habit of sinning is raised scarcely, and as it were with labour. It is also to be noted that public harm needs a public remedy; light and secret faults can be blotted out by a light and secret penance. The girl lying in the house rises with few witnesses, and is charged to tell no one. The young man is outside the gate, with a great crowd accompanying and seeing. Lazarus, called from the tomb, became so well known that for this reason the crowds went out to meet the Lord with palms, and: “many of the Jews went away, and believed in Jesus.” He heard of a fourth dead man announced by a disciple, but because there were no living people to pray for him: “Leave the dead, he said, to bury their dead.”
56_interl514: He keeps the sabbath badly who is idle from good works.
56_marg280: “How came this man by all these things?” etc. Strange blindness. They can know Christ from his deeds and words, and they despise him solely from knowing his family.
56_marg281: Bede. He who works by fire and by the Spirit. Whence: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire.” The craftsman is he who fashioned the dawn and the sun.
56_marg282: He is called ‘the son of the craftsman,’ and this is mystical: of the craftsman who fashioned the dawn and the sun, namely the first Church and the one that follows, in whose figure the woman and the girl are healed.
56_interl523: “A prophet shall the Lord God raise up to you.”
56_marg283: “A prophet is not without honor,” etc. It is almost natural for fellow citizens to envy one another, because they remember not his works but the childhood they saw.
56_marg284: Lowliness often accompanies origin, as in: “Who is the son of Isai?” But “the Lord looketh on the low: and the high he knoweth afar off.”
56_marg285: So that he would not condemn the unbelieving citizens more severely by doing many mighty works; or because he is despised in his own country. He did few mighty works and signs there, lest they be wholly excusable. Greater signs he does daily among the Gentiles, not so much in healing bodies as in souls.
56_marg286: Bede. He shows it not as unexpected but as something to be wondered at, since they believe neither the prophets nor him whom they see before them.
56_marg287: Jerome. The twelve apostles are sent, and the power and command to teach are given them, so that word and deed go together, and mighty works are mixed with invisible promises; and so, as they anoint the sick with oil, they strengthen weakness of faith by power.
56_marg288: The kind Lord and master does not begrudge his disciples and servants his power. But he himself works by his own power, while they, in their weakness, if they accomplish anything, confess the power of the Lord, saying: “In the name of Jesus, arise and walk.”
56_marg289: Let there be such trust in the Lord that they know most certainly nothing will be lacking, lest, while providing for themselves in temporal things, they provide less for others in eternal things.
56_marg290: Matthew and Luke record that the Lord told the disciples not to carry even a staff; Mark, that they should take nothing but a staff. But they actually take a staff. Mark understands by the staff the power of receiving what is necessary from those under them.
56_interl525: the power of living from the gospel.
56_marg291: Bede. That the foot be neither covered nor bare on the ground, that is, that the gospel be neither hidden, nor lean on earthly comforts.
56_interl529: lest, clothed with one, they should keep another for the future; not that we ought to be content with one tunic in icy places.
56_marg292: Bede. That is, that they walk simply, not doubly.
56_interl530: It is foreign to a preacher to run about from house to house and change the rights of hospitality.
56_marg293: Bede. Dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labour: that they entered the city, and that the preaching reached them. Or: that they received nothing for their necessary food from those who scorned the gospel.
56_marg294: having received the power and heard the commands from the Lord.
56_interl531: which is the first way of salvation.
56_marg295: Bede. James says: “Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” etc. Whence it is clear that this custom was handed down from the apostles: that the possessed and other sick are anointed with oil consecrated by a bishop.
56_interl533: because so many signs were being done.
56_marg296: Bede. Luke: “Now Herod, the tetrarch, heard of all things that were done by him; and he was in a doubt, because it was said by some, that John was risen from the dead: but by others, that Elias had appeared.” Whence it must be understood that he said it either, having been confirmed by the words of others and believing, or still hesitating: “John, whom I beheaded, he is risen again from the dead,” etc.
56_marg297: It is not lawful for a lamp to be hidden under a bushel.
56_marg298: “John the Baptist is risen again from the dead,” etc. Bede. Strange envy against the Lord: the Jews believe that John, of whom it is said that he did no sign, could have risen, with no one attesting it. Jesus, approved by signs and mighty works, at whose death the elements trembled, and whose resurrection and ascension angels, apostles, men and women have proclaimed, they preferred to believe had not risen but had been secretly carried off.
56_interl536: he thinks rightly about the resurrection: namely, that the saints will be of greater power after the resurrection.
56_interl538: not the lord of the prophets.
56_interl539: Bede. This statement is either affirmative or doubtful.
56_interl540: Jerome. He states it plainly, not by irony.
56_interl541: Bede. Tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis.
56_marg299: Bede. Ancient history relates that Philip was the son of the elder Herod and brother of Herod, under whom the Lord suffered, and that he had married Herodias, daughter of Aretas; and afterwards Aretas, quarrels having arisen, took back his daughter and joined her in marriage to Herod, enemy of Philip, to his grief. Hegesippus or Josephus, however, tell it far differently.
56_marg300: “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife,” etc. Bede. He who had come in the spirit and power of Elias rebukes Herod and Herodias, as Elias rebuked Achab and Jezabel, preferring to be in danger before the king rather than to be forgetful of God’s precept.
56_marg301: Herod and Pharaoh alone are read to have celebrated the day of their birth, and each stained the festival with blood. But Herod did so the more wickedly, by as much as he killed a holy man, teacher of the truth and herald of the heavenly King; and he was not ashamed to have the head of the slain man brought before the guests, at the wish of the dancing girl. Pharaoh killed a eunuch who had sinned. Yet by the example of both it is better and more useful for us always to fear the day of death, keeping it in mind, than to celebrate the day of birth in luxury. For man is born to labour, and the saints pass through death to rest.
56_marg302: “And he swore.” Bede. He is not excused of perjury by the oath. For perhaps he swore in order to find an occasion for killing. And if she had asked for the death of her father or mother, Herod would by no means have granted it.
56_interl545: Bede. She feared lest Herod at some time should reconsider, or become a friend to her brother.
56_interl547: a reward of blood, worthy of the dance.
56_marg303: Bede. As is the usual manner of Scripture, he is saddened, not in fact but in the opinion of many. As Joseph too is called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself, so Herod is called saddened because those at table thought it. The dissembler displayed sadness in his face, and hid joy in his mind. He excused the crime by the oath, so that under pretence of piety he might become impious.
56_marg304: He wishes them all together to be partners in his crime, so that at a luxurious banquet bloody feasts might be brought in.
56_marg305: Bede. Jerome. The head of the law, which is Christ, is cut off from its own body, that is, from the Jewish people, and is given to the girl, that is, to the Roman Church; and the girl gives it to her mother, the adulteress, that is, the Synagogue, which is to believe at the end. The body of John is buried, the head is placed on the dish, the letter is covered with earth, the spirit is honoured and received on the altar.
56_marg306: John is diminished in his head, that is, the fame by which Christ was believed by the people is shown to be lessened. Christ is exalted on the cross, because he who was believed to be only a prophet is known to be God and Lord of the prophets. Whence John himself: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” John, whom it was fitting to be diminished, was born when the days begin to decrease; Christ, who is the light of the world, when the days begin to increase.
56_marg307: Bede. Josephus relates that John was bound, led to the castle of Macheronta, and beheaded there. Church history relates it in the city of Sebaste in Palestine, formerly called Samaria. In the time of Julian, the pagans, envious of the Christians who devoutly frequented his tomb, invaded the monument and scattered his bones over the fields; then, gathering them, burned them and again scattered them over the fields. Monks from Jerusalem, however, were present; mingling with the pagans who were gathering the bones, they collected the greater part of them and carried them to Philip at Jerusalem, and he sent them to Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria; and they were afterwards kept there, until Theophilus, at the command of Theodosius, with all the temples of the nations destroyed and the temple of Serapis cleansed of filth, placed the same bones there and consecrated a basilica in honour of Saint John.
56_marg308: “And the apostles coming together unto Jesus,” etc. Jerome. “Unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return.” They always give thanks to God for what they have received.
56_marg309: All things that they had done: the apostles report to the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John suffered while they were teaching; either his own disciples or the disciples of this same John, as Matthew writes. Whence it follows: And he said
56_interl557: that you do not consent to evils.
56_marg310: Bede. Not only for the sake of rest, but mystically it signifies that Judea, having been left, which by not believing had taken the head of prophecy from itself, he was about to bestow the food of the word, as bread and a feast of fishes, in the desert of the Church, which had had no husband. For there the holy preachers, who were long pressed by grave tribulation among a Judea not believing but contradicting, obtained rest with the Gentiles brought to the faith.
56_marg311: He leads apart those whom he has chosen, so that among those living evil lives they do not take notice of evils, as Lot in Sodom, Job in the land of Hus, and Abdias in the house of Achab. And he says to them: “Rest a little,” like birds in the branches of the mustard. Brief is the rest here, long the labour for the saints; but afterwards it is said to them: “that they may rest from their labours.”
56_interl558: here a brief rest for the saints; long labour.
56_interl559: therefore it was fitting for the disciples to rest: “For there were many coming and going,” etc.
56_marg312: Jerome. In Noe’s ark the animals inside were sent out and those outside broke in. So in the Church Judas departed, a thief came in. As long as one withdraws from the faith, there is no rest for the Church without mourning: “Rachel weeping for her children,” etc. There is no feast here at which new wine is drunk, when the new song is sung in the new heaven. And on the new earth, by new men? With five loaves and two fishes five thousand men are fed in the evening of life; with twelve baskets full of fragments, gathered in the eighth power; with the twelve judging on twelve thrones, the twelve tribes of Israel, which are the fragments of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, when the remnant of Israel shall be saved; when we shall see God face to face, which we read of Christ in the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms. Whence, after the fourth watch of the night, Jesus Christ calms the swelling of the sea, walking upon it, and says: “Be of good heart: it is I”; because we shall see him as he is, then the wind and the storm will cease, Jesus sitting and reigning in the ship, which is the universal Church.
56_interl564: because the feast of these men is not yet.
56_interl565: not only the disciples but with the Lord, as Matthew says.
56_interl566: a fire that always shines is not hidden.
56_marg313: Bede. By seeking solitude he tests whether the crowds follow him in faith, and having tested them he rewards them with worthy recompense. The crowds, not with beasts or carriages but by the labour of their own feet, take up the way of the desert and show their desire for salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, teaching the unlearned, healing the sick and refreshing the fasting, he shows how much he delights in the devotion of believers.
56_marg314: Note that they did not arrive by boat at another shore of the sea or of the Jordan. But, having crossed some strait or lake, they went to nearby places of the same region, where even natives on foot could reach.
56_marg315: “And he had compassion, etc.” Bede. Matthew explains more fully how he had compassion, in this way: “And he had compassion on them, and healed their sick.” To have true compassion on the poor who have no shepherd is to open the way of truth, to cure the languid, and to refresh the fasting, encouraging them to praise heavenly bounty; the things that follow declare that he did this.
56_interl567: Evening. Whence in Luke: “And the day began to decline.”
56_marg316: The day declining, the Saviour refreshes the crowds, because either as the end of the age draws near, or when the sun of justice has set for us, we are freed from the long famine of the spirit.
56_marg317: Allegorically. Many troops of the faithful, leaving behind the walls of their former way of life and neglecting the protection of various doctrines, follow Christ as he seeks the deserts of the Gentiles; and when first “In Juda God is known,” then: “He is exalted above the heavens, and his glory above all the earth.”
56_interl568: as if it were your duty.
56_marg318: He provokes the apostles to break bread, so that, with them testifying that they have none, the greatness of the sign might become known. And by hinting that hungry hearts are to be fed daily through them, we are roused by their examples or words to love heavenly things.
56_marg319: It is to be noted that John, about to write of this miracle of the loaves, mentioned beforehand that the Passover was near. Matthew and Mark say that it was done straight after John was killed; whence it is gathered that John was beheaded as the Passover was approaching, and that the Lord was crucified at the following Passover.
56_marg320: Bede. Allegorically. The five loaves are the five books of the law of Moses, by which the knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the passing age, and the true religion of serving God were made known to the human race. The two fishes are the Psalms and the prophets, who fed the people taught in the law of God with the sweetness of the new grace, concerning the promise of the Lord’s incarnation, and in them the whole series of the Old Testament is comprised. Whence: “that all things must needs be fulfilled, which are written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.” And when he had opened their sense that they might understand the Scriptures, and hand them on faithfully to the hearers once understood, he, as it were blessing the apostolic loaves and fishes and multiplying them with the gift of inner sweetness, ordered them to be distributed to the crowds. And rightly, according to John, the “barley loaves” are said to be the food of beasts of burden, especially of country folk and servants, because when hearers are beginning, harsher and as it were coarser precepts are to be entrusted to them: “But the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God.” And so the Lord, bestowing gifts on each according to his strength and always calling them on to higher things, first feeds five thousand with five loaves, second feeds four thousand with seven loaves, third entrusted the mysteries of his flesh and blood to his disciples, and at last gives with great gift to the elect, that they may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.
56_marg321: Bede. Different reclinings: distinct orders of the churches, which make up one catholic church, by fifties and by hundreds. By fifties is the rest of the jubilee. A fifty multiplied twice makes a hundred. And so it signifies the perfection of both rests, namely of body and of mind. For he who rests from wicked deeds has rest of body, and he who rests from even perverse thoughts has rest of mind. Rightly also, those who recline on the green grass are fed with the food of God, who by the study of abstinence, trampling down the allurements of the flesh, devote their labour to hearing and fulfilling the words of God.
56_marg322: So some sit by fifties and some by hundreds, because one first rests from evil work, so that afterwards there may be rest in the mind also.
56_marg323: Since he is made flesh, he creates no new food; he preaches nothing other than what had been written, but shows that the law and the prophets are pregnant with mysteries.
56_interl575: signifies that the gaze of the mind is to be directed upward, to seek the light of knowledge
56_marg324: And he distributed to his disciples what was to be set before the crowds, because he revealed the sacraments to the holy teachers who preach these throughout the whole world.
56_interl576: who are the dispensers of the word
56_interl577: that they might lay them open
56_marg325: Bede. The more perfect diligently seek out the secret mysteries which the untrained cannot grasp. For “by twelve baskets” the apostles are signified, and “by the apostles” the teachers who follow, despised outwardly, but filled inwardly with the remnants of the saving food, heaped up to nourish the hearts of the humble. For in baskets servile work is done; but that bread of fragments filled them, which chose the weak things of the world to break or confound the strong.
56_marg326: Bede. On account of the five bodily senses. These, who followed the Lord, signify those who, still placed in secular dress, know how to make good use of the outward things they possess. Those who are rightly nourished with five loaves, because such people must still be instructed by the precepts of the law. But those who renounce the world altogether, the four thousand fed with seven loaves, that is, raised up by evangelical perfection and taught inwardly by spiritual grace.
56_interl578: because, as John immediately continues after this feeding: “They were about to come and take him, and make him king.”
56_marg327: He gives us an example, that in all the good things we do we should avoid seeking the return of human favour, lest the working of virtues bend us toward desire for temporal things. The Lord himself suggests this to us: when those who admired his virtues wanted to make him king, he fled to the mountain to pray, and readily met those who would crucify him; that is, so that we may be ready to bear adversity, wary of flatteries if they smile upon us, and, lest they soften us and deceive us if they abound, may beseech it from the Lord with frequent prayers.
56_marg328: Bede. Bethsaida is a city in Galilee of Andrew and Peter and Philip, near the lake of Genesareth. But Mark says that, the feeding being over, they came across the sea to Bethsaida. Luke says that the miracle was done in the places of Bethsaida, for he says: “And taking them, he went aside into a desert place, apart, which belongeth to Bethsaida. Which when the people knew, they followed him; and he received them,” etc., as far as that feeding. But perhaps Luke, in saying “a desert place which is Bethsaida,” meant not the neighbourhood of the city itself but the desert places pertaining to it. For Mark states plainly that they went before him to Bethsaida, where he marks the very limits of the city. But Luke does not say “into a desert place which is Bethsaida,” but “which is Bethsaide.” Perhaps he wished us to understand not the city itself but the desert place pertaining to it. John says that the crowds ate bread near Tiberias, and that the disciples, going up into the boat, came to Capharnaum across the sea; both of which are cities in Galilee near the lake of Genesareth, which is also called the lake of Tiberias, after the city of Tiberias.
56_marg329: He does not pray for himself, but obtains for me. He went up into the mountain to pray. Bede. He prays well who seeks God by praying, advancing from earthly things to higher, he ascends to the height of the loftier court. He who prays for the riches or honour of the world, or for the death of an enemy, lying low in the depths, sends base prayers to God. But the Lord prays not for himself but for me. For although the Father has put all things into the hand of the Son, the Son nevertheless, to fulfil the form of man, entreats the Father for us, who is our advocate; whence: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ.” If he is our advocate, he must intervene for our sins. So he does not entreat as one weak, but obtains as one who is loving. He can do all he wills, because he is our advocate and judge: the one is the office of mercy, the other the mark of power.
56_interl579: so the Church, in the waves of the world, heading for the shore of the heavenly homeland
56_marg330: And he alone, etc. He who seems at times to have utterly deserted the Church in its dangers. Whence: “Why, O Lord, hast thou retired afar off?” etc. But because he delays help, he does not take away support. Whence it follows: And about the fourth, etc.
56_interl580: by the look of mercy, that is, he strengthens
56_marg331: Bede. Military watches and vigils are divided by spans of hours. It is plain, then, that they laboured all night and had help when dawn was approaching, because when human frailty, beset with distresses, considers the smallness of its own strength, it sees in itself nothing but the darkness of straits and the surge of rising enemies. But when it lifts the mind to the light of the higher protection and to the gifts of everlasting reward, it suddenly sees, as it were amid the shadows of night, the rising of the morning star, which announces the approaching day, that is, Christ. For the morning star is said to light up three hours of the night, that is, the whole morning watch.
56_interl582: quelling all the dangers of the world
56_interl583: for an hour, so that the deliverance might be the more welcome
56_marg332: And he would have passed by them, etc. Bede. So that, for an hour indeed they are troubled, but at once delivered, they may marvel the more at the miracle of their deliverance and render greater thanks to their rescuer. So often the divine mercy seems in tribulation to have forsaken the faithful, as Jesus seemed to wish to pass by the disciples labouring on the sea. Whence: “Why hast thou cast me off? and why do I go sorrowful whilst the enemy afflicteth me?” But at once the Lord is present, as if he were to say: “When thou shalt pass through the waters, I will be with thee, and the rivers shall not cover thee: when thou shalt walk in the fire, thou shalt not be burnt, and the flames shall not burn in thee.” Whence it follows: And immediately he spoke with them, etc.
56_interl584: for they did not think a true body could walk upon the waters
56_marg333: Bede. Even now heretics think it was a phantasm, and that he did not take true flesh from the virgin. For Theodore, bishop of Pharan, wrote that the Lord had no bodily weight according to the flesh, but walked upon the sea without weight and without flesh. But the catholic faith teaches that he had weight according to the flesh, and that he walked upon the waters bearing bodily weight and burden, not with his feet sunk in. Whence Dionysius, in the little work On the Divine Names, says thus: We do not know in what manner, from virginal blood, he was formed by a law other than the natural one, and in what manner, not with his feet sunk in, bearing bodily weight and material burden, he walked upon the moist and unstable substance. And they cried out.
56_interl585: That is: “We shall see him as he is.”
56_marg334: The first help is to drive out fear; the second, by the power of his presence, to restrain the storm. Nor is it strange that when the Lord goes up into the boat the wind ceases, because wherever he is present in a heart by the grace of his love, at once all the wars of vices, and of the opposing world and of evil spirits, are quieted.
56_interl587: by the greatness of the miracles, not by knowledge of the godhead. And this is: For they understood not concerning the loaves, etc.
56_marg335: For they understood not concerning the loaves, etc. Bede. By the miracle of the loaves he showed that he was the maker of things. By walking on the waves he showed that his whole body was free from all the heaviness of sin. By calming the winds and waves he showed that he ruled the elements. But the disciples, still carnal, marvelled indeed at the greatness of the powers, but did not know the truth of divine majesty.
56_marg336: He was known by report, not by face; or by the greatness of his signs; he was also known to many by countenance.
56_interl590: wonderful faith! They are not content with the health of those present only; they send to those round about, so that all may run to the physician
56_marg337: Bede. The least commandment: whoever shall have broken it shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven. Or it is the taking on of flesh, through which we come to the word of God.
56_interl594: when sorrow and groaning shall flee away
56_marg338: Bede. It is plain how true is the Lord’s confession to the Father, in which he says: “Because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to the little ones.” The unlearned come, they bring the sick, that they may touch even the fringe of his garment, and so they obtain the health they desired. But the Pharisees and scribes, who ought to have been teachers of the people, ran not to hear the word, nor as to a physician, but to the wrangling of questions.
56_interl595: he states why they had come
56_marg339: Common. Jerome. Unclean or common hands signify the communion of the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the unwashed communion of the apostles: “It stretched forth its branches unto the sea.”
56_marg340: They find fault about hands not washed in body, when no uncleanness is found in their works. They themselves are washed outwardly with water; inwardly they are polluted with the bruising of conscience.
56_marg341: For the Pharisees and all the Jews, etc. Bede. Superstitious human tradition bids them wash more often before eating and the like. But the necessary doctrine of truth bids those who desire to eat “the living bread that came down from heaven” to cleanse their works often with the washing of almsdeeds and of the other fruits of justice.
56_interl601: they are baptized in vain in this way, while in the name of the Saviour they are not washed
56_marg342: They keep the baptisms of vessels in vain who neglect the filth of their hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, the correction of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.
56_marg343: Marvellous folly, that they accuse the Son of God, because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works, not of the body but of the soul, are to be washed, so that the word of God may come to be in them.
56_marg344: Jerome. The fork of reason restrains the barking of the Pharisees, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and Isaias, so that we too may be able to overcome heretics with the words of Scripture.
56_interl604: and because the heart is far away: In vain, etc.
56_interl611: you do superstitious and useless things
56_marg345: He refutes the false charge by true reasoning, as if you, for the sake of men’s tradition, despise and neglect the precepts of God. Why then do you accuse my disciples, who make light of the orders of the elders in order to keep the commandments of God?
56_interl613: not only by greeting and paying honour, but by giving; as in that: “Honour widows,” that is, give what is necessary
56_marg346: But you say, etc. Bede. The Lord, providing for the weakness, whether of age or of the want of parents, commanded that sons honour their fathers even in the necessities of this life. But the scribes and Pharisees, subverting this law so as to bring impiety in under the name of piety, taught their sons that if anyone wished to vow to God those things which are to be offered to parents, the offering to the Lord, who is the true Father, should be put first.
56_interl614: as if: he could well say
56_interl616: that I have vowed to God
56_marg348: Shall profit thee, etc. Isidore. What is sacrilege is spent on your own uses. Or interrogatively, as if: will it profit you? It ought not to. The fathers, fearing this, were brought to starvation.
56_interl620: who ought to be supported by the necessities of this life
56_interl621: as if in this you annul
56_interl626: the proud having been refuted, he calls and teaches the humble
56_marg349: Bede. Neither is a thing offered to idols unclean as food, nor as a creature of God; but the invoking of demons makes it unclean. Whence: “You cannot drink the chalice of the Lord, and the chalice of devils.”
56_marg350: The Jews boast that they are the portion of God; they call common those foods which all men use, such as oysters, hares, and such animals as do not cleave the hoof, nor chew the cud, nor are scaly among fishes.
56_interl628: or: communicate. For the Jews call what is common unclean
56_marg351: They are rebuked, because they think mystical what lies open of itself. From this we note that it is a faulty hearer who wants to understand obscure things plainly, or plainly stated things obscurely.
56_marg352: Bede. Hence some heretics slander, saying that the Lord, ignorant of natural science, thinks all foods go into the belly and are digested in the privy, whereas immediately once eaten they are poured through the limbs, veins, marrow and sinews. Whence also they say that many who suffer from a fault of the stomach, which keeps them in perpetual vomiting, at once vomit after suppers and meals, and yet are corpulent, because at the first touch the thinner food and drink is poured through the limbs. But although the most subtle humour and liquid food, when it has been cooked and digested in the veins and limbs, slips downward through hidden passages, which the Greeks call pores, and goes into the privy.
56_marg353: Some things so approach that they both change and are changed, as food itself, losing its form, is turned into our body, and we, being refreshed, are changed into strength.
56_interl635: in which is the seat of the soul
56_marg354: Bede. The seat of the soul is not in the brain, as Plato says, but in the heart, as Christ says. By this saying are refuted those who think that thoughts are sent in by the devil and not born of our own will. The devil can be the instigator and helper of evil thoughts; he cannot be their author. But if, always lying in ambush, he has kindled a slight spark of our thoughts with its own tinder, we ought not to suppose that he also searches out the secrets of the heart, but to judge from the bodily bearing and gestures what we are turning over within, so that if he sees us often gazing at a beautiful woman, he understands that we love her.
56_marg355: And rising from thence, etc. Having left behind the scribes and Pharisees, the slanderers, he withdrew into the parts of Tyre and Sidon so that he might heal the Tyrians and Sidonians.
56_marg356: Bede. Although he could not be hid, yet what he wished did not come about. But he gave an example to those to whom he gave the grace of healing the sick, that in their miracles they should shun, as far as they could, the glory of human favour, yet not cease from the holy work of virtues, since this is justly sought by the faith of good people, or necessarily compelled by the unbelief of the wicked. For this cause he entered the borders of Tyre and Sidon: to free the daughter of the Syrophenician from the devil, and by the faith of a Gentile woman to expose the faithlessness of the scribes and Pharisees.
56_marg357: Mark says the Lord was in the house when the woman came to him. Matthew says: “because she crieth after us,” by which he hints that she sent up her prayers after him as he walked. The woman therefore came to him into the house, but because Matthew says: “He answered her not a word,” he gives us to understand that both were silent and entered in silence. And so the rest are woven together, and they do not disagree in anything.
56_marg358: Allegorically. ‘Woman’ is our mother, the Roman Church. ‘Daughter’ is the demon-possessed Western barbarism, whose faith made a sheep out of a dog. It seeks the crumbs of understanding; it desires not the unbroken bread of the letter.
56_marg359: Allegorically. A Gentile woman, but coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the ‘church’ gathered from the Gentiles, who asks the Lord for her demon-possessed daughter, that is, for her peoples not yet believing, that they too may be freed from the deceits of the devil. She who, according to Matthew, came out from her borders, and according to Mark, went into the house and is said to have fallen at the Lord’s feet, so that from both it may be gathered that only those pray faithfully and rightly for the wandering who leave the old dwellings of their faithlessness and transfer themselves with pious devotion into the house of God, that is, the Church.
56_interl639: “At the hearing of the ear they have obeyed me.”
56_interl641: the cause for which the mother had come to Jesus
56_marg360: A Syrophenician, born of the Syrians and of the Phoenicians.
56_interl643: here, the faith by which she believes her daughter can be saved
56_marg361: As if to say: it will come about that you Gentiles also obtain salvation, but first the Jews, who by ancient election are called the sons of God, must be refreshed with heavenly bread, and so at last the food of life is to be given to the Gentiles.
56_marg362: Bede. A wonderful reversal. For Israel was once a son, not a dog. Because of the difference of faith the order of the names is changed: of those it is said, “Many dogs have encompassed me”; of us, “And other sheep I have, that are not of this fold.”
56_interl645: here, the patience by which she persists, though so often scorned, as Matthew says
56_interl646: here, the humility by which she compares herself not to dogs but to puppies
56_marg363: I am not worthy to receive whole foods; I am content with the leftovers of the puppies, so that I may thus come to the whole bread.
56_marg364: Allegorically. Of the crumbs, etc. The table: Scripture, whence: “Thou hast prepared a table before me,” etc. The crumbs of the children: the inner mysteries by which the hearts of the humble are refreshed, according to that: “and filleth thee with the fat of wheat.” For the puppies, converted to the faith, that is, those who were despised among the Gentiles, seek not the surface of the letter but the marrow of the spiritual senses. And this under the table of their masters, that is, while humbly submitted to the words of God, they place beneath themselves all the duties of heart and body that are to be fulfilled as written, so that they may raise themselves, by the merit of humility, to hope for the heavenly rewards in heaven promised by the Lord.
56_marg365: “And why then didst thou not give my money into the bank, where things that can be sold are set out?”
56_interl652: Jerome. Prudent and humble, she merits what she asks.
56_marg366: Bede. Hence an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, because by the faith and confession of their parents, little ones who cannot yet of themselves know or do anything good or evil are freed from the devil in baptism.
56_marg367: Jerome. Tyre, meaning ‘distress,’ signifies Judea, to which the Lord says: “The bed is straitened, it is short; thy covering cannot cover both,” so that he might transfer himself to the other nations.
56_marg368: Jerome. Sidon, ‘hunting’: our region is an untamed wild beast.
56_marg369: Of Decapolis: Decapolis is the region of ten cities beyond the Jordan to the east, over against Galilee.
56_marg370: Bede. The region of ten cities beyond the Jordan to the east. But that which is said, “came … to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis,” does not signify that he entered those borders themselves; for it is not said that he sailed across the sea, but that he came as far as the sea, and to the place which looked upon the midst of the borders of Decapolis, lying far beyond the sea.
56_marg371: Jerome. The Saviour is led by the apostles to save the Gentiles, and he teaches what he answered the young man who asked him: “Thou knowest the commandments; do these, and thou shalt live.”
56_marg372: Bede. The one who indeed opens neither his ears to hear the words of God nor his mouth to speak them. Such as these must be offered for the Lord to heal by those who have learned, through long practice, to hear and to speak the word of God, so that the right hand of grace may save those whom human frailty cannot.
56_marg373: Jerome. The human race, like one man consumed by a various plague in the first-formed man: it goes blind while it sees; becomes deaf while it hears; is wiped clean while it smells; falls mute while it speaks; becomes maimed while it raises its hand; is bent over while it is raised up; becomes dropsical while it lusts; is lame while it advances; is covered with leprosy while it is cleansed; is filled with a demon while it grasps at divinity. It dies a death while it boldly excuses itself. And they besought him, etc.: the prophets and patriarchs were longing for the Lord’s incarnation. And taking him, etc.: he who deserves to be healed is led apart from turbulent thoughts, disordered deeds and unseemly words. The fingers put into the ears are the words of the Holy Ghost, of whom it is said: “This is the finger of God,” and: “The works of thy fingers are the heavens.” He touched the tongue, etc. The spittle of the Lord’s flesh is divine wisdom, which dissolves the ignorance of the human race, so that it may say: ‘I believe in God the Father almighty,’ etc.
56_interl663: the patriarchs and prophets, desiring the Lord’s incarnation
56_interl666: from the noise of the world
56_marg374: Bede. The first way of salvation is to be led out of the crowd. The Lord leads the sick man out of the crowd when, by visiting, he enlightens a mind weakened by sins, and calls him away from the customs of his former manner of life, and urges him to follow his precepts. But he puts his fingers into the ears when, through the gifts of the Holy Ghost, he opens the ears of the heart to understand and receive the words of salvation. And because confession must follow the knowledge of the truth, there follows: And spitting, he touched his tongue, namely when he instructs the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith. For the spittle of the Lord is the savour of wisdom, which says: “I came out of the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn.” Whence, with his spittle mixed with earth, the blind man is enlightened. For the spittle which came down from the head of the Lord expresses his divine nature, which is from God. The portion of earth mixed with the spittle signifies human nature. So then, with a remedy compounded of spittle and earth, he opened the eyes of the man born blind, because he draws the human race, through the confession of both its natures, out of the innate darkness of errors. Spitting, then, upon the tongue of the mute man, that he may be able to speak, he forms with the contact of his mercy a mouth long dumb, to utter the words of wisdom.
56_interl667: that is, the words of the Spirit
56_interl669: so that he may say: “I believe in God, the Father,” etc.
56_interl671: because thence he teaches that words are for the dumb, hearing for the deaf, and healing for all the sick, and teaches the heart to be directed to the Lord
56_marg375: Jerome. He groaned: he taught us to groan, and to raise up to heaven the treasure of our heart, which by the compunction of the heart is cleansed from the frivolous joy of the flesh, as it is said: “I roared with the groaning of my heart,” etc., “Lord, all my desire is before thee,” etc. And he said to him: Ephphatha, which is, to open. “For with the heart we believe unto justice,” etc. And immediately the ears were opened, etc.: the ears are opened to hymns and canticles and psalms. The tongue is loosed to belch forth “a good word,” which neither mind nor words can restrain or forbid. Whence Paul: “but the word of God is not bound.” And he commanded them not to tell anyone, he taught that one must glory not in virtues but in the cross and in humiliation. For the more he charged them, etc.: a city placed on a mountain, seen on every side, cannot be hidden. Humility always goes before glory.
56_interl672: he taught us to groan, praying either for our own or for the sins of our people
56_interl673: he healed with one word, because he is God
56_interl674: to hymns and canticles and psalms
56_marg377: Properly, to the ears. For the ears had to be opened for hearing, and the tongue had to be loosed so that it could speak. Whence it follows: And immediately, etc.
56_interl675: that it may belch forth a good word
56_marg378: Bede. He alone speaks rightly, either by confessing the Lord or by preaching to others, whose hearing divine grace opens, so that, being cleansed, he may hear and obey the heavenly things; whose tongue the Lord instructs for speaking by the touch of wisdom, which is himself. Such a one can say: “O Lord, thou wilt open my lips,” etc.
56_interl676: because one must not glory in the high things, but in the cross and humility
56_marg379: But the more he charged them, etc. He who knows all things before they happen knew that they would preach the more. And by commanding this he wished to show the sluggish how much more zealously, how much more often, and how much more fervently they ought to preach; he bids them preach, since those who were forbidden to keep silent could not.
56_interl679: he sets down the matter of the miracle beforehand
56_marg380: Because he is true man, he has pity and suffers with the affection of human frailty. That he satisfied four thousand men with seven loaves and a few small fishes is a work of divine power, against the error of Eutyches.
56_marg381: Why they endured for three days, Matthew says thus: “And going up into a mountain, he sat there. And there came to him great multitudes, having with them the dumb, the blind, the lame, the maimed, and many others: and they cast them down at his feet, and he healed them.” The crowd waits upon the Lord for three days on account of the healing of its sick, when the elect, each shining with the faith of the holy Trinity, pray instantly to the Lord for their own sins and those of their people, that is, for the languors of the sinning soul.
56_marg382: Likewise. The great crowd waits upon the Lord for three days, when the multitude of believers, turning from their sins through penance, converts itself to the Lord in deed, in speech and in thought.
56_marg383: Mystically. By this miracle is signified that we cannot pass safely through the way of the present age unless Christ refreshes us with the food of his word. But typologically, there is a difference between this refreshment and that of the five loaves and two fishes: there the letter of the Old Testament is fully signified in its spiritual grace; here the truth and grace of the New Testament are shown to be dispensed. Both refreshments were celebrated on a mountain, as the account of the other evangelists declares, because each Scripture, rightly understood, proclaims the height of heavenly precepts and rewards, and the height of Christ, who is the mountain on the top of mountains. For he lifts up the city built upon himself, that is, the Church, to the height of good works, and makes it manifest to all. He himself refreshes with bread of heaven the one drawn away from the lowest delights, and kindles his appetite for supreme sweetness by giving the pledge of spiritual food.
56_marg384: Because converted sinners faint on the way of this present life if they are sent away, in their own conscience, without the food of teaching.
56_marg385: The Jews, taught from nearby by the law and the prophets; the Gentiles come from afar to Christ, with no teachers having forewarned them of his faith.
56_marg386: From afar. Morally. He who, having experienced no carnal corruption, hastens to the service of God, does not come from afar; nor does he who, untainted by any impurity or shameful deed, has experienced only marriage; nor is this one from afar. Others come after many shameful deeds, and therefore from afar.
56_marg387: Bede. It is a mystery of the New Testament, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is more fully believed and given. Nor are they barley loaves, like those five by which five thousand men were fed, lest, as in the law, the food of the living soul should be veiled by bodily sacraments. For the marrow of barley is covered by a very tenacious chaff.
56_marg388: Jerome. The seven loaves: ‘the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost.’ The four thousand: ‘the year of the New Testament with its four seasons.’ The seven baskets: ‘the seven first churches.’ The fragments of the loaves: ‘are the mystical understandings of the first week.’ The small fishes blessed: ‘the books of the New Testament,’ just as, rising again, he asks for a part of a roasted fish, and offers to the disciples at the catch of fishes a fish laid upon the coals.
56_marg389: Bede. In the refreshment of the five loaves the crowd reclined upon the grass, but this crowd, which is to be fed with the seven loaves, is bidden to recline upon the earth. Upon the earth they are commanded to recline, because through the law we are bidden to trample down the desire of the flesh, which is the grass: “All flesh is grass.” But in the New Testament we are bidden to leave behind even the flesh itself and temporal goods. Or, because the mountain on which Christ’s refreshment takes place signifies height, there he is refreshed above the grass, here above the earth, because there the height of Christ is governed, on account of carnal men and earthly Jerusalem, by carnal hope and desire; here, however, with all carnal cupidity removed, the firmament of enduring hope, like the very solidity of the mountain, with no grass interposed, holds the guests of the New Testament.
56_interl681: Jerome. The seven gifts of the Holy Ghost.
56_interl682: he shows how much he rejoices at our salvation, and teaches us to give thanks for the carnal and spiritual refreshment
56_interl684: because he handed on spiritual knowledge to them, and through them to others
56_interl685: the books of the New Testament
56_marg390: Bede. The saints of that time, through whom this same Scripture was composed, or whose faith, life and sufferings the Scripture itself contains, who, snatched from the waves of the age and consecrated by divine blessing, have furnished us with refreshment, lest we faint in the course of this world, by the example of their life and of their death.
56_marg391: Bede. There are many who, though they have left all their possessions and cannot fulfil the higher things of this world, yet, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, are satisfied when, hearing the commandments of God, they come to eternal life.
56_interl687: “The poor shall eat, and shall be filled.”
56_marg392: Bede. The higher precepts, or exhortations and counsels, which the general multitude of the faithful cannot attain: as here, “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all that thou hast,” etc.
56_marg393: Seven baskets: “filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost.” For baskets are made of rush and the leaves of palms. The rush grows over the waters; the palm crowns the victor. The saints too, lest they dry up from the moisture of eternity, place themselves in the very fountain of life, and await the palm of eternal reward.
56_interl692: so that in that very number they may be taught that they have been fed by the precepts of the Gospel.
56_marg394: In place of this, Matthew has: “he went up into a boat, and came into the coasts of Magedan.” But there is no doubt that it is the same place under either name; for most copies have Magedan, also in Mark.
56_marg396: As if what they had seen were not signs. But what they were asking for is defined: a sign from heaven, or, after the manner of Elias, fire from on high; or, like Samuel, thunder roaring in summer time, or lightning or rain, as if they could not also calumniate these things, who calumniated what they had seen with their eyes, touched with their hands, and felt in its usefulness. Whence John says that the crowds, after the meal of loaves, asked: “What dost thou work? Our fathers did eat manna in the desert,” etc.

56_marg397: Augustine. On the Harmony of the Gospels. He declares that it is written thus in Mark: and a sign shall not be given it.
56_marg398: “To this generation”: that is, to those who tempt God and gainsay his words, no sign from heaven will be given, which they seek by tempting him, although to them he gave many heavenly signs on earth. But to the generation of those who seek the Lord, he showed a sign from heaven, when, the apostles looking on, he ascended into heaven and sent the Spirit; and at the laying on of the apostles’ hands he poured the grace of the Holy Ghost from heaven upon many believers.
56_marg399: Bede. With the seven baskets just filled, they at once went up into the boat and came to the coasts of Magedan; and there, as they sailed, it was said to them that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. But Scripture says that they forgot to take bread, by which it is shown how little care for the flesh they had, being intent on the presence of the Lord.
56_interl700: Mystically. Christ, the bread of life, by whom those who are refreshed care less, out of love, for earthly bread.
56_interl701: that is, to put the law of God after the traditions of men; to preach with words and to fight with deeds; to tempt the Lord; not to believe his teaching or his works.
