For if the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod signifies perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, why would the food by which the people of God was nourished not signify true and entire doctrine?
56_interl709: Jerome. House of the valley, that is, the world, which is a valley of tears.
56_interl710: Who does not see what was, what is, and what will be.

56_interl715: so that they may see the will of the Lord through the breath of the Holy Ghost.
56_marg401: And spitting upon his eyes, etc. Bede. The spittle comes from within, from the head of the Lord; the hands are the members of the body, placed outside. So, spitting into the blind man’s eyes, he lays on his hands so that he may see, because by the invisible gifts of divine mercy and by the sacraments shown outwardly of the humanity he assumed, he wiped away the blindness of the human race.
56_marg402: Whom with one word he could have healed all at once, he heals little by little, so as to show the greatness of human blindness, and that it returns to the light scarcely and, as it were, by degrees; and he shows us his grace, by which he helps each single increment of perfection.
56_interl717: of majesty; for the Creator is known from the greatness of the creature.
56_marg403: Jerome. He judges himself unworthy, esteeming all others above himself, as David did, who called himself not a man but “a dead dog and one flea.”
56_marg404: At first he sees men as it were trees, walking; that is, the shape of their bodies, so that it is not easy to tell whether it is a man or a tree. For the first progress in virtue is to look into the strength, the life, and the customs of others: to imitate the good and to beware of the evil. But because he has been out of his wits through long darkness, and cannot yet tell between good and evil, faith and faithlessness, sincerity and pretence, he sees men walking like trees, because he sees their deeds without the light of discernment. To him the Lord, by a second laying on of hands, restored the light of seeing all things clearly: namely, what is to be believed, how to live, and what rewards are to be hoped for.
56_marg405: Then again, etc. Jerome. That he might see all things clearly, that is, through visible works understand invisible things, and “which eye hath not seen”; and that he might contemplate with the eye of a clean heart the clear state of his soul after the rust of sin: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.”
56_marg406: Jerome. That he might see within himself what he had not seen before; for a man in despair about salvation does not think he can do at all what, enlightened by hope, he is able to accomplish.
56_marg407: Mystically. The Lord admonishes all who are enlightened by knowledge of the truth to return to the heart, to weigh with an anxious mind how much had been given to them, and to answer the benefits of God with fitting works.
56_marg408: That is: proclaim the blindness of your heart, not the power. Whence Paul: “I was a blasphemer, and I persecuted the Church of God.”
56_marg409: Tell no one, etc. Bede. That he commands the healing to be kept silent is an example to his own: that, if they do wonderful things, they should not seek favour, but be content to please the divine gaze.
56_marg410: Philip, brother of Herod, tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, in honour of Tiberius Caesar named Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Paneas, imitating his father Herod, who in honour of Caesar Augustus named Caesarea, which was formerly called the Tower of Straton. Caesarea Philippi is where the Jordan rises at the roots of Lebanon, and it has two springs, one Ior and the other Dan, which, mixed together, make up the name of the Jordan.
56_interl720: nor does he cease to teach as he goes.
56_marg411: Whom do men say that I am, etc. Beautifully, he first asks the opinion of men, so that their confession may appear to be founded not on popular opinion but on recognition of the truth, lest they be thought to hesitate, as Herod did, about what they had heard. Whence he says to Peter, according to Matthew: “because flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee,” that is, the teaching of men.
56_marg412: Beautifully, those who give differing opinions of the Lord in the manner of men are called men. For those who with a devout mind know the truth of his power deserve to be called not men but gods. Whence he says to them: “But whom do you say that I am?” As if to say: those men, thinking human thoughts; but you, gods, whom do you say that I am?
56_interl721: not thinking him to be the Lord of the prophets.
56_interl723: Bede. One for all. For they all knew the same thing.
56_marg413: Thou art the Christ, etc. Bede. He embraces everything who expresses both nature and name, in which lies the sum of virtues. Paul says: “For I judged not myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Peter thought nothing more was to be confessed than the Son of God. We probe, by the contemplation of human weakness, when and how he was born and how great he is. The end of my faith is therefore Christ; the end of my faith is the Son of God. It is not permitted me to know the line of his generation. Yet it is not permitted me to be ignorant of the faith of his generation.
56_marg414: Bede. He did not will himself to be preached before his passion and resurrection, because, when the sacrament of blood was completed, he said to the apostles, more fittingly: “Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” For it would not profit to proclaim publicly him whom they were to see scourged and crucified, and who was to suffer much.
56_interl724: that he is the Son of God.
56_interl725: he forewarns them, lest they fail in the passion.
56_interl726: the reason why they should not say it.
56_interl727: Note that he calls him whom it behoves to suffer so much the Son of man, because the passion was in Christ’s flesh; the divinity remained impassible.
56_marg415: That the Son of man must suffer many things, etc. Jerome. As a skilled helmsman, foreseeing the storm in calm, wants his sailors to be ready. As elsewhere: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself.”
56_interl728: he strengthens them with the hope of resurrection.
56_marg416: Bede. Speaking out of loving affection: “Lord, be it far from thee.” Or, as is better in the Greek: “Be merciful, Lord; this shall not be.” That is, it cannot happen, nor do my ears admit that the Son of God should be killed.
56_marg417: And Peter taking him, etc. Because he loves the Lord too much; and because in confessing he said, Thou art the Christ, he heard his reward according to Matthew: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona,” etc. He does not want his confession destroyed, nor does he think it possible that the Son of God should be killed; so he seizes him out of affection, or leads him aside, lest, with the others present, he seem to rebuke the master.
56_interl733: an adversary or opponent, because you speak things contrary to my will.
56_marg418: Bede. Many think that it was not Peter but the adversary spirit who was rebuked, at whose prompting the Apostle said this. But to me the apostle’s error, coming from a devout affection, was never an incentive.
56_marg419: To the devil it is said: “Go behind me, Satan.” To Peter: “Go behind me,” that is, follow my judgment.
56_interl734: that I may die for the salvation of men.
56_marg420: Things that are of God, etc. It is my will and the Father’s that I die for the salvation of men. You do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth and bring forth much fruit.
56_interl735: He had before spoken the higher mysteries only to the disciples.
56_marg421: If any man will, etc. Bede. Having shown the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he exhorts all to imitate the example of his passion, and promises salvation of souls to all. But to the more perfect he revealed how much he was to suffer and that he was to rise from the dead, giving a rule for preaching, so that each may be instructed in his own way, and higher things are not entrusted to the weak.
56_marg422: He cannot grasp what lies beyond him, if he does not know how to slay what he is. Unless a man fails in himself, he does not draw near to God, who is above himself.
56_interl737: let him strip off the old man and put on the new. Whence Paul: “I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me.”
56_marg423: Either by abstinence, mortifying the body, or by compassion of soul. Of the body Paul says: “But I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection,” etc. Of compassion of soul, the same: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”
56_interl739: as if it were said to the farmer: “If you keep the grain, you lose it.”
56_marg424: Bede. It signifies two times of the Church: one of persecution, when the soul is to be laid down; the other of peace, when earthly desires are to be broken. Whence follows: “For what shall it profit a man,” etc.
56_interl740: If you sow it, you renew it.
56_interl741: as if the soul is to be lost in adversity; but in peace the heart is to be fortified with all watchfulness in time of peace, because it is permitted to live, and permitted to seek advantage.
56_interl742: in heart, in mouth, in deed.
56_marg425: Because many overcome avarice and despise passing things, but, hindered by shame, do not express the uprightness of faith which they have; so he adds, in words: “For he that shall be ashamed of me,” etc.
56_marg426: Amen, I say to you, etc. Bede. Since he was speaking of the life to come, it was necessary that he should promise this about the present life, so that the disciples, still unlearned, might be strengthened by this comfort; as is said of the Jewish people: “And he gave them the lands of the Gentiles: and they possessed the labours of the people: That they might observe his justifications, and seek after his law.”
56_interl745: those who for a time are to dwell in eternal life.
56_marg427: The kingdom of God, etc. That is, the Church, raised up against the glory of this world. Or the future blessedness in heaven, which they saw on the mountain. This was done by pious providence, so that eternal joy, though tasted beforehand for a brief moment, might more strongly encourage them to bear adversity.
56_marg428: And after six days, etc. Jerome. After the threat of the cross, the glory of the resurrection is shown. Whence follows: “And after six days,” etc., so that they should not fear the reproaches of the cross, who with their own eyes had seen the glory of the future resurrection.
56_marg429: And after six days. Luke: “And it came to pass about eight days after these words,” etc. On the eighth day he displays the glory of the resurrection, so that, having shown the sweetness of the heavenly life, he may refresh the hearts of all who can hear this, and by the number eight teach that the joy of the true time of resurrection is to come. For he himself rose from the dead after the sixth day of the sabbath, on which he ascended the cross, and the seventh, on which he rested in the tomb; and we, after the six ages of this world in which we rejoice to suffer for the Lord, and after the seventh age of souls, which meanwhile is passing in the other life, shall rise in the eighth age. But that Matthew and Mark say the Lord was transfigured after six days, they differ neither in time nor in mystery, for they count only the days in between. Whence they also say, absolutely, that it happened after six days. Here Luke adds both the first day on which the Lord promised this and the last on which he fulfilled it, and therefore says more cautiously: “about eight days.” And mystically: they signify that after the six ages of the world the saints are to rest from all labour; but here, in the eighth time, it is signified that they are to rise. Whence the sixth Psalm is inscribed for the eighth: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation,” etc., because through the six ages in which it is lawful to labour, we must persevere in prayers, lest in the eighth time of retribution we be rebuked by the angry judge.
56_interl749: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”
56_marg430: Bede. “Went up into a mountain to pray,” according to Luke. About to pray on the mountain, and so to be transfigured, he ascended, teaching those who look for the fruit of the resurrection, and who desire to see the King in his beauty, to keep the mind on high and to persevere in continual prayers. He takes with him only three disciples, either because “many are called, but few are chosen,” or because those who have kept the faith of the holy Trinity with an uncorrupted mind will then deserve to rejoice in his eternal vision.
56_interl750: he did not lose the true substance of flesh.
56_interl751: he showed the glory of the resurrection.
56_marg431: Bede. He did not lose the true substance of flesh, but showed the glory of his future resurrection, or ours. Such he will appear after judgment to all the elect. In judgment, in the form of a servant, to both good and bad, so that the impious may be able to recognize as judge the one whom they despised, whom the Jews denied, whom the soldiers crucified, whom Pilate and Herod judged.
56_marg432: The garments of the Lord are the saints. Whence: “For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.” These, while the Lord remained in the world, were seen as despised; but when he sought the mountain they shine with new whiteness: “Now we are the sons of God; and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, that, when he shall appear, we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is.” Whence it is added: “so as no fuller upon earth can make white.”
56_interl753: Of which: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity.”
56_interl754: cannot on earth give to his faithful the brightness which he keeps for them in heaven.
56_marg433: And there appeared to them, etc. Moses, holy, dead; Elias, taken up alive into heaven; seen in majesty with the Lord, as Luke says, signify the future glory of all the saints in him, who at the time of judgment will be found either living in the flesh or dead.
56_marg434: Bede. The lawgiver and the outstanding one of the prophets appear. They speak with the Lord in living flesh, showing him to be the one whom the law and the prophets promised. Not in the lowest places but on the mountain with him, because those who pass beyond earthly desires in mind see the majesty of holy Scripture unveiled, which is fulfilled in the Lord.
56_marg435: Rabbi, etc. Although astonished, he nonetheless shows the affection implanted in him, forgetting that the saints are promised a kingdom not on earth but in heaven, and that he and his fellow apostles, clothed in mortal flesh, cannot undergo the state of immortal life, and that a house made by hands is not necessary. He also desires to make three tabernacles for the law, the prophets and the gospel, though they cannot be separated, having one tabernacle, that is, the Church of God.
56_marg436: Much better, then, to be among the choirs of the saints and enjoy the vision of the Godhead, if the transfigured humanity of Christ and the fellowship of the two delight us so much, shown for a moment.
56_interl756: although astonished, he nevertheless shows the affection implanted in him
56_marg437: Whence, because he sought a material tabernacle, he received the shade of a cloud, so that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the covering of houses but by the Holy Ghost.
56_interl758: of the Father, answering for the Son
56_interl759: Moses and Elias are servants: a tabernacle is to be made for this one, and he is to be served, not they
56_marg438: As if saying: this is truly the one whom Moses promised you; listen to him, and bid all to listen. Note that as at the baptism, so on the mountain the mystery of the Trinity is declared, because the glory of him which we believers confess in baptism we shall praise together, seeing it in the resurrection. Here the Spirit is in a bright cloud, there in a dove, because whoever keeps with a simple heart the faith he has received will then contemplate by the light of open vision what he had believed, and will himself be illumined by grace and protected for ever.
56_interl760: and Moses: as you would hear myself
56_interl761: where the Son began to be pointed out, at once the servants departed, lest the voice be thought to have been made to them; and immediately looking around
56_marg439: Bede. When the voice came over the Son of man, he was found alone, because when he shall have revealed himself to the elect, “God shall be all in all,” rather he himself, one with his own in all things, Christ, that is, the head with the body, will shine forth. Whence: “No man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.”
56_marg440: He does not want the glory of the future kingdom and the triumph which he had shown on the mountain to be proclaimed publicly, lest it be incredible because of its greatness, and lest the cross that followed, after so great a glory, cause a scandal among simple minds.
56_marg441: Jerome. That is, when death has been swallowed up in victory, “the former things shall not be in remembrance,” when the Lord has taken away the filth of the daughter of Sion, wiping away every tear from the eyes of the saints.
56_interl765: as if: if you have already appeared in glory; Why then
56_interl766: Why then do they say: The scribes hand down, according to Malachi, that Elias comes before the coming of the Saviour, and will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, and will restore all things to their former state. The disciples therefore think this is the glory of the coming which they saw on the mountain, and they say: If you have now come in glory, why does your forerunner not appear? Especially because they see that Elias has departed.
56_interl767: the second coming is not so, unless he goes before
56_interl768: as if: this is not the coming you think, which Elias will precede: for when Elias has come, etc.
56_marg442: He shall restore all things, etc., namely, “he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers.” For he will restore to death what he owes, and what he took away by living long. Whence he adds: And as it is written, as if saying: as the prophets wrote in many ways about the passion of Christ, so Elias too is to suffer much. He will therefore restore all things: first the hearts of men of that time to believe in Christ and resist Antichrist; then he will lay down his soul for Christ.
56_interl770: as if: Elias himself is to come in body, but also he “has come in the spirit and power,” that is, John
56_marg443: Jerome. There is no rest under the sun; envy always strikes down the little ones; lightnings strike the great mountains. Some come to the Church learning with faith, others envying with pride.
56_marg444: Bede. The evangelist does not say what they were questioning about. But it can be understood that the question arose about this: why could the disciples not free the demoniac who was in their midst? For this can be gathered from what follows: And he asked them, etc.
56_marg445: Bede. Note that the places fit the events. On the mountain he prays, is transfigured, opens to the disciples the secrets of his majesty; nay, he is received by the crowd and beaten by the weeping of the wretched. Above, he unlocks to the disciples the mysteries of the kingdom; below, he reproaches the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he reveals the voice of the Father to those who could hear; below, he drives out evil spirits. Thus, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease to lead some up and to let others come down.
56_interl774: the unlearned, not the wise scribes
56_marg446: Jerome. He knows, and asks, so that confession may bring salvation, and the murmur of our heart is first loosed in words, as it is said: “Tell thou first thy iniquities, that thou mayst be justified.”
56_interl778: by beseeching, through complaint, he sets out the troubles of the son
56_interl779: Jerome. Allegorically, the foolishness of sinners foams
56_marg447: He secretly shifts the blame onto the disciples, since often a cure is hindered not by the fault of the healers but of those to be healed.
56_interl782: as if your unbelief hinders salvation
56_marg448: He is not angry with the man but with the fault. He says this not from a feeling of weariness, but as a doctor speaks to a patient acting against orders. And through one man he rebukes the Jews for unbelief.
56_interl783: the boy, not the demon, so that he shows him delivered to the demon on account of his own sin or his parents’
56_marg449: Because while we wish to turn to the Lord after sin, we are attacked all the more by the devil, so that he either shakes our strength or avenges his expulsion.
56_marg450: He asked not as one ignorant, but so that the length of the sickness, being shown, may make the cure more welcome.
56_interl784: Morally: of anger or of lust
56_marg451: Jerome. It signifies the Gentile people, in whom the worship of idols grew from birth, so that they foolishly sacrificed their sons to demons. Whence it follows: “And oftentimes hath he cast him into the fire and into waters.” For some worshipped fire, others water.
56_interl787: which are asked in the name of Jesus
56_interl788: or without the prefix in-: credulity
56_marg452: Jerome. Our belief, like a beaked tongue, is weak unless it leans on the help of God. Faith with tears takes up the desired vows, as it is said: “According to your faith be it done unto you.”
56_interl789: a threat is an exercise of power
56_marg453: He charges to the spirit what it does to the man: while he heard, he could not speak, which the penitent sinner hears and speaks: “Go out of him, and enter not any more into him,” etc. A spirit going out of a man never returns if the man has locked his heart with the key of humility and held the door with the bolt of defence; whence: “Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a place of strength: that thou mayst make me safe.”
56_interl790: for whom to command is to do
56_marg454: Jerome. The devil tears apart those who draw near to salvation, which is his favourite food, whom he wants to drag into his belly through terrors and losses, as with Job.
56_marg455: Isidore. Rabanus. etc. For to the healed it is said: “For you are dead; and your life is hid with Christ in God.” Whence the sickness of Christians is not death, but a likeness of death.
56_marg456: Jerome. Foolishness pertains to the lust of the flesh and is healed by fasting. Anger and sloth are driven away by prayer. The remedy proper to each wound must be applied to it. What heals the eye does not heal the heel: bodily passions are healed by fasting, the plagues of the mind by prayer.
56_marg457: He mingles sad things with happy ones, so that when they come, minds are not carried away unprepared. If it saddens them that he is to be killed, it ought to gladden them that he is to rise on the third day.
56_marg458: Not so much from dullness of mind as from love: because they had known him as the true God, they could not believe he would die. And because he was accustomed to speak to them in figures, shrinking from his death, they thought he spoke figuratively in these words too.
56_marg459: Jerome. A village of consolation. It fits the sentence just stated: “Killed, he will rise on the third day.” A grain of wheat dies that it may be gathered back more abundantly. “Unless the grain of wheat die, itself remaineth alone.”
56_marg460: Jerome. On the way they were discussing leadership; a similar discussion fits the place. For leadership enters by force, so it is abandoned; and while it is held it slips away, and it is uncertain at what stage, that is, on what day, it will end. Whence he says: “If any man desire to be first, etc.”
56_marg461: Bede. From this the dispute seems to have arisen, because they had seen Peter and James and John led apart up the mountain, and believed some secret was there; and also because to Peter, as Matthew says, the keys of the kingdom of heaven were promised, and the Church was to be built upon the rock of faith, from which he received his name. They therefore thought that either those three were preferred to the rest, or Peter was preferred to all.
56_marg462: Going along, they were disputing about leadership, and he, sitting down, teaches humility. For princes labour; the humble rest.
56_marg463: He wishes to heal the desire for glory by humility, and first he admonishes with a simple command, then with the example of childlike innocence.

Therefore he does not deny that he himself is good, but signifies that he is God. Nor does he testify that he is not a good master, but that without God no good exists at all.

56_marg514: Bede. On this occasion some teach the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the just, when all that we have left for God is to be repaid to us with manifold interest, and eternal life besides. They do not see how foolish they are, at least about the hundred wives according to the other evangelists, especially since the Lord says: neither do they marry, nor are they given in marriage; and that those things are to be repaid in this time with persecutions, which after the resurrection will be none at all for the just. Whence: “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul”; and “all things were common unto them.” Otherwise. The hundred, moved from the left hand to the right, although in the bending of the fingers it seems to keep the same meaning or figure as the ten in the left hand, yet surpasses it in magnitude of quantity; because all who for the sake of the kingdom of God despise temporal things, even in this life, which is full of persecutions, taste beforehand with sure faith the joy of the kingdom; and in expectation of the heavenly country, which is signified by the right hand, they enjoy, in most true love, all the elect alike.

56_marg528: Jerome. Jericho is the moon, or a curse, which fits one drawing near to the passion. The failing of Christ’s flesh is the preparation of the heavenly Jerusalem. Whence, leaving Jericho, they draw near to Jerusalem, that is, to the vision of peace.
56_marg529: Bede. Because, with the Lord ascending to heaven and all the faithful following, that is the elect who from the beginning of the world entered the heavenly kingdom with him, the people of the nations, long blind in unbelief, on hearing of Christ’s coming, began to hope for the light of salvation. Sitting by the way he begs, because not yet recognising the road of truth, he strives by diligent inquiry of desire to come to it, as Cornelius, who prayed with frequent prayers to the God he worshipped, that he would deign to enlighten him. Passing by, he hears; standing still, he enlightens, because by his humanity, in which he was born, suffered, rose and ascended, he shows mercy, which is a temporal and transitory action. And standing, he enlightens the blind man, because the eternity of the Word does not pass, and remaining in itself renews all things. To stand is God’s, to arrange all changeable things by an unchangeable disposition. Why then does he hear while passing and enlighten while standing? Because he who for our sake endured temporal things gives us light from the very place where he does not know how to have the passing of change.
56_marg530: Matthew in this place says that two blind men sitting by the way were enlightened. Luke, when he drew near to Jericho, has one enlightened in like manner. But Luke writes what Matthew omitted. As for Matthew here saying two, Mark says one and does not deny the other. It must be understood that one of them was very well known, whence Mark records his name and his father’s name, which he does not do elsewhere except when he names Jairus, because that man too was noble. So this one, cast down from some former prosperity, was of most notorious and famous misery. He sat there not only blind but also a beggar. Mark therefore describes this one’s enlightenment, because by this miracle he gained greater fame.
56_marg531: Therefore, drawing near to Jericho, he enlightened one blind man, because coming in the flesh and nearing his passion he did not bring many to faith. For not at first, but a few years before he suffered, did he show the light of the word. But setting out from Jericho he enlightened two blind men, because rising from the dead and ascending into heaven he sent the Holy Ghost to the apostles, and scattered them into the world for the enlightenment of all peoples.
56_marg532: Typologically. He enlightens one, drawing near to Jericho, because before his passion he preached to one people only, the Jews. And setting out from Jericho, two, because after the resurrection through the apostles he preached to both Jews and Gentiles, and revealed the secrets of his eternal divinity and assumed humanity. Mark writes of one because he looks to the Gentiles to whom he was writing, who were wholly alien from the light, whose blindness is the more famous, the more gracious the enlightenment. Matthew two, because he was writing the gospel for believing Hebrews, which was also to come to the knowledge of the Gentiles, so that he might teach that one grace of faith pertains to both alike. Hence also Matthew reports the she-ass and the colt; the others, three, who write for converted Gentiles, say that only the ass was led to the Lord.
56_marg533: The blind whom the Lord enlightened are men ignorant of the light above, which is Christ; yet by his bestowal they are pricked to confess their blindness and to seek the light of truth. Jericho is the moon, which signifies the failing of our changeableness. Whence: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” etc.
56_marg534: Jerome. The blindness of the Jews, which will be enlightened at the end, at the coming of Elias and Henoch.
56_marg535: Who when he had heard, etc. The people of the nations, having heard the report of Christ, sought to become partakers of him. Many objected, first the Jews and afterwards also the Gentiles, lest the world, which was to be enlightened and healed, should call upon Christ; yet the fury of the opponents could not hinder those predestined to eternal life.
56_marg536: Jerome. Through the merits of the patriarchs the Jewish people is enlightened; God is present to them, merciful and compassionate, enlightening the blind and raising up those who are crushed.
56_marg537: As the war grows heavier, the hands of the vices must be lifted with a cry to the stone of help, that is, to Jesus.
56_marg538: A fitting order of salvation. We hear first; then we cry out through faith; we are called through the apostles; we rise through penance; we are stripped through baptism; we are asked through the will. Whence he who has cast off his garment is said to leap up, naked of the old man, like a young hart leaping over the mountains, putting aside sloth, looking to the patriarchs and prophets, and to the apostles on the heights.
56_marg539: And they call the blind man, etc. Bede. Allegorically. The Lord calls the blind man crying out, while through holy preachers he entrusts the word of faith to the people of the nations who desire the knowledge of truth. They, calling the blind man, bid him be of good courage and rise, and come to him, since by preaching they bid him have hope of salvation, rise from the torpor of vices, and gird himself for the pursuit of virtues by which he may deserve to be enlightened, as if: “Come ye to him and be enlightened,” and: “Rise, thou that sleepest,” etc. He who has cast off his garment, that is, the cares of the world cast aside, hastens with the step of his mind unhindered to the giver of light.

56_marg611: A barren woman, who dies last of the seven brothers and leaves no seed, signifies the Synagogue, left as if dead by the sevenfold Spirit, who filled the seven patriarchs, who did not leave to her the seed of Abraham, which is Christ. For though born to the Jews, he was given to the Gentiles. This woman, dead to Christ, will be joined to none of the seven in the resurrection. For the universality of the perfect is signified by the number seven. As is said in turn through Isaias: “And seven women shall take hold of one man.” The seven are the Churches, which the one Lord loves, reproves and chastises, for they adore in one faith. Here are the seven baskets full of fragments of loaves. The loaves are “the words of the Holy Ghost,” the baskets “the Church.” Jesus, blessing, broke the loaves, and his disciples divided them to the crowds; when on the seventh day he blessed his works, resting in them. Whence: light, made on the first day, is of wisdom; the firmament on the second, of understanding; the dry land on the third, of counsel; the lights on the fourth, the virtues; the flying things and fishes on the fifth, of knowledge; the animals and living soul on the sixth, that is, man made to the image of God, is of piety; on the seventh day, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, who abides holy for ever and ever and fills the earth. The holy Church is filled, having no spot or wrinkle. Therefore the Church is filled with the sevenfold, that is, perfect, fear, because scarcely will the just man be saved who prays: “Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord, for in thy sight no man living shall be justified.” David recalls these seven qualities of the spirit: what our negligence has brought forth, what our diligence has sought, what divine providence has bestowed, what the enemy’s instigation has defrauded, what slippery forgetfulness has withdrawn, what human frailty has brought in, what improvident ignorance has deceived. We find all these affections in the psalms. The first: “He hath conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity.” The second: “I prevented the dawning of the day, and cried.” The third: “The uncertain and the hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me.” The fourth is: “My enemies have surrounded my soul.” The fifth: “I am forgotten as one dead from the heart.” The sixth: “For my loins are filled with illusions.” The seventh: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember, O Lord.” These affections the sevenfold Spirit weakens or eliminates and illumines. Whence seven lamps, burning from the south, illumine the northern darkness in the tabernacle of the Lord. The Spirit of wisdom drives negligence out of the sluggard. The Spirit of understanding reasonably seeks diligence. The Spirit of counsel prudently finds divine providence. The Spirit of virtue strongly beats back instigations. The Spirit of knowledge does not allow slippery forgetfulness to last long. The Spirit of piety mercifully indulges human frailty. The Spirit of fear ardently and thoroughly consumes improvident ignorance and fills well. Wisdom builds the house. Understanding finds the rudders. Counsel makes good things discreet. Virtue possesses the soul in patience. Through knowledge the riches of faith and the gifts of salvation are acquired. By piety the prosperity of present and future life consists; by fear humility is kept and every sin is expelled, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
