56_interl1056: The former name remains, so that the power of the healer may appear. For he had been a leper, but was cured by the Lord.
56_marg683: Jerome. Simon the leper signifies the world, first unbelieving and afterwards faithful.
56_marg684: And he was at meat, etc. Jerome. He himself reclining, that is, humbling himself, so that the faith of the sinful woman might touch him, which goes up from his feet to his head, descends from the head through faith, that is, from Christ to his members.
56_interl1057: Jerome. The Church, having faith, which says: “My spikenard sent forth the odour thereof.”
56_marg685: Bede. Mary Magdalen, sister of Lazarus whom the Lord raised. John says this happened six days before the Pasch, the day before he came to Jerusalem sitting on an ass. For she is the very one, not another, who once, still a sinner, as Luke writes, watered the feet of the Lord and anointed them with ointment; now justified and made familiar. She poured it not only on the feet, as John says, but also on the head, as Matthew and Mark report, with holy oil.
56_marg686: An alabaster box, etc. Alabaster is white marble, spotted with various drops, which keeps ointments uncorrupted.
56_marg687: Nard: an aromatic shrub, which, they say, is fragrant in smell and has a thick root and a small, dense leaf, whose tops spread out into ears.
56_marg688: Pistic nard is called mixed, because it was made up not only of the root but of the ears and the leaves, and is precious.
56_marg689: Jerome. The house filled with the odour is heaven and earth. The broken alabaster is carnal desire, which is broken at the head, from which the whole body is fastened together.
56_marg690: Mystically. The devotion of Mary designates the faith and piety of the Church, which says: “While the king was at his repose, my spikenard sent forth the odour of sweetness.” This she fulfilled literally with Mary’s hands, and daily spiritually in her members never ceases to fulfil, boasting in the whole world and saying: “Now thanks be to God, who always maketh us to triumph in Christ Jesus, and manifesteth the odour of his knowledge by us in every place. For we are the good odour of Christ unto God.” When with fitting reverence she confesses the power of his divinity, which is one with the Father, she praises and preaches it. She pours precious ointment on his head when she receives his humanity with fitting reverence. She pours pistic ointment, that is, faithful and true, on his feet, because that nature of his by which he deigned to touch the earth, that is, to be kept among men, she venerates with pious preaching and devout services.
56_interl1060: Jerome. By synecdoche one is said for many, and many for one.
56_marg691: Bede. By synecdoche he put the plural for the singular. John says that Judas said this: “because he was a thief, and having the purse, carried the things that were put therein.” Perhaps also the other disciples either felt this, or said it, or were persuaded by Judas saying it, and Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all in words. But Judas, because he was a thief; and the others, out of care for the poor. John, however, wished to mention him alone, whose habit of stealing for this reason he took care to make known.
56_marg692: Jerome. The lost one found perdition out of salvation, so that on the fruitful fig tree he might obtain the noose of death.
56_marg693: For this ointment might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, etc. Jerome. He speaks a mystery of faith under the pretext of avarice. For our faith is bought for three hundred pence, that is, the ten senses tripled through body and soul and spirit; so that we too, taking up the number of three hundred men like Gedeon, may destroy the camps of the Philistines, poor in spirit, with our broken jars, with trumpets and lamps; and, like Abraham with three hundred men, divide the spoils at evening.
56_interl1061: Bede. This is said of Judas alone, by synecdoche.
56_marg694: Jerome. He who believes in God is reckoned to him as a work of justice. For it is one thing to believe him, another to believe in him, that is, to cast oneself wholly into him.
56_marg695: Bede. Joined to us in bodily presence and familiarity, as now. Whence the Apostle: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh; but now we know him so no longer.” Spiritually, however, he is always with us. Whence: “Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.”
56_marg696: Jerome. It is to be understood thus: “But me you will not always have” in bodily presence, as before, in fellowship and familiarity. Whence also through the Apostle: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh; but now we know him so no longer.”
56_interl1062: Jerome. Let us not seek elsewhere what we have in ourselves.
56_marg697: What you think is the waste of the ointment is the office of burial. Nor is it strange if she gave me the good odour of faith, since I am about to shed my blood for her.
56_interl1063: that is, before one came who would exclude her.
56_interl1064: Not invited, not compelled, he also set the price in the will of the buyers, as of a worthless slave: “What will you give me” etc.
56_marg698: Bede. Note in Christ the knowledge of things to come. About to suffer after a few days, he foresees that his gospel is to be preached throughout the whole world.
56_marg699: It is to be noted that just as Mary, throughout the whole world where the Church is spread, earned glory from the devoted service she offered the Lord, so Judas, who spoke against her, is infamous far and wide for his treachery. But the Lord rewards the good with pious praise, and is silent about the future insults of the impious.
56_interl1065: Remigius. He wishes to make up for the loss of the poured-out ointment with the master’s price.
56_marg700: One of the twelve, etc. Jerome. One in number, not in merit; in name, not in divinity; in body, not in soul. Whence the bridegroom to the bride: “Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, with one of thy eyes, and with one hair of thy neck.” The eye and the hair are wisdom and virtue, since of Judas with the rest it is said: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God,” and: “I have given you power to tread,” etc.
56_marg701: He went to the chief priests, and after he went out, Satan entered into him. Here night indicates knowledge to night. Each animal is joined to its like. Mary runs to the apostles, that day may utter speech to day; Judas to the Jews, that night may show knowledge to night.
56_interl1066: They lost life rather than money; he receives it when he loses life.
56_interl1067: The opportunity for deceit is never found; for it is pointed out here or there.
56_marg702: And he sought how he might conveniently betray him, etc. Jerome. He promises to betray, as his master said before: “To thee will I give all this power.”
56_marg703: Many today abhor the crime of Judas, yet do not guard against it. For when for bribes they give false testimony against anyone, because for money they deny the truth, they sell God for money, who says: “I am the truth and the life.” When by some discord they stain the partnership of brotherhood, they betray God, because “God is charity.” And what is worse, not from infirmity, not from ignorance, but like Judas they seek opportunity, so that, the witnesses removed, they may change truth by lying and virtue by crime.
56_marg704: Bede. The fourteenth moon, when the leaven having been put away the lamb was killed at evening. Expounding this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our pasch is sacrificed.” For although he was crucified on the following day, the fifteenth moon, yet on this night, on which the lamb was sacrificed, he gave his disciples his body and blood, and, held and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of that same immolation, that is, of his passion.
56_marg705: Unleavened bread is eaten with bitterness, which is our redemption. For bitterness is the passion of the Lord.
56_interl1068: Jerome. That we may direct our steps by the will of God.
56_marg706: Bede. It is a proof of divine foreknowledge that he, speaking with his disciples, also knows what is done elsewhere. Beautifully, a man carrying a jar or amphora of water, according to another evangelist, meets those preparing the Pasch, to show that the mystery of this Pasch is to be celebrated for the washing away of the world. For water signifies the laver of grace, and the jar signifies the frailty of those through whom this grace was to be ministered to the world. Whence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” The disciples prepare the Pasch where the jar of water is carried in, to indicate that the time is at hand in which, for the worshippers of the old Pasch, the typical blood is taken away from the threshold and doorposts, and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated to take away the sins of the world.
56_marg707: The city is the Church, which is girded with the wall of faith; the man who meets them is the primitive people; the jar of water is the law of the letter.
56_marg708: A vessel of clay and for water.
56_marg709: Bede. Advisedly the words “bearer of the water” and “the house of the Lord” are left unnamed, so that opportunity is signified to be given to all who wish to celebrate the true Pasch, that is, to be steeped in the sacraments of Christ, and seek to receive him in the hospitality of their mind.
56_marg710: Follow him, etc. Jerome. He leads them up on high, where Christ’s refreshment is. Whence Rahab bids the spies not to go by the low places, but by the high ones.
56_marg712: Jerome. The great Church, which proclaims the name of the Lord, spread with a variety of virtues and tongues, whence: “clothed about with variety,” is where the Pasch is prepared for the Lord. The lord of the house is Peter the apostle, to whom the Lord entrusted his house, so that there might be one faith under one shepherd.
56_marg713: The upper room is the spiritual law, which, coming out from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Saviour in a lofty place. For whoever has still kept the letter that kills, who has understood in the lamb nothing but a sheep, makes the Pasch in the depths, because he does not grasp the majesty of the Spirit in the words of God. But whoever has followed the water-bearer, that is, the herald of grace, into the house of the Church, transcending through the spirit of knowledge that illumines the surface of the letter, prepares a refreshment for Christ on the high throne of the mind, because he knows that all the sacraments of the Pasch and the other decrees of the law are his sacraments.
56_marg714: Jerome. The evening of the day indicates the evening of the world. For about the eleventh hour come the last, who receive the penny of eternal life first; because before the cross Abraham was in hell, and after the cross the thief was in paradise.
56_interl1076: Jerome. Many do good, as Judas does, but nothing profits them.
56_marg715: As he had foretold of the passion, so he foretells of the betrayer, giving room for repentance, so that, having understood that his thoughts were known to God, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not name him, lest, openly rebuked, he become more shameless. He casts the accusation into the general number, so that the guilty one may do penance.
56_marg716: One of you, etc. When falsehood is charged, the truth is proved and fulfilled: “who ate my bread, hath greatly supplanted me.” All are touched, so that there may be harmony in the lyre. All the well-strung strings respond with a consonant voice: “Is it I, Lord?” One lax and affected by love of money said: “Is it I, Rabbi?”
56_marg717: The eleven know that they had thought nothing evil against the Lord, but they trust the master more than themselves; fearing their own frailty, they sadly ask about their sin, of which they had no awareness.
56_marg718: Jerome. The wolf separates off the sheep that it seizes. A sheep that goes out of the fold lies open to the wolf’s bites.
56_marg719: Who dippeth with me his hand in the dish, etc. Bede. Wonderful is the patience of the Lord. Earlier he said: “One of you shall betray me.” The traitor persists in evil. He argues more openly, and yet is not properly named. Judas, while the others are grieved and draw back their hands from the food, with the rashness and shamelessness with which he betrays the Lord, even puts his hand into the dish with the master, so that by his audacity he may counterfeit a good conscience.
56_interl1077: Jerome. Many do good, as Judas does, but it does not profit them.
56_marg720: But woe to that man, etc. Bede. Woe for ever to that man who comes unworthily to the table of the Lord. For after the example of Judas he betrays the Son of man, not indeed to sinful Jews, but yet to sinful members, namely his own, he who rashly presumes to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body. He sells the Lord who, neglecting fear and love of him, does not fear to love and cherish earthly and fleeting things in his place, or rather even criminal ones.
56_marg721: But woe to that man, etc. Neither at first nor at second correction does he repent, but the patience of the Lord feeds his impudence and stores up wrath for himself. The punishment is foretold, so that he who is not conquered by shame may be corrected by fear.
56_interl1079: Lying hidden in the mother’s womb: it is better not to be than to exist for torments.
56_marg722: Bede. Once the old Pasch, which was celebrated in commemoration of the liberation of God’s people from Egypt, was finished, he passes to the new, which he wished the Church to frequent in memory of his own redemption; that is, in place of the flesh of the lamb and its blood he substituted the sacrament of his body and blood, and showed himself to be the one of whom “The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever,” etc. He himself breaks the bread which he hands to the disciples, because the breaking of his body comes of its own accord and by his own arrangement. Whence: “I have power to lay down my soul,” etc. Before he broke it, he blessed it, because the human nature which he assumed to suffer he filled, together with the Father and the Holy Ghost, with the grace of divine power. He blessed the bread and broke it, because he so subjected the man he had assumed to death that he showed the power of divine immortality truly to be in him, and therefore he was to be raised from death more swiftly.
56_marg723: Jerome. Figuring his body in the bread, which is the present Church, which is received in faith, blessed in number, broken in sufferings, given in examples, taken in teachings. Forming his blood in the chalice, mixed of wine and water, so that by the one we are cleansed from faults, and by the other redeemed from punishments. For by the blood of the lamb the houses are kept from the striking of the angel, and by the water of the Red Sea the enemies are extinguished; which are the mysteries of Christ’s Church.
56_marg724: Mystically. The bread, which strengthens the heart of man, is referred to the body; the wine, which produces blood, to the blood. But because we ought to abide in Christ and Christ in us, the wine is mixed with water, because, as John witnesses, “The waters ... are peoples”; and it is lawful for no one to offer water alone, or wine alone, just as neither grain alone without the kneading of water into bread, lest the head seem to be separated from the members, or Christ to have been able to suffer without love of our redemption, or we to be saved without his passion.
56_interl1081: Jerome. We are saved by God by grace, not by merits.
56_marg725: He gave thanks and blessed, already near to the passion, he who takes on the punishment of another’s wickedness, he who had done nothing worthy of the passion, so as to show with how calm a mind each one ought to bear the scourges of his own fault.
56_marg726: Jerome. A happy drunkenness, a healthful satiety, which the more abundantly it is taken, the more it deigns to give sobriety to minds. And Judas drank, but is not satisfied, nor does the fire of eternal punishment quench his thirst; because whoever receives the mysteries of Christ unworthily is shown here, as a spot on the moon, which is never wiped away. Rightly the Church is compared to the moon, which has no brightness of its own but receives light from the sun in fixed measures, that is, from Christ, who abides for ever. For there are some in the Church whom no sacrifice cleanses, but foolish thought leads them into faults; they have mingled themselves in the mire of cruelty. For the blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many, does not cleanse all.
56_interl1082: Not of the Old, of which this is the blood of the testament, which God hath enjoined unto you.
56_marg727: Shed for many, but does not cleanse all.
56_marg728: Jerome. Here he changes the sacrifice, but does not change the time, so that we never hold the supper of Jesus before the fourteenth moon. He who makes the resurrection on the fourteenth makes the Lord’s supper on the eleventh; which has never been found either in the New or in the Old Testament.
56_marg729: The vine, etc. Bede. The vine, or vineyard, is the synagogue of the Lord. Whence Isaias: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” Of this the Lord drank for a long time, although many branches were turned into bitterness; yet he delighted in the pious thoughts and highest virtues of some. But after the Lord’s passion the figures were translated into a spiritual sense. Therefore, about to go to the passion, he said: “I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine, until that day when I shall drink it new in the kingdom of God.” That is, I will no longer delight in the carnal ceremonies of the synagogue, in which was also the sacrament of the paschal lamb, which is pre-eminent. There will come a time when, placed in the kingdom of God, raised up in immortal glory, I shall be filled with new joy with you over the salvation of the same people, regenerated by baptism.
56_marg730: They shall praise the Lord that seek him, and have adored him; and all the fat ones of the earth have eaten.
56_marg731: Bede. It can be understood that the hymn he sang, giving thanks to the Father, according to John, was one in which, with his eyes lifted up, he prayed both for himself and for his disciples and for those who were to believe through their word. And beautifully he leads out the disciples, imbued with the sacrament of his body and blood and commended to the Father by the hymn said, to the Mount of Olives, to teach us that we ought to climb, through receiving the sacraments and by the help of his intercession, to the higher gifts of virtues and the charisms of the Holy Ghost, by which we are anointed in the heart.
56_marg732: Jerome. On the Mount of Olives Jesus is held, and thence he ascended to heaven, so that we may know that thence we ascend to heaven, whence we watch, and pray, and are bound, and do not resist on earth.
56_marg733: Bede. He foretells what they are to suffer, so that when they have suffered they may not despair but repent: “In this night they that are drunk are drunk in the night”; and they that are scandalized are scandalized in the night, that is, darkened in mind.
56_marg734: All fall, but not all lie down: “Shall he that sleepeth rise again no more?” To fall is fleshly; to lie down is devilish.
56_marg735: Jerome. Strike the shepherd. The prophet asks for the passion of the Lord; the Father answers: “I will strike the shepherd.” By the prayers of the saints the Son is sent by the Father, that is, is made flesh, and is struck, and suffers; the sheep are scattered when the shepherd is taken. The resurrection is promised, so that hope may not be extinguished.
56_interl1084: Jerome. The resurrection is promised, lest they despair.
56_interl1085: Bede. It is not rashness nor lying, but faith and ardent affection.
56_marg736: Jerome. A bird without feathers strives to fly aloft, but the body weighs down the soul, so that by the fear of human death the fear of the Lord may be overcome.
56_interl1086: Peter promised from the ardour of faith, but Christ, as God, had foreknown the future.
56_marg737: Bede. Others simply: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.” Mark: “Before the cock twice give voice, thou shalt deny me thrice.” This is not contrary. For the whole of Peter’s denial is a threefold denial, and he remained in that purpose of mind until he wept bitterly. If the whole had begun after the first cock-crow, the three evangelists who said that the Lord had said, “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice,” would seem to have spoken falsely. Likewise, if he had finished the whole before the cock began to crow, Mark would have said superfluously, in the Lord’s person: “Before the cock twice give voice, thou shalt deny me thrice.” But because it was begun before the first cock-crow, the three attended not to when he would complete it but to when it was to be, when it was to begin, since the threefold denial began before the cock-crow. It can also be understood that before the first cock-crow the whole was in his mind; for although in words it was begun before the first cock-crow and completed before the second, yet in the affection and fear of Peter’s mind the whole was begun before the first cock-crow, just as also that: “Whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her, hath already committed adultery with her in his heart,” etc.
56_marg738: The cock crows, Peter denies thrice. The cock, herald of light, is the Holy Ghost, by whose voice, in the prophets and apostles, we are told of the threefold denial by which we denied knowing the Lord; terrified by the voice of the maidservant, we are exhorted to the bitterest weeping after the fall, we who thought ill of God, spoke ill to our neighbour, and did ill to ourselves.
56_interl1087: Jerome. Note that Peter denies, and denies a third time; but after the cock had crowed, and as the darkness departed, the near light was announced, he, turning, wept bitterly and with tears washed away the filth of his threefold denial.
56_marg739: Farm: an estate or a field.
56_marg740: Gethsemani, that is, the valley of the fat ones, where “fat bulls have besieged him, and many calves have surrounded him.”
56_marg741: Gethsemani is interpreted as the fattest valley.
56_marg742: Isidore. They are separated in prayer who are separated in suffering, because he prays, they sleep, oppressed by the fatness of heart.
56_marg743: Bede. When the Lord prays on the mountain, he admonishes us also to seek the lofty things, that is, the heavenly, by praying. But when he is in the valley, and this the valley of the fat ones or of fatness, he warns us to have humility in our prayers and the fatness of inward love. And beautifully, drawing near to death, he prays in the valley of the fat ones, because through the valley of humility and the fatness of charity he underwent death for us. Whence: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death”; and: “Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
56_marg744: And he began to fear, etc. Jerome: We are taught to be dismayed and sorrowful before the judgment of death, we who cannot say, except through him: “For the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
56_marg745: Bede. He is not sorrowful on account of death, because it is not the fear of death that disturbs him, but the condition of bodily feeling. For he who took up a body ought to undergo all that belongs to the body: that he should hunger and thirst, be troubled and be made sad. But the divinity does not know how to be changed by these affections.
56_marg746: My soul is sorrowful, etc. Christ fears; Peter does not fear; indeed he says: “I will lay down my life for thee.” Christ says: “My soul is troubled,” “even unto death.” Peter, as a man, is ignorant of the power of death. Christ, because, being God established in a body, sets forth the frailty of the flesh so that he may appear as true man, says: “My soul is sorrowful.” He took on the sadness and the will of man, as also the pain of man; he who had nothing for himself to grieve over, the delight of the eternal divinity being set aside, is affected by the weariness of human infirmity.
56_marg747: Stay you here, etc. Bede. He does not command them to refrain from sleep, for which there is no time with the danger at hand, but from the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of mind.
56_interl1088: He shows humility of mind by the posture of his body.
56_marg748: Bede. This voice is the sound of our infirmity. Many are saddened by approaching death, but have a right heart and avoid death as much as they can. But if they cannot, let them say what Christ himself said: “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me.” Behold, you have the human will expressed. See the right heart: “But not what I will, but what thou wilt.” Whence: “I came not to do my own will,” that is, which I assumed in time from the virgin, “but the will of him that sent me,” which I, being eternal, had with the Father. He prays that the chalice pass, because he is man; but, recalling that for which he was sent, he accomplishes the dispensation and says: “Not what I will, but what thou wilt”; as if to say: if death should die, I not dying according to the flesh, let the chalice pass; but since it cannot otherwise be done, not what I will but what thou wilt.
56_marg749: This is against the Eutychians, who say there is one operation only in Christ, and one will. But here he shows the human will, which through the weakness of the flesh refuses the passion, and the divine, which is ready to accomplish the dispensation.
56_interl1089: Jerome. In Hebrew and in Greek, because there is no distinction of the Jew and the Greek.
56_marg750: Jerome. Even to the end he does not cease to teach us to obey our fathers, and to set their will before ours.
56_interl1090: Jerome. As they sleep in mind, so they sleep in body.
56_marg751: And he said to Peter, etc. He who had said: “Yea, though I should die with thee, I will not deny thee”; and “Although all shall be scandalized, yet not I,” now, through the greatness of sorrow, cannot overcome sleep.
56_marg752: He did not say, “that you be not tempted,” but: “that you enter not into temptation”; that is, that temptation not overcome you, nor hold you within its snares.
56_marg753: He enters into temptation who neglects to pray. Thrice the disciples sleep, thrice the Lord, praying, rouses them. The threefold sleep signifies the three dead whom the Lord raised: the first in the house, the second at the tomb, the third out of the tomb. The threefold vigil of the Lord teaches us to hold three persons in prayer, and to ask pardon for past, present, and future.
56_marg754: He restrains the rash, who think they can attain whatever they believe; but as much as we trust in the ardour of mind, so much let us fear the frailty of the flesh; yet nevertheless, according to the Apostle, by the spirit let us mortify the deeds of the flesh.
56_interl1091: The eyes of the apostles grow heavy, the denial being near.
56_marg755: Note that after this saying he kept silence for a little while, and they rested. Whence it is said: “It is enough,” as if you had rested. Then he added: “Behold, the hour is come,” etc.
56_marg756: After he had prayed the third time, and had taught that the fear of the apostles was to be corrected by penitence, he goes securely to the passion, saying: “Rise up, let us go”; as if they should not find us fearful, but let us go of our own accord to meet them, so that they may see us about to suffer with joy and confidence.
56_interl1092: Jerome. He trusts in the power of the world who despairs of the help of God.
56_marg757: Jerome. He gives the sign of a kiss with the poison of the devil, as Cain offered a crafty and rejected sacrifice. Whence they put wine with vinegar on the cross.
56_marg758: Bede. Shameless and wicked boldness calls him master and forces a kiss upon him whom he betrays. Yet it has something of a disciple’s shame, because he does not hand him over openly to the persecutors, but by the sign of a kiss. The Lord receives the kiss, not so as to teach us to pretend, but lest he seem to flee the betrayal. He also fulfils that: “With them that hated peace” etc.
56_marg759: Joseph is here, bound and sold by his brothers, and: “The iron pierced his soul.”
56_marg760: Bede. Peter, according to John, with the same burning of mind as in the rest. For he knew how Phinees, punishing the sacrilegious, had received the reward of justice and of an everlasting priesthood. Luke says: “that the Lord, touching the ear, healed it.” For he never forgets pity; he does not suffer even his enemies to be wounded.
56_marg761: Mystically. Teaching that those who, in consenting to his death, have contracted a wound of the soul, can merit salvation if they repent worthily.
56_interl1093: Jerome. Peter’s preaching cut off from the Jews the hearing of the kingdom of God.
56_marg762: Bede. As if to say: it is foolish to seize with swords and clubs him who of his own accord gives himself up to you, and to search for him in the night as if he were hiding, through a betrayer, when he teaches daily in the temple. But therefore you gather against me in darkness, because your power is in darkness.
56_interl1094: Jerome. It is fulfilled: “Friend and neighbour thou hast put far from me: and my acquaintance, because of misery.”
56_marg763: Bede. It is fulfilled what he said, that all would be scandalized in him that night. For though, according to John, they fled with the crowd’s permission at the Lord’s request, yet they showed fear of mind, and were readier for flight than for confidence to suffer.
56_marg764: Then the disciples, etc. Bede. As Peter, who washed away his denial with tears and, by the threefold confession of the Lord’s love, utterly uprooted it, shows the recovery of those who fall in martyrdom; so the other disciples, who by fleeing anticipated the moment of seizure, teach caution in flight to those who feel themselves less fit for punishments, for whom it is safer to lie hidden than to set themselves against danger. So too the young man who, leaving the linen cloth, fled naked from the impious designates the work and the soul of those who, so as to be safer, cast away all worldly things, and have learned to serve the Lord naked rather than, by adhering to the world, to give the adversaries matter for tempting and calling away from God.
56_marg765: Who that evangelist was he does not say. But that he loved the Lord more than the rest the thing itself has shown: while the others fled, he, bound by the bond of charity, did not cease to follow the Lord until he himself was seized by the enemy. Yet he who could flee even when held had not yet perfect charity. We may nevertheless understand this to be John, loved by the master above the others, whom the judgment of his long later life shows to have been a youth at that time. It may have happened that, having slipped away for an hour, he soon returned after putting on a garment, and in the uncertain light of night mingled himself with the crowds leading Jesus, as one of them, so as to come to the high priest’s court, where he was known, as he himself says.
56_interl1095: he had no garments but only the linen cloth
56_marg766: Clothed with a linen cloth over the naked: “body” is understood, that is, over the naked body, since he had no other garment than only the linen cloth.
56_marg767: As Joseph, leaving his cloak behind, fled naked from the hands of the shameless mistress. But whoever wishes to flee the hands of the wicked, leaving behind in mind the things of the world, let him flee after Jesus.
56_marg768: He detested both their presence and their deeds; not from the Lord, whose love he kept fixed in his mind even when absent in body.
56_marg769: Caiphas, namely the one who, according to John, “was the high priest of that year”; of whom Josephus fittingly writes that he bought the high priesthood for himself from the Roman prince, without any worthiness of dignity. What wonder then if an unjust high priest judges unjustly?
56_interl1097: Jerome. It is made “the congregation of bulls with the kine of the people.”
56_interl1098: Jerome. “A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways”; fear draws back, love draws forward.
56_marg770: Afar off, etc. Bede. Because he was near to denial; had he been near to Christ, he would not have denied. Yet in this he is to be admired, that he did not leave the Lord even though he feared. That he feared is of nature; that he follows is of devotion; that he denies is of stealthy lapse; that he repents is of faith.
56_marg771: Allegorically. That Peter follows from afar the Lord going to the passion signifies that the Church indeed will follow the Lord’s passion, but very differently. For the Church suffers for itself; he suffers for the Church.
56_marg772: The court of the high priest, etc. Jerome. The court is “the worldly circuit”; the servants are “demons”; the fire is “carnal desire”; he who remains with them cannot weep over his sins.
56_marg773: And he warmed himself at the fire, etc. Bede. There is a fire of charity, of which it is said: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?” There is also a fire of cupidity, of which it is said: “They are all adulterers, their hearts like an oven.” The former, descending upon the believers, taught them to praise the Lord in various tongues. The latter, kindled in Caiphas’ court by the prompting of the evil spirit, was arming the tongues of the faithless to deny and blaspheme the Lord. For what the evil council was doing inside the house, this fire kindled in the court amid the cold of the night was prefiguring. Let him who extinguished the flame of this fire in the praetorium say: “For I am become like a bottle in the frost,” etc. But those in whom the rivers of vices have overwhelmed the flame of charity, let them hear from the Lord: “Because iniquity hath abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold.” Peter, numbed by this cold for a while, wished to be warmed by the coals of Caiphas’ servants, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage through the company of the faithless. But, looked upon by the Lord, he left the fire of the faithless with his body, and their unbelief with his mind. And after the Lord’s resurrection, refreshed by the holy fire, he thoroughly purged the excess of the threefold denial by a threefold confession of love. For then, when that memorable catch of fish was completed, when he came to the Lord, he saw with his disciples coals laid down, and a fish laid over them, and bread; and at once he kindled the secrets of his heart with the coals of love.
56_interl1099: “Iniquity hath lied to itself,” as the queen against Joseph, the priests against Susanna; but fire without fuel dies out.
56_marg774: Bede. He is false who does not understand words in the sense in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken of the temple of his body, but they slander him in the very words, with a few things added or changed.
56_marg775: It is the custom of heretics to draw a shadow from the truth. He did not say what they say, but a similar word: of the temple of his body, which he raised up after three days. The Lord said: “Destroy you”—but not I, since no one ought to bring death upon himself. They add this so that he may seem to have spoken properly of the Jewish temple.
56_marg776: The Lord said: “Destroy you, but not I, because no one ought to bring death upon himself.”
56_interl1101: They add this so that he may seem to have spoken properly of the Jewish temple.
56_interl1102: The Lord said: “I will raise up a living animal, a temple signifying and breathing.”
56_marg777: And rising, etc. Angry, because he found no place for accusation, he shows by the movement of his body the madness of his mind.
56_marg778: He provokes him to answer, so that from any occasion of speech he may find a place for accusing. But Jesus did not answer, because he foresaw that whatever he answered would be turned into calumny.
56_interl1103: “As a sheep is led to the slaughter”; and: “He was struck dumb and kept silence from good things.”
56_marg779: Art thou the Christ the Son, etc. Jerome. He whom he awaited from afar he did not see when near, as Isaac with dimmed eyes did not recognize Jacob under his hands; but afterwards, from afar, he sings of him the things that were to come.
56_interl1105: Jerome. That they may be inexcusable.
56_interl1106: Bede. Mark: “I am”; Matthew: “Thou hast said it.” Which is the same.
56_marg780: And you shall see, etc. The priest asks about the Son of God. Jesus answered “the Son of man,” that we may understand the same to be Son of God and Son of man, lest we make a quaternity in the Trinity, and that man may be in God and God in man.
56_interl1107: Jerome. Reigning in eternal life and by divine power.
56_marg781: Sitting at the right hand of the power of God. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. For which cause God also hath exalted him, and hath given him a name which is above all names.”
56_marg782: With the clouds of heaven. Jerome. He ascended in a cloud; he will come with a cloud, that is, he ascended with his body alone, which he took from the virgin, and he will come to judgment with the many-formed Church, which is his body and fulness. As Matthew says: “And when the Son of man shall come in his majesty, and all the angels with him,” etc.
56_marg783: Bede. The same madness that had driven him from his seat provokes him to tear his garments, to show that the Jews had lost priestly glory and that the seat is empty.
56_marg784: It was the custom of the Jews, when they hear something of blasphemy, as if against God, to tear their garments. Paul and Barnabas also did this when, in Lycaonia, they were honored as if they were gods.
56_marg785: His garments, etc. Jerome. This is the ephod, in which the Jews had honor; they lost it. Here is Samuel, with the mantle torn from Saul’s hand, that is, the kingdom. The Gentile soldiers did not tear the tunic of Christ, but the priest tore the dignity of his priesthood.
56_marg786: It was done by a great mystery that at the Lord’s passion the high priest tore his garments, when the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. For it was foreshown that the priesthood of the Jews was to be torn for the sins of its priests. But the solidity of the Church, which is the vesture of its Redeemer, can never be torn asunder. For although Jews, Gentiles, heretics, and bad Catholics despise the Lord’s humility, his inviolate purity nevertheless remains until the end of the age in those whom the lot of election finds.
56_marg787: Who all condemned him, etc. Jerome. By that condemnation of his he might loose our guilt, and take away the veil of our hearts by the veil of his face, and by receiving spittle wash the face of our soul, and by the blows with which he was struck on the head heal the head of the human race, which is Adam; and by the slaps with which he was buffeted, the greatest praise of him might applaud from our hands and lips, whence: “O clap your hands, all ye nations.” And by his cross he might loose our torment, and by his death kill our death, because, the staff having become a serpent, the other serpents were swallowed up; whence: “O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite.” His reproaches have blocked our reproach; his chains have made us free. By the crown of thorns on his head, we have gained the diadem of the kingdom. By his wounds we are healed; by his burial we rise again; by his descent to hell we ascend to heaven. Here is found honey in the mouth of the dead lion. Hence the prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord, for all the things that he hath rendered to me?”
56_interl1109: “I have not turned away my face from them that spit upon me.”
56_interl1111: that he might take away the veils of hearts.
56_marg788: To cover his face, etc. Not so that he should not see their crimes, but so that they, as once they did to Moses, might hide from themselves the grace of knowing him. This veil, which is taken away for those who believe in Christ, remains to this day over their heart. Whence at his death the veil of the temple was torn, and the secrets of the holy of holies laid open.
56_interl1112: that he might heal our head, which is Adam.
56_marg789: According to others: “Who struck thee?” They do this in insult to him who wished to be held a prophet. But he arranged this so that he who endured it for us might prepare us to bear mockery for his name.
56_interl1114: that we may applaud him with our hands.
56_interl1115: “I gave my cheek to the blows.”
56_marg790: Bede. He who was then struck with blows is now struck with the blasphemies of false Christians. He who was spat upon with the spittle of unbelievers is now dishonored with the mad reproaches of the faithful.
56_marg791: Now when Peter was, etc. The maidservant first betrays Peter, when men might rather recognize him, so that this sex also seems to have sinned in the death of the Lord and was redeemed by the Lord’s passion. And therefore woman first received the mystery of the resurrection and keeps the commandments, so that she might abolish the old error of transgression.
56_marg792: Note that he denies Christ who denies that he is his disciple. For the Lord did not say, “You will deny my disciple,” but “You will deny me.” Therefore he denied him when he denied that he was his disciple.
56_marg793: And he went forth before the court, etc. Jerome. Peter, without the Spirit, yielded to a servant’s voice; with the Spirit, he yields neither to kings nor to the princes of the earth. The first maidservant was wavering, the second assent, the third the man’s act. This threefold denial the remembrance of Christ’s word washed away with tears. But the cock crows for us when the preacher calls our hearts back to compunction. Then we begin to weep when we are set on fire within by a spark of knowledge, and go forth outside what we were.
56_interl1117: the preacher who says: “Awake, ye just, and sin not.”
56_marg794: Of this crowing of the cock others are silent, yet do not deny it, as with many other things that some say and others pass over.
56_interl1119: not the same as before. Whence Matthew: “another maid seeing him.”
56_marg795: For thou art also a Galilean, etc. Bede. The language is the same for the Galileans and the people of Jerusalem, but still every province and region has its own sound of speech which it cannot change. Whence, when the apostles spoke in all tongues, it is reported that among others who dwelt in Judea [they said]: “Behold, are not all these, that speak, Galileans? And how have we heard, every man our own tongue wherein we were born?” And Peter, speaking to the brethren in Jerusalem, said: “And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their tongue, Haceldama.” This is said because that name sounded one way to the Jerusalemites and another way to the Galileans.
56_marg796: And Peter remembered, etc. Bede. Peter denies by night; at the crowing of the cock he repents. In the day he professed three times, bitterly, that he loved him whom he had denied three times. For what he had erred in the darkness of forgetfulness, he corrected by the remembrance of the light now hoped for; and, with his presence now attained, he fully raised up all that had wavered.
56_marg797: Bede. How harmful are the evil conversations among the faithful: he denied that he knew a man whom among his fellow disciples he had already confessed as Son of God. But in the court of Caiphas he cannot do penance; he goes out, as the other evangelists relate, so that, withdrawn from the impious, he may more freely wash away the guilt of his denial with weeping.
56_interl1122: See how diligent they are in evil: they kept watch the whole night that they might commit murder.
56_marg798: Binding Jesus, etc. It was the custom of the Jews that whom they had adjudged to death they handed over to the judge bound. And it is to be noted that they had not bound him for the first time then, but had bound him at once when he was seized by night in the garden, as John says: “And they led him away to Annas first.”
56_marg799: Here is Samson, bound by Delilah. Samson is interpreted “sun” of those to whom the sun has set at midday. Delilah is interpreted “bucket,” that is, the synagogue, which, like a bucket, does not hold clear liquid, and gathers filthy refuse. Our Samson here, with the jawbone of his word, lays low countless troops of Jews and demons, and opens to us thirsting the fountain of perennial life, that is, his body.
56_interl1123: he was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, that each might mock him.
56_marg800: When Pilate asks of him no charge except whether he is king of the Jews, the impiety of those is exposed who find not even a false charge to bring.
56_marg801: So he tempers his answer that he says what is true, yet is not exposed to calumny. And note that he answered Pilate in some part, who reluctantly passes sentence; but to the priests and princes he would not answer, judging them unworthy of his speech.
56_marg802: See in how many things, etc. The Gentile condemns Jesus, but refers the cause back to the Jewish people: “See in how many things they accuse thee,” etc.
56_interl1124: lest by refuting the charge he be released by the governor, and the benefit of the cross be deferred.
56_marg803: Bede. Their request clings to the Jews to this day, which they obtained with all their effort. For when the option was given them, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a killer instead of the Savior. Rightly therefore they lost salvation and life, and so submitted themselves to robberies and seditions that they lost kingdom and country, and never recovered freedom of body and soul.
56_marg804: Pilate gave many occasions for freeing the Savior: first by setting the just man against the robber, then by adding: “What then will you have me do to the king of the Jews?” And when they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not at once consent, but, following the prompting of his wife, who had sent him word, as Matthew says, “Have thou nothing to do with that just man,” he answered: “For what evil has he done?” By saying this he absolved Jesus.
56_interl1127: by saying this he absolved Jesus.
56_interl1128: satisfying their madness, not answering the governor’s question.
56_marg805: David: “For many dogs have encompassed me: the council of the malignant hath besieged me.” Isaias: “I expected that he would do judgment, but they have done iniquity and injustice and a cry.” Jeremias: “My inheritance is become to me as a lion lying in wait; they have given their voice against me.”
56_marg806: Jerome. These are the two goats: one, apopompaeus, that is the scapegoat, absolved, is sent away into the wilderness of hell with the sin of the people; the other is slain like a lamb for the sins of the absolved. The part of the Lord is always slain; the part of the devil, who is their master, is hurled unbridled into Tartarus.
56_marg807: That he might free us from scourges. Whence: “Nor shall the scourge come near thy dwelling.” Whereas before it was said: “Many are the scourges of the sinner.”
56_marg808: Jesus, scourged. He was scourged by Pilate himself. Whence John: “Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.” And afterwards he adds: “And the soldiers platting a crown of thorns,” etc., and he gave him over to be mocked by the soldiers. He did this so that they, sated with his pains and reproaches, might not thirst beyond death.
56_interl1131: that he might free us from torments.
56_marg809: Bede. Matthew says: “And stripping him, they put a scarlet cloak about him,” which is the same. For instead of royal purple a cloak was given him by the mockers; and there is a certain red purple very like scarlet. It may also be seen that Mark mentioned the purple which the cloak had, although it was scarlet.
56_marg810: He is stripped of his own garments, that is, the Jews. He is clothed in purple, that is, the Gentile Church gathered from bitter peoples. Likewise, when she offends him, he is stripped; at the end he is clothed again with the Jewish people: “For when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, then all Israel shall be saved.”
56_marg811: Because he was called king, and the priests and scribes imposed this, that he was usurping rule over the people, they clothe him in mockery with the purple which kings use. For a diadem, a crown of thorns; for a royal sceptre they give a reed, as Matthew says: and they bow before him as before a king, etc.
56_marg812: As Caiphas, not knowing, said: “That it was expedient that one man should die for the people”, so the soldiers, not knowing, do all things mystically. Purple is his flesh made red by sufferings, whence: “Why then is thy apparel red, and thy garments like theirs that tread in the winepress?” He bears the crown of thorns, because being made mortal for us he took up our sins, whence: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.” That thorns signify sins the Lord shows thus: “Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee”, that is, your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and stings of vices. But that according to Luke he is clothed in a white garment by Herod, and according to others with a scarlet or purple garment by Pilate’s soldiers: in the one is signified innocence and the chastity of his humanity; in the other is expressed the truth of the passion, through which he came to the glory of an immortal kingdom. For purple signifies both passion and kingdom. But because, as the Apostle says: “For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ”, and Isaias: “Thou shalt be clothed with these as with an ornament”, in either garment can be designated the multitude of the elect, which, shameful indeed by the judgment of enemies but most glorious by the Lord’s choice, is distinguished into martyrs and the other faithful. He is clothed in white when he is surrounded with the pure confession of the just. He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he glories in the triumph of the glorious martyrs.
56_interl1133: that we may be made kings
56_marg813: ‘The head of Christ is God.’ They therefore strike the head of Christ who deny that he is God. And those who defend their error by the authority of Scripture, since Scripture is usually made with a reed, strike his head as with a reed. They spit in his face who reject the presence of his grace with execrable words conceived from the inner madness of a blinded mind, and deny that he came in the flesh.
56_marg814: As if he had falsely said he was God. But today, which is of graver madness, some adore him with sure faith as the true God, yet by perverse deeds soon despise his words as if they were fables, and set the promises of that kingdom behind temporal enticements.
56_interl1136: as the brother of Cain led Abel out into the field
56_marg815: Jerome. Here Abel is led out into the field by his brother to be slain. Here is Isaac with the wood, and Abraham with the ram held fast by the thorns. Here is Joseph with the tunic dyed with blood. Here is Moses with the rod and the serpent hung on a tree. Here a cluster is carried on a tree. Here is Eliseus with the wood to seek the axe that had sunk to the bottom and floated up to the wood, that is, the human race, which fell into hell from the forbidden tree, and through the wood of Christ’s cross and through the baptism of water swam up to paradise. Here is Jonas, cast out of the wood of the ship into the sea and into the belly of the whale for three days.
56_marg816: Jerome. What is the very form of the cross but the shape of the squared world? The east shines from its strength, the north holds the right hand, the south stands on the left, the west is fixed beneath the feet. Whence the Apostle: “That we may know what is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth.” Birds fly to the heavens in the form of a cross, man worships and swims in the form of a cross, and the ship is driven across the seas with its yard likened to the cross. The letter Thau shows the sign of salvation and of the cross.
56_marg817: Bede. The Lord himself first carried his cross, as John says; afterwards this Simon, of whom the others also speak, in a fitting order of mystery: “Because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow his steps.” And because it was not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian from the city of Libya, through him the Gentiles are rightly signified, who once were strangers and guests of the testaments, but now by obeying are citizens and household of God, as elsewhere: “Heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ.” Hence Simon is interpreted ‘obedient’, Cyrenian ‘heir’. And note that he is said to come from a village. For a village in Greek is pagos, whence we call them ‘pagans’, whom we see as alien from the city of God and lacking in urbane conversation. But Simon, coming out of the village, carries the cross of Jesus, when the people of the nations, with pagan rites left behind, obediently embrace the footprints of the Lord’s passion.
56_marg818: Simon who carries the cross under compulsion, this is the one who labors for human praise. Men compel him to this labor, whom the fear or love of God does not compel.
56_marg819: This Simon seems to have been of great reputation, since his sons too are designated by name as known to all.
56_marg820: Some are recalled for the merits of their fathers, others for the merits of their sons. But this Simon who carries the cross under compulsion is recalled for the merits of his sons, who were disciples. Through this, fathers in the present life are admonished to be helped by the merits of their sons, as the Jewish people is often recalled through the merits of the patriarchs, prophets and apostles. For the sweetness of the olive arises from the bitterness of the root. Whence Jeremias: “The Lord called thy name, a plentiful olive tree, fair, fruitful, and beautiful.”
56_marg821: Jerome. The Jews relate that on this hill of the place the ram was sacrificed in place of Isaac, so that Christ might be made bald there, that is, be separated from his own flesh, namely the carnal Jewish people.
56_marg822: Outside the gate the heads of the condemned were cut off, and the places of the beheaded are called Calvary. Therefore the Lord was crucified there, where was the area of the condemned, so that there the standards of the martyrs might be raised. And since the curse of the cross was made for us, and he was scourged and crucified for the salvation of all, he willed to be crucified as a guilty man among the guilty.
56_interl1137: A bitter vine makes bitter wine and offers it to Jesus. Whence: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”
56_marg824: Bede. Matthew has “mingled with gall”, which is the same thing. For he put gall for bitterness. For myrrhed wine is most bitter, although it could happen that gall and myrrh together made the wine most bitter.
56_marg825: And they gave, etc. By this vinegar the deadly juice of the apple is wiped away. And he did not accept that for which he suffers. Whence of him: “Then did I pay that which I took not away.”
56_interl1138: “He would not drink,” according to Matthew.
56_marg826: Matthew: “And when he had tasted, he would not drink.” Matthew shows that he tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose on the third day.
56_interl1139: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” He was made accursed, that he might take away our curse.
56_marg827: And crucifying him, etc. Jerome: Here salvation is fixed to the wood. First death was fixed to a wood, the first tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The second is for us a tree of good only and of life. The stretching out of the first hand to the wood grasped death; the stretching out of the second found the life that had perished. By this wood we are carried across the wavy sea to the land of the living.
56_interl1140: into four groups. Into four parts, according to John.
56_interl1141: the commandments and the rest, except the tunic
56_marg828: His garments, etc. Bede: Christ’s garment, divided into four parts according to the number of soldiers, signifies the Church, distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, among the four parts of the world.
56_marg829: The garments of the Lord are the commandments by which his body is covered, which is the Church, because they are divided among the soldiers of the Gentiles into four orders, so that there are four orders though there is one faith: the married, the widowed, the prelates, and the separated. They cast lots for the tunic which is undivided, which is peace and truth in all, in the manner of a royal mantle or ring.
56_marg830: Jerome. Namely over the tunic, which was seamless. This lot of all parts signifies the unity which is held together by one bond of charity, because that which surpasses all knowledge and is above all precepts is as it were woven from above. In the lot the grace of God is commended, for thus it comes to all in one, since the lot pleases everyone, because the grace of God comes to all in unity; and the lot comes or falls by the judgment of God alone.
56_marg831: Jerome. This is proper to Mark. For at the sixth hour darkness covered the earth, so that no one could move his head. For Mark rises from the thirtyfold fruit to the hundredfold, that is, from the third hour of the cross to the third hour of the resurrection, which was after three days. The thirtyfold fruit is on the cross, the sixtyfold in hell, the hundredfold in paradise.
56_marg832: As if to say that the soldiers crucified him, which was done about the sixth hour according to John; but first the Jews crucified him at the third hour, who are rather to be said to have crucified him, although they strive to hide it, than the soldiers, who by their duty obeyed their leader.
56_marg833: Bede. The title shows that by killing him they could not bring it about that he was not their king, whence: “But I am appointed king by him over Sion his holy mountain, preaching his commandment,” etc. For he is at the same time king and priest, since on the altar of the cross he offered to the Father the choice sacrifice of his flesh, and by the title he set forth the dignity of a king, so as to make known to all that through the gibbet of the cross he did not lose but confirmed his empire.
56_marg834: What is prefixed in the titles of the psalms, “Unto the end, destroy not”, and with three tongues: malchus of the Jews, basileos exomolisson, king of confessors. These three tongues were joined together on the gibbet of the cross, so that every tongue might recall the perfidy of the Jews.
56_marg835: Bede. As the Apostle says: “Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin may be destroyed, that sin may no longer have dominion over us.” As long, then, as our works are doing this, that the body of sin may be made void, as long as the outward man is corrupted that the inward man may be renewed, it is the time of the cross. These are indeed also good works, yet still laborious, whose reward is his rest. But so it is said: “Rejoicing in hope,” that we may await the future rest with cheerfulness in our labors. The breadth of the cross in the transverse wood, where the hands are fixed, signifies this cheerfulness. For by the hands we understand works, and by the breadth the cheerfulness of the one working, because sadness makes narrowness. By the height, to which the head is joined, the expectation of reward from the sublime justice of God. By the length, by which the whole body is stretched out, endurance, whence they are called long-suffering. By the depth, which is fixed in the earth, the very secret of the sacrament. Whence the Apostle: “That being rooted and founded in charity, you may be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth.”
56_interl1144: Two thieves. Bede: The thieves who were crucified with the Lord signify those who undergo, by faith and confession of Christ, or by the struggle of their martyrdom, or by any strict continence. And those who do this for eternal glory are signified by the merit and faith of the right-hand thief. But those who do so for human glory, or with any less worthy intention, imitate the mind and deeds of the left-hand thief.
56_marg836: Truth, reckoned with the wicked, leaves one on the left and takes the other on the right; so will he do on the day of judgment: from a like crime they draw unlike ways. One goes before Peter into paradise, the other before Judas into hell. A brief confession gains a long life, and blasphemy, once ended, is punished with eternal punishment. Here Juda’s colt is tied to the vine: ‘anabologium’, that is, the garment is dyed in the blood of the grape; here the kids tear the vineyard.
56_marg837: Jerome. The death of the wicked is sent forth when the chains of hell are stirred up to the neck, which is the neck of the human race.
56_interl1150: the wicked mock at the salvation which he had begun
56_marg838: Even unwilling, they confess that he saved others, and they condemn themselves by their own sentence, because he saved others and could have saved himself if he wished.
56_marg839: It is more to rise from the tomb, and yet they did not believe. These: “They are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together.”
56_marg840: And they that were crucified with him reviled him, etc. Bede: According to Luke, one of the thieves blasphemed, saying: “If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.” The other rebuked him and says: “Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom.” So today those who carry the sacraments of the Lord’s passion with a feigned heart and a feigned mind desire to be freed by the Lord for the joys of the world, and therefore are despised by the Lord, nor judged worthy of any answer. But those who with the Apostle glory in the cross of Christ rather choose so to be stripped of present woes that they may commend their holy spirit into the hands of God, and desire to be partakers with Christ of the heavenly kingdom. Whence the Lord piously heard the prayer of him who sought salvation, because those who, placed in tribulations, seek from the Lord only temporal consolations are separated from temporal things and deprived of eternal ones. Those who seek heavenly things undoubtedly arrive at them, with Christ mediating and showing mercy.
56_marg841: Bede. It is to be noted that he was crucified at the sixth hour, that is, when the sun was about to recede from the centre of the world, and he rose when the sun rose at dawn, because “he was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification.” For concerning Adam sinning it is said that he heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise in the breeze after noon, the light of faith being now inclined; the breeze, the heat of charity having cooled. But he was heard walking, because he had withdrawn from the sinning man. The order of reason, or rather of divine piety, therefore required that at the same moment of time in which he had shut the gate of paradise on the transgressing Adam, he should open it for the penitent thief. And at the very hour when the first Adam by sinning brought death into the world, the same hour the second Adam by dying would destroy death.
56_marg842: Jerome. Here is Noe, drunk and naked, covered by a dark mantle of heaven and earth, and mocked by a man; here blood dripped from the wood.

56_marg845: Bede. John says more fully: “Afterwards Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst. Now there was a vessel set there full of vinegar,” etc. As if: you have done this lesser thing; give what you are. For they were vinegar, degenerate from the wine of the prophets and patriarchs, as if from a full vessel, full of the iniquity of this world, having a heart like a sponge, deceitful in hollow and winding hiding-places. Around hyssop they placed a sponge full of vinegar. Hyssop, a humble herb that cleanses the breast, signifies the humility of Christ, which they surrounded and thought they had surrounded. Whence: “Thou shalt sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” For we are cleansed by the humility of Christ, because, unless he had humbled “himself, becoming obedient unto death, even to the death of the cross,” his blood, poured out for our cleansing, would not have been. Through the reed on which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, which is fulfilled by this deed, because it is written with a reed; as speech, which is formed by the tongue, is called ‘tongue,’ whence we say the Greek and the Latin tongue.
56_marg846: And one running. He found a likeness of them: a sponge hollow, dry with age, apt for fires. 56_marg848: And Jesus, etc. For his flesh being weakened, the divine power at once grew strong, which says: ‘Open to me the gates of justice,’ etc. But we die with no voice or with one voice, we who are of the earth. For he who came down from heaven breathed out his last with a loud voice.

Before it was said: ‘God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel.’ Now however: “Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth.” And in the Gospel earlier: ‘Go not into the way of the Gentiles,’ and after the passion: ‘Go and teach all nations,’ etc.
56_marg850: It is shown why the centurion marvels: because he saw him thus breathe his last, that is, send forth his spirit. For no one has the power to send forth the spirit except the creator of souls.
56_interl1164: The last shall be first: the Gentile people confesses, the blinded Jewish people denies, so that its error becomes worse than the former.
56_interl1165: Bede. He confesses him man and God.
56_marg851: Indeed, etc. Jerome. Note that the centurion, before the cross, in the very scandal of the passion, truly confesses the Son of God, while Arius preaches a creature in the Church. Whence the centurion rightly signifies ‘the faith of the Church,’ which, with the veil of the heavenly mysteries opened by the death of the Lord, at once confirms Jesus both as a truly just man and as the truly Son of God, while the Synagogue keeps silent.
56_marg852: Jerome. As the female sex is not excluded from salvation through the Virgin Mary, so it is not barred from the mystery of the cross, of knowledge, and of the resurrection, through the widow Mary Magdalen and the other mothers.
56_interl1166: to distinguish him from James the son of Zebedee, who was called among the first apostles and chosen by the Lord: James the less
56_marg853: By the less James he means James the son of Alphaeus, who is also the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of Mary, the Lord’s aunt on his mother’s side. Of her John says: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen.” ‘Cleophas’ seems to name her from her father or from her kindred.
56_interl1167: Bede. It was the custom for women to minister to their teachers from their own means.
56_marg855: ‘Parasceve’ is Greek, ‘preparation’ is Latin. By this name the Jews, dwelling among the Greeks, called the sixth day of the sabbath, because on it they prepared what was necessary for the sabbath, according to what is said about the manna: ‘On the sixth day you shall gather a double portion,’ etc. Since, therefore, man was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from all his work, he wished this sabbath, that is, rest, to be so called; and rightly the Saviour, crucified on that same sixth day, restored man. And therefore, when he had taken the vinegar, he said: “It is consummated,” that is, the work of the sixth day was completed, which I undertook for the repair of the world. Resting on the sabbath in the tomb, he waited for the outcome of the resurrection, which was to come on the eighth day, where the example of our devotion and reward shines forth: those who must suffer for the Lord in this sixth age and necessarily be crucified to the world. In the seventh age, that is, when each one has paid the debt of death, the bodies indeed in tombs, but the souls in secret peace are to rejoice with the Lord, and after good works ought to rest; until, the eighth age coming, the bodies themselves, glorified in resurrection, together with the souls receive the incorruption of the eternal inheritance.
56_marg856: Jerome. Joseph came late on the Parasceve from Arimathea, which is interpreted ‘laying down,’ to lay down the body of Christ in the tomb. A noble decurion, waiting for the redemption of God. He went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Joseph wrapped it in a linen cloth; wrapping the body in the cloth, he put it into the tomb which had been hewn out of the rock, and rolled the stone to the door of the tomb. The Marys look on where it was to be laid. All these things fit the Jewish people, who at the end believe, who is ennobled by faith, so as to be a son of Abraham, lays down despair, awaits the kingdom of God, comes to the Christians that he may be baptized; which the name Pilate signifies, that is, ‘mouth of the hammerer,’ that is, one who tames the wild nations, so that he may rule them with an iron rod; and he asks for the sacrifice that is given to penitents at the end, that is, viaticum. And, with a pure heart and dead to sins, he wraps him in the defence of faith, closing him with the lid of faith by works of charity: “For the end of the commandment is charity.” The elect, who are the stars of the sea, look on from afar, when, if it were possible, even the elect would be scandalized.
56_interl1170: which is also Ramatha, the city of Elcana and Samuel
56_marg857: Administering the office of the council, of great dignity in the world, he is read to have been greater before God. For such a man ought to be the one who would bury the body of the Lord: one who would be worthy both through justice and by the nobility of worldly power would obtain the means. For an unknown or ordinary man could not approach the governor and obtain the body of the crucified.
56_marg858: He is called a decurion because he is of the order of the council and administers the office of the council; he is also usually called a councillor, from managing civic duties.
56_interl1175: a pure heart and dead to sins
56_marg859: And Joseph, etc. Bede. From the simple burial of the Lord, the ambition of the rich is condemned, who cannot even in tombs do without riches.
56_marg860: Allegorically, the body of Christ is to be wrapped not in gold, not in gems or silk, but in pure linen. Morally, however: he wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth who receives him with a pure mind. Hence the Church celebrates the sacrifice of the altar not with silk nor with dyed cloth, but with earthly linen, just as the body of the Lord was buried in a clean cloth; so it was ordained by Pope Sylvester.
56_marg861: Which was hewed out of a rock, etc. Bede. It is said that the Lord’s tomb was a round house, hewn from the rock beneath it, of such height that a man standing upright can scarcely reach the top with an outstretched hand. It has its entrance from the east, against which that great stone was rolled and set. In its northern part is the sepulchre itself, that is, the place of the Lord’s body, made from the same rock, seven feet long, standing a measure of three palms higher than the floor. This place is open not from above but along the whole of the south side, whence the body was carried in. The colour of the tomb and of the niche is said to be a mixture of white and red.
56_interl1181: the elect, who are the stars of the sea
56_marg862: Bede. Luke says: “For all his acquaintance stood afar off, and the women that had followed him.” But when the others, the body having been put down, returned to their own homes, only the women who loved him more closely followed the funeral, and took care to see how it was placed, so that at a fitting time they might offer him the gift of devotion.
56_marg863: Morally. The holy women do the same on the day of the Parasceve, that is, of preparation: humble souls who, the more they are aware of their own weakness, the more they burn with love of the Saviour, diligently attend upon the footsteps of his passion in this world, in which rest is to be prepared for the future. And if perhaps they are able to imitate with pious curiosity, they weigh in what order his passion is to be embraced.
56_interl1182: from afar, because even the elect will be scandalized, if it were possible

56_marg864: And when the sabbath was past, etc. Bede. Luke says that, returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments, and rested on the sabbath, because it was commanded that the silence of the sabbath be kept from evening until evening. Therefore the devout women, while the Lord was buried, while it was permitted to work, that is, until sunset, prepared ointments, as Luke says. And because they could not finish for lack of time, as soon as the sabbath was past, that is, at sunset, when the permission to work returned, they hurried to buy spices, as Mark says, so that coming in the morning they might anoint Jesus. Nor on the evening of the sabbath, the moment of night already coming on, were they able to approach the tomb.
56_interl1184: the elect, who are the stars of the sea
56_marg865: Morally. The holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices, and attend upon him whom they loved living, even when dead, with the zeal of humanity. And we, therefore, believing in him who is dead, if refreshed by the fragrance of virtues, seek the Lord with the reputation of good works, and come to his tomb with spices. But that they come very early to the tomb, when the sun had already risen, that is, when the sky was already growing white on the side of the east, which happens by the nearness of the rising sun, literally shows a great fervour of love in seeking and finding the Lord. Mystically, however, an example is given us: with face illumined, the darkness of vices shaken off, to offer to the Lord the fragrance of good works and the sweetness of prayers.
56_marg866: Now with fragrant spices we sprinkle the book, that is, the bed of our mind, with the bride and the young women who run after her. Now the King leads us into his cellars: “Now the beloved Mary rises; winter is gone, the rain is past, the flowers have appeared, the voice of the turtle is heard in our land, the flowering vines have given fragrance.” The Bridegroom has returned from the shade under which they sleep at midday. After the sad sabbaths the happy day dawns, which holds the first place among the days, the first light shining in it, and the Lord rising in it with triumph and saying: “This is the day which the Lord hath made,” etc.
56_marg867: Jerome. What another calls ‘at dawn.’ Dawn is between the darkness of night and the brightness of day, in which salvation came to be made known in the Church, after the manner of the sun, which, rising, sends forth the rosy dawn, so that such splendour might be seen by prepared eyes, when the time of the Lord’s resurrection dawned; so that then the whole Church would sing the praises of Christ through the holy women, when he gave life and poured in the light of belief.
56_interl1185: that is, the first from the sabbath. The same first of the sabbath is said; now it is called ‘the Lord’s Day.’

56_marg869: Bede. How the stone was rolled back by the angel, Matthew tells. For the law was written on stone; with its covering removed, the glory of the resurrection has been shown, and the abolition of ancient death and the everlasting life to be hoped for by us began to be preached throughout the whole world.

56_marg877: Salvation. But because many were named by this name not in substance but by name only, he specifies by place: Nazarene; and adds the cause: Crucified. And he adds: “He is risen, he is not here,” by bodily presence; he who is nevertheless nowhere absent by the presence of majesty.
